articles.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
articles.standfirst: A household using a typical amount of energy would see its annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if this level was sustained for a year.
paragraphs: Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

Regulator Ofgem said typical bills will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although individual households costs will depend on how much they use at the coldest time of year, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter.

For a household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit for gas and electricity, the increase would push annual bills from £1,723 to £2,166 if it was sustained for a year.
The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.
Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

Ofgem said the rise in the cap, which is set every three months, had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices, paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months which is the period used to set the January to March cap.
The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.
"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said: "Conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher, and we know this price increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches."

He said Ofgem had written to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable.
Suppliers said their own profits are also capped, and everyone was feeling the "impact of our exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets".
Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the UK needed to develop more domestic clean power and accelerate the electrification of our homes and transport.
The increase is the largest seen since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices significantly. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest and use is peaking.
Individual usage differs, so for every £100 spent on energy now, the new cost will be about £126.
People on prepayment meters will be hit as their spending comes when energy is needed, rather than the cost being spread over the year as with direct debits.
The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means:
For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p.
Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine.
Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.
The cap is set every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system.

It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but it will be in April's.

Campaign Groups Friends of the Earth and Global Witness said major oil and energy companies are making huge profits because of spiralling oil costs, hurting households. The industry said suppliers, which send your bill, have profits capped and do not see the same benefit as international energy generating companies.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills.
"For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said.

Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher.
"Labour are utterly out of touch and could fix this tomorrow if they had the backbone."
Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing
Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, said dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, £400 more than last year.
Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.
She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.
She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house.
The rise has been forecast for a while, allowing the government time to prepare some support measures.
They include the £100 pound payment going to millions of households in council bands A to D in England to help cover the winter costs, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.
Ministers have released more details, including:
Confirmation payments will begin on 4 January
Anyone paying council tax by direct debit will receive the money directly into bank accounts automatically
Others will be contacted by their council and offered payment via bank transfer or as credit on council tax.
But Citizens Advice said the money will disappear quickly, particularly for those on prepayment meters, leading to a wave of requests for emergency help.
Energy UK said the funding was poorly targeted and insufficient to stem rising levels of customer debt.
The government said councils had a £100m discretionary fund to support vulnerable households which fell outside of the main scheme.
How is the cost of energy affecting your quality of life? What questions do you have?

articles.title: US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
articles.standfirst: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
paragraphs: Tariffs are a signature policy of Trump's office
The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.
The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.
The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.
While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.
Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.
The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.
Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year
In the run up to the Shenzhen summit, the US accused China of not fully living up to the terms of what it agreed in October 2025.
Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.
The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

articles.title: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
articles.standfirst: Regulator Ofgem is raising the cap affecting the energy bills of millions of households.
paragraphs: Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.
The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.
It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.
The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.
It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months.
It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.
Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.
The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill.
Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.
Customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it.
From January, for those on variable tariffs:
For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p
Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine
Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas
The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs will not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.
Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.

As well as how much energy you use and how you pay for it, where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.
The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.
The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.
In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.
Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.
Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.
This is especially important when prices go up.
Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.
Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region and payment method.
Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers are 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.
From January, daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.
The electricity standing charge is lower than the amount charged over the previous three months, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.

Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.
The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen
Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.
You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.
Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.

Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills.
Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households.
However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.

In December 2025, Ofgem approved a £28bn investment to improve the electricity and gas grids in Great Britain to strengthen energy supplies and protect customers against volatile energy prices. It will also reduce Britain's dependence on gas.
Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional £108 added to energy bills by 2031.
These charges started to appear from April 2026, adding about £6 a month to the bill for a typical household covered by the energy cap.
Suppliers must offer customers affordable payment plans or repayment holidays if they are struggling to pay their bills. Most also offer hardship grants.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, and since then unpaid bills and charges have shot up.
Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, has advice for people who may be struggling:
Take stock of all household money coming in and going out.
Look closely at how much energy you are using, and be alert to estimated bills, which might prove to be inaccurate.
Tell your supplier if you think you are going to struggle.
It is often best to try to talk to someone who can fully understand your situation.
Energy UK has a list of support schemes.

Heating oil is not covered by the energy cap. About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil and they have already seen a sharp increase in bills since the Middle East conflict triggered a jump in oil prices. Some users have seen costs more than double.
The issue is particularly acute in Northern Ireland, where about 500,000 homes use heating all, almost two-thirds of all households.
In March, the government announced a £53m support package to help low-income households in rural communities who use heating oil.
How are rising costs caused by the Iran war affecting your quality of life or business?

articles.title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
articles.standfirst: The BBC speaks to three people about steps they take to keep their energy bills under control.
paragraphs: Domestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.
With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?
The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.
Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heating
Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.
The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.
She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.
The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.
To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill.
The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.
They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.
"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.
Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing
Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.
Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.
She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.
She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.
"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."
Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.

"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.
"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."

To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.
Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.
Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.
Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.
Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell & Bernadette McCague.
What are you doing to cope with rising energy bills?

articles.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.standfirst: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
paragraphs: This video can not be played
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.
"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he made "terrible mistakes" and is now in therapy for 90 minutes per day.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
articles.standfirst: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
paragraphs: Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement.
"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

articles.title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain
articles.standfirst: Household energy bills are about to increase but there are ways to keep a lid on your expenditure.
paragraphs: Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating bills
Energy bills will soar by 26% in the new year as the war in Iran pushes up wholesale prices.
Typical household bills will rise by £37 per month as Ofgem's latest price cap comes into force from January to March, but experts say it is possible to keep rising bills in check.
Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase.
Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.
So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.
With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.
Research foundation Nesta suggests:
turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently
turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use
turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum
closing all curtains at night
lowering radiator valves outside of the living room
turning off the heating before April
These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.
Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.
Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.
Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.

Customers on prepayment schemes  - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.
Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.

Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.
The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.

Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.
Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.

The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.
There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes.
This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.
Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.
Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.
Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme can help you repay energy debt.
You can get more advice from Ofgem, Citizens Advice, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes.
People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.
But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.
How is the cost of energy affecting your quality of life? What questions do you have?

articles.title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
articles.standfirst: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.
paragraphs: As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
Rising food prices hurt the poor the most
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onionomics: Peeling away the layers of India's food economy
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.

The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, India remains vulnerable to erratic monsoons
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.

Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.

"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.
India has ample buffer food stocks

At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.

Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.

India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

Revisiting New Zealand's Public Service Act
No

The Institute for Government has long argued that the UK government should strengthen civil service legislation because the current settlement leaves too much ambiguity about who leads the civil service, how responsibilities are allocated, and how impartiality and performance should be protected. New Zealand’s State Sector Act 1988, Public Service Act 2020, and the amendments that came into force on 3 June 2026, offer a useful case study: not because the UK should copy New Zealand, but because they show both the value and the limits of codifying Westminster conventions.

articles.title: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
articles.standfirst: There were legitimate fears before Huang's abrupt exit from Nvidia - and his return won't fix it
paragraphs: As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.
Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.
The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.
Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.
The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.
Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.
Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.
This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.
The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?
The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.
In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.
It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.
The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

articles.title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
articles.standfirst: Here is what you need to know about the payment that millions will receive from January.
paragraphs: Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.
Here's what you need to know about the payment.
For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.
A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by £443 a year from January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight.
Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.
Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.
As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.
If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.
The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.
The Scottish and Welsh governments have confirmed they will use the funding to introduce equivalent or similar payment schemes.
The Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.
If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into your bank account.
Those who don't pay by direct debit will be contacted by their council and given the choice to receive the £100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill.
The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May.
Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.
However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.
Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way to give them the payments.
This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.
The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.
The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy.
But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts so you could choose to spend it on something else, while some people may choose to receive the £100 as a credit on their council tax bill.
The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.
The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.

articles.title: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it
articles.standfirst: Busy mothers on both sides of the Atlantic are paying companies to handle their to-do lists.
paragraphs: Maxine Dillon says she needed help to get through her to-do list
Maxine Dillon, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.
Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.
"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.
Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load".

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.
Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.
"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.
Amanda says she and her husband made a conscious decision to spend more quality time with their family
With such companies also increasingly available in the US, another busy working mother, Amanda Sims Nichols in Austin, Texas, has also employed a firm to look after her life admin.
Amanda, who is a business consultant, has three children with her attorney husband, and decided to start paying for help with life admin after moving house, away from her family support network.
She pays $2,250 (£1,750) a month for 25 hours, and says she relishes offloading regular chores including the weekly food shop and clothes washing.
"Money cannot buy you everything, but it can buy you back some of your time," says the 45-year-old.
The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.
The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.
Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.
Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.
Staff of life admin companies will do most jobs around the house for a client
Jess Baker, a UK chartered psychologist, says the appeal of such providers is understandable.
"Using a life PA, if you can afford one, takes the pressure off having to keep hundreds of to-dos swimming around your head, or on lists you might forget to look at," she says.
"Otherwise, the cognitive load can lead to feelings of being overwhelmed, excess worry and exhaustion."
While paying for help with such tasks may seem a luxury, for some people support with life's everyday trials is a lifeline.
Anna Allington sought help after her husband died. "My husband passed away. I was 47," she says.
"And the same week he passed away, I got leukaemia. There was a lot to sort out and I was very, very unwell."
Anna, now 51, still suffers the after-effects of her cancer. "I can't function executively like I used to," she says.
She pays £1,200 a month for 40 hours of help from Cheshire-based company Vi-Va. Her personal assistant helps her respond to emails, manage her diary and make travel plans and bookings.
"We meet twice a week on Zoom," says Anna, who lives in the Cotswolds, so they can go through all her tasks.
Many of us would love for someone else to do our laundry
Many more women than men use these companies.
Queen of To Do says just 20% of its clients are male, while only one of Life Laundry's 25 clients is a man.
Some of that disparity is likely due to mothers still looking after the lion's share of household admin, as studies continue to show.
However, Life Laundry's Forbes wonders if some men are too proud to ask for assistance.
"Men are struggling as well, but I think they're less likely to ask for help."

articles.title: Worried about next week’s price cap? Here’s what it means for January
articles.standfirst:
There’s a lot of (understandable) nervousness around about Ofgem’s upcoming Price Cap announcement next week, as memories of the winter of 2022-23 have yet to fade. So, we wanted to figure out what the new price cap will likely mean for a typical household’s bills; how far the support that Government is offering will go; … Continued
The post Worried about next week’s price cap? Here’s what it means for January appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: There’s a lot of (understandable) nervousness around about Ofgem’s upcoming Price Cap announcement next week, as memories of the winter of 2022-23 have yet to fade. So, we wanted to figure out what the new price cap will likely mean for a typical household’s bills; how far the support that Government is offering will go; and which families we should be most concerned about.

Ofgem’s announcement next week will set the cap for prices between January and March 2027. Those months – you don’t need me to tell you – are the coldest of the year, when we most need the radiators switched on. So it’s a particularly painful time for the cap to rise from £1,723 (as it is currently) to £2,166, as forecasters expect.

We’ve modelled monthly energy costs for a typical dual fuel household, and on our numbers, they will be spending a staggering £62 a week on energy in January.[1] At that rate, the £100 Household Energy Payment paid out to those in homes in Council Tax bands A to D this winter would be used up by a typical family in just 11 days.

Unfortunately, once you adjust for inflation, a typical family will be spending around £50 more this January than they did in December 2022 and January 2023, at the height of the 2022-23 energy price crisis. That comparison takes account of the £400 Energy Bills Support Scheme discount households received that winter: it’s the far more generous support back then that tips the balance.

Families also have less room for manoeuvre than they did in 2022-23, because household gas and electricity consumption are down 18 and 13 per cent respectively on pre-pandemic averages. People have already turned down the thermostat to offset higher prices, and they have less scope to cut back further than they had in 2022-23.

At the risk of stating the obvious, it’s the poorest households who will find it hardest to heat their homes adequately over the chilly winter months. In 2024-25, nearly 2 million of the poorest two-fifths of families said they already could not afford to heat their home properly, compared with around half a million in the richest two-fifths. And we know from the last crisis how quickly that can get worse: after the steep price rises of winter 2022-23, the share of households in the poorest two-fifths of the income distribution that were unable to heat their homes rose by 8 percentage points, compared with a 2 percentage point rise among the richest fifth.

Our worry is that the Government’s £100 Household Energy Payment is spread far too thinly to make much difference to these families. Around 80 per cent of households in England live in homes in Council Tax bands A to D and will be eligible for support. Choosing to help most households means they all get a little, when it would have been far better to give half as many households twice as much instead.

On top of that, the payment is allocated using Council Tax bands based on property valuations that are 35 years out of date. Around one-in-eight households in the bottom half of the income distribution, around 1.6 million in total, will miss out.

If high prices persist, this won’t be the last winter where families need help. As people have been saying since the last painful energy price spike, the Government needs to build a better way of reaching struggling families than using Council Tax bands or its other default, the benefits system. As with the gas standing charge, the lesson is that without a proper way of targeting support, help either ends up spread across many households, as with Council Tax bands, or misses many of the people at the sharp end. The benefits system reaches only about a quarter of households, leaving out roughly 7 million low-income families in the poorest two-fifths who don’t receive means-tested benefits. A social tariff is the obvious place to start, and we’ve set out how one could work.
Jonathan Marshall is a Principal Economist at the Resolution Foundation.

[1] Our analysis estimates monthly gas and electricity costs from April 2019 to March 2027 for a typical dual fuel household in Great Britain paying by Direct Debit on the energy price cap. It uses Ofgem’s price cap levels up to Q4 2026 and Cornwall Insight’s forecast for Q1 2027, published on 18 November 2026. Comparisons over time are in real terms, in July-September 2026 prices.

articles.title: What did we learn from the CBI conference speeches?
articles.standfirst:
What did we learn from the CBI conference speeches? ellie.slee.lamb Tue, 24/11/2026 - 14:04 Louise Haigh is clearer about her attitude to markets than Kemi Badenoch. 6 Comment Giles Wilkes Institute for Government Yes Louise Haigh speaks at the CBI conference Public finances Public services Public spending Internal market Business Trade Burnham government
No

“This is not about whether markets work. They do”. Uttered by first secretary of state Louise Haigh to the CBI Annual Conference, these words would have been uncontroversial to most of those listening. For the past few hundred years – a period of world-changing growth – the essentials of life have been mostly provided to British consumers by markets. That is not going to change. 

Haigh cleared up the Labour position on public ownership somewhat

Public ownership is always the exception. We do not expect our groceries, car, phone, cinema ticket, newspaper or shirt to be provided by the state. Even the parts that are publicly financed rely on private ingenuity to work: the state may own railway concessions and pay for the NHS, but it is profit-maximising businesses that discover new drugs, build train engines and so forth. 

Perhaps it is not ideal that Haigh felt the need to spell this out – a reflection of the confusion wrought by Andy Burnham’s repeated praise for public ownership and disdain for what he calls 40 years of neo-liberalism. But I doubt most of the audience were ever worried about either politician coming for their assets. There are elements of the Labour movement that lament how markets provide the basics of life and see profit as pure extraction, always going to someone else. But these ideas rarely proceed from lip-service to legislation. 

Haigh’s speech was instead about a far narrower set of markets where the privatised model has come under fire: certain essential services that tend towards monopoly and were often publicly owned for a good chunk of the 20th century. The chargesheet is familiar. Staggering along in a deluded state of would-be competition, they adopt the worst features of free market capitalism, the profit-extraction, while under-delivering on the best, the provision of choice to the consumer. As she said, “where competition exists, it should be left to thrive”. The problem is that the conditions for thriving are not always in place. 

But she did take aim at ‘essential services’ like water and energy

To cut to the specifics: Louise Haigh means water and energy (particularly networks), and little beyond that. This is where consumer unhappiness is most acute, where regulation has mushroomed – and where England’s fully privatised approach is a genuine international outlier. Community- or government-owned energy is quite common in the US, and European states often own not only their own utilities, but a fair chunk of ours too. 

It is where there is a decent case to be made for state ownership actually to improve certainty for customers – for while nobody should assume that public sector managers are smarter, their behaviour may be more predictable than the profit-chasing sort, operating in a monopoly and spending most of their time second-guessing the next move of the regulator. Years-long queues for grid connections and new reservoirs demonstrate why reform is needed. 

There is the outline of a case for more public control or ownership here, and nothing to object to with principles like affordability, investability and accountability. It is refreshing to hear a Labour politician argue that users and not producers should be the priority. Haigh was also candid about the state’s role in creating friction and uncertainty, promising to cut down the number of arm’s-length bodies currently complicating the landscape, and tiresome procurement rules. Time is a tax, as she repeatedly acknowledged. 

The limits of voicing principles

Nevertheless, an elucidation of principles can only go a certain way towards reassuring a business audience. More political control swaps in one form of uncertainty for another. When Haigh calls for “good actors” to be backed, and “fair returns” for all, she sets in motion an argument for what is good and fair. Values like clarity, certainty, consistency and fairness do not align perfectly, and into the gaps will rush lobbyists and campaigners. There is a reason politicians in the past have delegated questions of a fair return on capital to technocrats, which they sometimes need to experience to appreciate. 

At the least, though, I would argue that Haigh has helped to clear up somewhat the question of what Labour thinks about markets – they are a nice idea, if they work. 

Kemi Badenoch showed less clarity on the subject

Curiously the next political speaker, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, was marginally less clear on the subject. This reflected the more ambiguous attitude to business that the Conservatives have shown ever since the great falling out over Brexit. On the one hand, Badenoch had to show that she fully understands why lower trading barriers and bigger markets are a good thing – on the other, she is choosing to maintain her party’s position against any renegotiation of a Brexit deal that undermines these principles, that the British public largely believes to be a failure, and few businesses see the advantage of. 

Badenoch returned to her attack-mode comfort zone

This tension was a constant theme throughout her appearance, which Badenoch attempted to soften through regular jibes at some of the government’s more business-unfriendly measures, like the rise in employer NICs and higher national minimum wage. Another device was to point at various bad-news stories – the closure of Denby Pottery, the departure of Compass Group from the UK stock market – and ask, with a dollop of derision, what these have to do with membership of the EU. 

An even less plausible line was to explain to business that a mere 8% of their number actually export to Europe. But these are the biggest and most productivity-driving companies, the ones most exposed to global competition, and it felt rather unconservative to suggest their small number rendered their problems unimportant. 

The Conservatives’ formula of lower energy costs, less regulation, light taxes and flexible labour markets ought to please business, but it is one they would have heard constantly over the 14 years to 2024. Badenoch’s answer to the obvious audience question – why wasn’t this all done before, then? – was both weak and overconfident: “well, it would have had I been in charge”. 

This kind of naivety about the real political difficulties of doing the right thing is acceptable for an opposition party a few years away from office, but “sheer political will” is a worse answer than none once in government. 

A return to mercantilism?

What is more confusing is the flavour of anti-market mercantilism that has begun to infect Conservative rhetoric in recent days. One of Badenoch’s lines of attack against moving closer to the EU was the triumphant declaration that it is not just the UK that sells to the EU, but the EU sells back to us – and more! The idea that running a deficit is reason to downplay the advantage of trade is embarrassing outside of the Trump White House, particularly on the 250th anniversary of Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations. This follows a foray into the “Lump of Labour” Fallacy at PMQs last week, when Badenoch challenged the prime minister to explain where the jobs for 100,000 EU migrants might come from. That is Old Labour thinking, to be kind. 

On business, Labour and the Conservatives are not so far apart

There is much in common between Labour and Conservative business policies. Both are frustrated by a clogged-up state and high energy prices, and both appear to realise that business taxes have risen about as far as they should or can. They might even each agree on how elements of utility regulation have gone wrong. Business has recently faced a choice between the Scylla of an anti-market Labour Party, and the Charybdis of the truculently anti-Europe Conservatives. At present, it is Labour that appears closest to proving the more attractive. 

This year’s CBI conference featured keynotes from Louise Haigh, first secretary of state in the Burnham government, and the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch. Perhaps surprisingly, Giles Wilkes says it was the Labour speaker who articulated a clearer attitude towards markets than the Conservative. Louise Haigh Kemi Badenoch Off Public finances

On the one hand, Badenoch had to show that she fully understands why lower trading barriers and bigger markets are a good thing – on the other, she is choosing to maintain her party’s position against any renegotiation of a Brexit deal that undermines these principles, that the British public largely believes to be a failure, and few businesses see the advantage of.

This tension was a constant theme throughout her appearance, which Badenoch attempted to soften through regular jibes at some of the government’s more business-unfriendly measures, like the rise in employer NICs and higher national minimum wage. Another device was to point at various bad-news stories – the closure of Denby Pottery, the departure of Compass Group from the UK stock market – and ask, with a dollop of derision, what these have to do with membership of the EU.

An even less plausible line was to explain to business that a mere 8% of their number actually export to Europe. But these are the biggest and most productivity-driving companies, the ones most exposed to global competition, and it felt rather unconservative to suggest their small number rendered their problems unimportant.

The Conservatives’ formula of lower energy costs, less regulation, light taxes and flexible labour markets ought to please business, but it is one they would have heard constantly over the 14 years to 2024. Badenoch’s answer to the obvious audience question – why wasn’t this all done before, then? – was both weak and overconfident: “well, it would have had I been in charge”.

This kind of naivety about the real political difficulties of doing the right thing is acceptable for an opposition party a few years away from office, but “sheer political will” is a worse answer than none once in government.

What is more confusing is the flavour of anti-market mercantilism that has begun to infect Conservative rhetoric in recent days. One of Badenoch’s lines of attack against moving closer to the EU was the triumphant declaration that it is not just the UK that sells to the EU, but the EU sells back to us – and more! The idea that running a deficit is reason to downplay the advantage of trade is embarrassing outside of the Trump White House, particularly on the 250th anniversary of Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations. This follows a foray into the “Lump of Labour” Fallacy at PMQs last week, when Badenoch challenged the prime minister to explain where the jobs for 100,000 EU migrants might come from. That is Old Labour thinking, to be kind.

There is much in common between Labour and Conservative business policies. Both are frustrated by a clogged-up state and high energy prices, and both appear to realise that business taxes have risen about as far as they should or can. They might even each agree on how elements of utility regulation have gone wrong. Business has recently faced a choice between the Scylla of an anti-market Labour Party, and the Charybdis of the truculently anti-Europe Conservatives. At present, it is Labour that appears closest to proving the more attractive.
This prime minister has largely completed Keir Starmer’s EU legacy.

Public spending Spending review Budget Public sector NHS Schools Criminal justice Local government Labour Chancellor of the exchequer Institute for Government Monday 07 December 2026, 09:30 GMT Public services How will John Healey ensure that new plans for ringfenced prevention spending are implemented correctly?

John Healey’s budget unveiled plans for a Preventative Departmental Expenditure Limit (PDEL) to "ringfence prevention spending that brings down costs in the future" – a reform which the IfG has championed for years.  

Focusing on early intervention and limiting demand for acute services like hospitals and prisons could be transformational for both public spending and public services – but a ringfence will only work if government gets the definition and implementation right.

articles.title: Why Poland Should Abandon Its Proposed Digital Services Tax
articles.standfirst: Experiences across European countries indicate that digital services taxes typically generate relatively modest amounts of revenue.
paragraphs: In connection with the draft Act on a Compensatory Tax on Certain Services (UD385), announced by the Ministry of Digital Affairs and commonly referred to as the “digital tax,” Tax Foundation Europe hereby submits its position on the proposal.

Tax Foundation Europe is a think tank that conducts research and analysis on taxation and advocates for tax policy grounded in four core principles: simplicity, neutrality, transparency, and stability. In light of these principles, and with regard to the draft Act on a Compensatory Tax on Certain Services, Tax Foundation Europe wishes to draw attention to the following issues and their potential economic implications.

Unlike the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. (CIT), a digital services tax is levied on revenue rather than profits, meaning that it does not take into account a company’s profitability (profit margin). As a result, an apparently modest tax rate (3%) can translate into a substantial effective tax burden in practice.

For example, if a company generates PLN 100 in revenue and incurs PLN 85 in costs, its profit amounts to PLN 15 (a 15% profit margin). Under a 3% digital services tax, the company would pay PLN 3 in tax (3% of PLN 100 in revenue), resulting in an effective tax rate on profit of 20% (PLN 3 in tax relative to PLN 15 in profit).

The chart below illustrates how different profit margins translate into markedly different effective tax burdens, assuming the same revenue of PLN 100. At a profit margin of 25%, the effective tax burden is 12%, whereas at a profit margin of 5%, the effective tax rate rises to 60%.

Under a revenue-based tax, companies generating the same level of revenue may face significantly different effective tax burdens depending on their cost structures and profit margins. As a result, firms with relatively low profit margins may bear a disproportionately high tax burden compared to more profitable businesses.

Recent research suggests that taxing digital platforms may fail to achieve its intended objectives if the economic burden of the tax is ultimately passed on to consumers. Such effects are particularly likely in the case of services that users perceive as highly valuable and that are provided in a small, open economy such as Poland, where domestic substitutes are often limited.

For example, Google explicitly states that in countries that have introduced digital services taxes, an additional fee reflecting the amount of the digital services tax is added to the price of advertising services.

Digital services taxes, which in some respects operate similarly to tariffs imposed on specific services, are inherently discriminatory because they target particular sectors dominated by U.S. companies. The United States government has opposed digital services taxes for more than a decade. During President Trump’s first term, the Administration challenged such measures through investigations conducted under Section 301, while more recently the U.S. Congress considered retaliatory action through the tax measures proposed in Section 899. Although Section 899 was ultimately removed from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, digital services taxes remain a sensitive issue in bilateral political and economic relations.

Until an international consensus is reached on the taxation of the modern digital economy, any retaliatory measures adopted in response to digital services taxes are likely to result in adverse economic consequences for all parties involved.

Experiences across European countries indicate that digital services taxes typically generate relatively modest amounts of revenue. In the most recent year for which data are available, revenues from these taxes in Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom ranged from €137 million in Austria to €1.04 billion in the United Kingdom. Turkey’s digital services tax, levied at a rate of 5% (7.5% in 2024 and 2025), generates the highest level of revenue relative to total government receipts, amounting to approximately 0.24% of government revenue.
Even if Poland were to achieve the projected revenue from the proposed digital tax, the resulting proceeds would account for less than 1% of total government revenue.

According to simulations conducted by Tax Foundation Europe, Belgium’s proposed digital services tax would generate relatively limited budgetary revenue while at the same time producing adverse economic effects. The estimates are based on a 3 percent digital services tax, comparable to the proposal put forward in Belgium in April 2026. Under this scenario, annual tax revenues would amount to approximately €148 million, representing less than 0.06 percent of Belgium’s total tax revenues. At the same time, Belgium’s GDP would decline by around 0.056 percent, equivalent to approximately €342 million per year. Investment would fall by 0.073 percent, while wages and employment (or, alternatively, hours worked) would decrease by 0.03 percent, and total labor income would decline by 0.053 percent.

These effects reflect the tendency for taxes imposed on digital activities to be passed on to other economic actors, reducing incentives to invest and ultimately affecting workers through lower wages and reduced employment.

Most importantly, the economic costs of the proposed measure may outweigh its direct fiscal benefits. Tax Foundation Europe’s simulations indicate that the economic distortions associated with the proposed digital services tax could exceed the expected budgetary gains. The estimated reduction in economic output of approximately €342 million is around 2.3 times greater than the projected annual tax revenue of €148 million. This suggests that the resulting contraction of the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. could offset a significant share of the additional revenue generated by the tax and, once lower receipts from other taxes are taken into account, could ultimately lead to a negative net fiscal effect.

It is important to design the tax system in a way that raises government revenue as efficiently as possible while minimizing the non-tax costs associated with economic growth. In economic literature, consumption taxation is generally regarded as a less distortive form of taxation. OECD research suggests that there remains scope for reform in this area within the Polish tax system.

For example, Poland ranks fourth in Europe in terms of foregone VAT revenue resulting from reduced rates and exemptions. Estimates indicate that broadening the VAT base by eliminating reduced rates and exemptions could generate nearly PLN 220 billion (€50.4 billion) in additional government revenue. Even a small fraction of this amount would exceed the revenue that could realistically be generated by a digital services tax.

Compared with digital services taxes, VAT offers several important economic advantages, including tax neutrality, a broad tax base, the absence of tax cascading, consistency with international tax frameworks, and greater revenue-raising capacity.
Taking into account the shortcomings of the digital tax discussed above, as well as its potential adverse economic effects, Tax Foundation Europe recommends abandoning this proposal.
