Anna Leszczyłowska is a Research Fellow at Tax Foundation Europe and Assistant Professor at the Poznań University of Economics and Business, Poland.

articles.title: Movers and Shakers in the 2027 State Tax Competitiveness Index
articles.standfirst: In the spirit of change and improvement, it’s worth looking back to see which states have truly embraced tax competitiveness since 2020, and which ones have lagged behind.
paragraphs: The TaxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. Foundation’s State Tax Competitiveness Index enables policymakers, taxpayers, and business leaders to see how their states’ tax systems measure up across a wide range of tax measures. While there are many ways to show how much state governments collect in taxes, the Index evaluates how well states structure their tax systems and provides a road map for improvement.

The Tax Foundation has published this study, previously called the State Business Tax Climate Index, since 2003. In 2024, we updated the methodology to more comprehensively address a range of emerging tax issues. As with any methodological changes, we apply them to prior years as well to allow for an apples-to-apples comparison across years. Currently, backcasting under the new methodology stretches back to fiscal year 2020 (July 1, 2019).
In the spirit of change and improvement, it’s worth looking back to see which states have truly embraced tax competitiveness since 2020, and which ones have lagged behind.

Amidst a country-wide flat tax revolution, the states that saw the greatest Index ranking improvements consolidated their individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source brackets and reduced rates across multiple major taxes, making their tax codes more attractive to businesses and individuals alike.

Tennessee reduced the rates of its corporate gross receipts taxGross receipts taxes are applied to a company’s gross sales, without deductions for a firm’s business expenses, like compensation, costs of goods sold, and overhead costs. Unlike a sales tax, a gross receipts tax is assessed on businesses and applies to transactions at every stage of the production process, leading to tax pyramiding., improved its treatment of business expensing, and fully phased out its tax on individual interest and dividends income, becoming one of eight states to have no individual income tax.

Iowa has been working toward comprehensive tax reform for several years, and its dedication is paying off. Since our 2020 ranking, the state repealed its alternative minimum tax, reduced its top corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. rate from 12 percent to 7.1 percent, and consolidated four brackets into two. On the individual side, the state reduced its top income tax rate from 8.53 percent in 2019 (and 8.98 percent before reforms adopted in 2018) to a highly competitive 3.8 percent and converted a nine-bracket system to a flat taxAn income tax is referred to as a “flat tax” when all taxable income is subject to the same tax rate, regardless of income level or assets..

Louisiana, too, has been working toward comprehensive tax reform for many years. Since the 2020 ranking, the state has eliminated its uncompetitive throwout rule and its policy of federal deductibility, eliminated its corporation franchise tax, brought down the individual income tax rate from 6 percent to 3 percent, and consolidated five corporate income tax bracketsA tax bracket is the range of incomes taxed at given rates, which typically differ depending on filing status. In a progressive individual or corporate income tax system, rates rise as income increases. There are seven federal individual income tax brackets; the federal corporate income tax system is flat. into one, with a top rate reduction from 8 to 5.5 percent. Louisiana is also one of three states to adopt permanent full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. separate from the federal provision.

Arkansas saw rate reductions and bracket consolidation as well. Lawmakers reduced the top marginal corporate and individual income tax rates from 6.5 and 6.9 percent to 4.3 and 3.7 percent, respectively. The corporate income tax now features only four brackets, and the individual income tax has only two, while both previously had six. The state also improved its nonresident income tax provisions, among other reforms. The corporate rate will continue to fall to 4.1 percent in 2027, helping the state’s future scores.

Nebraska began a phasedown of its individual and corporate income tax rates in 2022, accelerating and extending that phasedown—in addition to consolidating the state’s corporate income tax brackets—through a 2023 law. Since 2022, the 7.81 percent top corporate and 6.84 percent top individual income tax rates both dropped to 4.55 percent and will reach 3.99 percent on January 1, 2027.

Oregon adopted a modified gross receipts tax in addition to its normal corporate income tax. This new tax has relatively high rates, which compounds the tax pyramidingTax pyramiding occurs when the same final good or service is taxed multiple times along the production process. This yields vastly different effective tax rates depending on the length of the supply chain and disproportionately harms low-margin firms. Gross receipts taxes are a prime example of tax pyramiding in action. caused by typical gross receipts taxes.

Washington previously had no income tax at all, and its individual income tax rank bolstered its overall Index score. However, in 2022, the state instituted a tax on individual capital gains income over $250,000 (adjusted annually for inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin). Then, in 2025, the state added a new top marginal rate of 9.9 percent on capital gains exceeding $1 million. Without the help of a strong income tax score, the state’s other categories weighed down its overall rank, which quickly plummeted. This year, lawmakers also adopted a 9.9 percent tax on general income above $1 million, which is scheduled to go into effect in 2028 and will further harm Washington’s score.

Michigan has historically ranked well on the Index (between 12th and 16th) and did not make the large, negative changes of other states in this list. However, the state fell behind by standing still. While other states lowered their individual and corporate income tax rates, increased their tangible personal property de minimis exemptions, and improved their expensing provisions in line with the OBBBA, the Great Lakes State maintained its historical treatment. Michigan also newly exempted tipped and overtime income in 2026, narrowing its income tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates..

Colorado did not make the significant negative changes of Washington, Oregon, or Maine—at least, not in the time period in question. Instead, like Michigan, it demonstrates a cautionary tale of resting on laurels at a time when states are strongly competing for the best tax code. Colorado was sitting comfortably at 22nd on the Index in 2020 because of its relatively low-rate flat taxes—and the state even reduced its income tax rate from a statutory rate of 4.63 percent to a statutory rate of 4.4 percent, with additional temporary reductions due to the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights (TABOR). However, unlike other states, Colorado did not address some of the inefficiencies in its tax code, like its throwback rule and taxation of net CFC-tested income (NCTI, formerly GILTI). The state has also failed to address its lack of a uniform sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. base and unified point of administration. Notably, Colorado’s score is set to decrease substantially in coming years, as voters recently approved an income tax increase for both businesses and individuals that will raise the top marginal corporate and individual income tax rates to 8.4 percent, abandoning Colorado’s flat tax structure.

Maine has seen its rankings slide gradually since 2020 but experienced a sudden seven-place drop this year with its adoption of a 2 percent “high-income surcharge.” This surcharge brings the state’s top marginal individual income tax rate to 9.15 percent on incomes over $1 million and includes a marriage penaltyA marriage penalty is when a household’s overall tax bill increases due to a couple marrying and filing taxes jointly. A marriage penalty typically occurs when two individuals with similar incomes marry; this is true for both high- and low-income couples.. The state also failed to conform to the improved expensing provisions passed by the OBBBA while increasing various excise taxes.

A state’s ranking is not a permanent label—instead, it is meant to show states where they have done well and where they can still improve. If state legislators make pro-growth changes, they can jump up in the rankings, as these states prove. And many states have done just that in the last seven years, truly prioritizing tax reform in such a way as to leave behind those states that are simply standing still. Every state can benefit from a simple, neutral, transparent, pro-growth tax structure.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Janelle Fritts is a Senior Policy Analyst with the Tax Foundation’s Center for State Tax Policy. She is the lead researcher on the annual State Tax Competitiveness Index and serves as a resource to policymakers in their efforts to modernize and improve the structures of their state tax codes. Her work has been cited in The New York Times, the Associated Press, Bloomberg, and numerous state media outlets across the country.

articles.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
articles.standfirst: The Nvidia chief executive has been at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.
paragraphs: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.
The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.
Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".
Following the announcement of Huang's return, Musk posted: "The mistake has been corrected."
Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment platform XTB, said Huang's return suggested he was "the godfather" of AI and has the status to shift "the dial for corporate finance".

"Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet? His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out, and the market loves it," she added.
However, Huang's return to Nvidia does not solve the wider issues rattling the tech stock markets in recent weeks.
Investors had taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

However, investment in AI is still expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.
President Donald Trump hailed Huang as a "great patriot and national treasure" after his reappointment and pointed to the chief executive's wider impact.
"The country needs Jensen's leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy," he wrote on Truth Social.
Nvidia said its leadership had received input from "senior levels of the United States government and was "confident that Mr Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk".

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.standfirst: AI employees in the industry's epicentre - San Francisco - worry that the sector is overheated.
paragraphs: The city of San Francisco is the heart of the AI sector
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Lauren Goldboss walks dogs for AI workers

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
Huge data centres are being built across the US to power AI

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing, which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title: How Value-Added in Trade Complicates the Tariff Picture
articles.standfirst: Although President Trump’s current tariffs apply to nearly every US trading partner, he has often advocated for tariffs to reduce US exposure to China. However, standard trade statistics might not capture China’s true role in global trade.
paragraphs: Although President Trump’s current tariffs apply to nearly every US trading partner, he has often advocated for tariffs to reduce US exposure to China. However, standard trade statistics might not capture China’s true role in global trade. Goods imported from China may contain components (i.e., “value-added”) made in other countries, while goods exported by other countries may contain more Chinese-made components than the statistics show.
Accounting for these factors presents a more complex picture of supply chains and further complicates the effects of tariffs on trade and the US economy.

To illustrate the complexity, consider the iPhone (a product that just so happens to be exempt from the president’s tariffs). Among its 178 components, the chips are manufactured in Taiwan (and some domestically at an affiliate facility in Arizona), the memory and storage components mostly in Japan and Korea, the glass display in Kentucky, and the camera in Japan. The final product, however, is assembled in China.

For the purposes of trade statistics, a product is said to originate from a country if it undergoes a “substantial transformation” there. When iPhones are imported from abroad by Apple to be sold in its stores, the entire value of the iPhone is classified as an import from China, even though it was assembled with parts from around the world, including the US. And this does not even account for the intellectual property and other “intangibles,” such as the specific design of the iPhone, that largely originate in the US as well.

While other countries contribute a larger share of value-added to Chinese exports than the conventional trade statistics show, China may also comprise a large value-added of other countries’ exports. For instance, some evidence suggests that supply chains shifted from China to Vietnam and Mexico following the tariffs that Trump imposed on China in 2018.

The table below presents 2022 value-added shares using the OECD’s “Trade in Value-Added” database. Across the top 10 goods exporters to the US, we can see that a country’s own share of value-added ranges from a low of 50.2 percent for Vietnam to a high of 82.2 percent for China. For Mexico, only 59 percent of the value-added is generated within its borders—about 14 percent of the value-added of its goods exports to the US is generated by the US, while another 8.5 percent comes from China. For Vietnam, China comprises a large share of its value-added at 17 percent.

The president’s current tariffs, if they remain permanent, would likely lead to further shifts in supply chains. Throughout 2025, China faced tariffs higher than many other countries, and the effect of those tariffs was to reduce imports by about $130 billion compared to the previous year. China tariffs still remain higher than other countries even after the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year, as the Section 301 tariffTariffs are taxes imposed by one country on goods imported from another country. Tariffs are trade barriers that raise prices, reduce available quantities of goods and services for US businesses and consumers, and create an economic burden on foreign exporters. imposed in July applies an across-the-board tariff of 12.5 percent on Chinese imports that stacks on top of the Section 301 tariffs imposed on China in 2018. This leaves some goods facing a tariff rate as high as 37.5 percent.

Altogether, accounting for value-added in trade shows that it can be surprisingly difficult to target tariffs at one particular country, and that many countries beyond the targeted country can be affected due to the complexities of modern supply chains. Policymakers should be aware of these complexities when shaping trade policy.

articles.title: Europe Doesn’t Need New EU Taxes. Policymakers Should Fix the Existing System
articles.standfirst: Policymakers calling for higher EU spending need to make their case. And if they make it, the path forward should run through well-designed policies.
paragraphs: Every seven years, EU Member States debate Brussels’ long-term budget: how much to spend and who will pay. At this year’s Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) negotiations, which will cover the bloc’s collective expenses from 2028 through 2034, European Council President António Costa has been calling for additional revenue sources and to finalize discussions by year’s end.

As policymakers gather in Brussels this Thursday to satisfy this ambitious deadline, the question they must answer is how to raise these funds. While Costa aims to avoid burdening Member States with the bill, the money must come from somewhere. In reality, if the revenue collection policies are not designed accordingly, the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. burden will be passed on to EU taxpayers and businesses—whether it’s collected by Member States or Brussels.
But policymakers can choose to collect this revenue efficiently. To do this, the EU should set three goals for this debate.

In recent weeks, Costa has taken the Corporate Own Resource for Europe (CORE) plan off the table. This is welcome news. The CORE would have charged businesses a fixed tax based on their revenues instead of their profits. A company struggling to make money would pay a heavier share of what they earn while a highly successful business would have a low tax bill. This is not how tax policy should work.

And yet, after removing the CORE, Costa has reintroduced the concept of a 3 percent digital services tax (DST) on revenues of companies with more than €50 million in annual revenue within the EU and €750 million in global revenue. Recent Tax Foundation Europe modeling of similar policies and proposals in the United Kingdom and Belgium demonstrate that the economic costs are larger than the revenues raised by such taxes.

And, as with any tax that applies to revenue rather than profits, higher profit margins mean lower effective tax rates. As my colleague Cristina Enache described in her testimony to the European Parliament’s Budget Committee in July:

“…a company with €100 in revenue and €15 in profit faces a 3 percent DST (€3 in tax), which translates into a 20 percent tax on profits. If the profit margin is lower, the effective tax rate rises dramatically—up to 60 percent or more.”

Or consider the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which is a charge on the carbon content of imports. This, too, is a flawed approach. By not offering rebates for exporters, it increases costs for EU producers who compete abroad. Even though we are in early days of implementation, CBAM has already drawn widespread international criticism from the US and BRICS nations.
Both proposals are complicated and raise costs in the EU market. A better approach would be to reform the effective tools that are already in place.

Today, much of the EU budget is funded by two sources: contributions based on each Member State’s gross national income (GNI), and their value-added tax (VAT). Together, they finance more than 80 percent of it. Crucially, both are dependent on how well Member States run their domestic tax policies. This makes VAT policy particularly important for national revenues.
Fortunately for Costa and policymakers seeking new revenue, the old VAT system has plenty to fix.

Member States fail to collect roughly EUR 128 billion under existing rules, which is often called “the compliance gap.” They also give up EUR 742 billion through exemptions and special rates in VAT rules, or “the policy gap.” By comparison, the new revenue being sought in the EU budget is only roughly EUR 60 billion.

Closing the compliance and policy gaps—collecting what is already owed while trimming exemptions and special rules—and adjusting how the EU budget raises funds from VAT would be far easier than building something new.

Tax policy shouldn’t only focus, though, on revenue. When designing the MFF, Costa and Member States should ask each policy to pass a simple test: will this make Europe more or less competitive? The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) recent World Economic Outlook shows that governments have options to raise additional revenue while minimizing economic costs, ideally through broad-based consumption taxes, well-designed income taxes, and policies built with tax administration in mind.

Relying on revenues from policies like DST or CBAM makes that task harder. But by focusing on simplicity, Member States can refine their own policies rather than worrying about special new levies out of Brussels. Brussels should continue to identify how Member States could patch up their VAT systems that are currently leaving money on the table.

Policymakers calling for higher EU spending need to make their case. And if they make it, the path forward should run through well-designed policies. Improving existing systems at the Member State level should be step one. If Costa instead adds more complexity and tax hikes into the fold, the EU will end up with an inefficient system run from the top while serious problems with national tax systems persist, putting a further drag on the economy.
If we don’t start here, policymakers might waste precious time designing policies that will be more effective at preventing EU growth than raising revenue.

Daniel has been with the organization since 2018 and, prior to becoming President, successfully built its Center for Global Tax Policy, expanding the Tax Foundation’s reach and impact around the world. articles.title: Online Sports Betting Taxes by State, 2026
articles.standfirst: The market for sports betting will likely continue to grow substantially as more states allow legal operations or expand existing operations to online services. State governments are often enticed by potential tax revenues. As the tax base grows, tax policy design becomes increasingly important.
paragraphs: Legal sports betting has grown rapidly since the 2018 Supreme Court decision Murphy v. NCAA recognized the federal prohibition as unlawful, enabling states to establish legal markets. Under the previous prohibition, consumers could only bet legally in a few states, but there is now some form of legal sports betting in 40 states and the District of Columbia.

Across these states, sports betting markets vary substantially. States levy a range of different taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. rates and structures, sometimes differentiating between online wagers and brick-and-mortar wagers, and access to legal sports betting can be strictly limited.

While 40 states have legalized sports wagering in some form, consumers only have statewide access to online sports betting platforms in 30 states and the District of Columbia. These other states limit wagers to those placed within brick-and-mortar casinos, on tribal lands, or other physical restrictions—even for wagers placed digitally online. The highest tax rates are levied in New Hampshire, New York, Oregon, and Rhode Island at 51 percent of sportsbooks revenues. Nevada and Iowa levy the lowest tax rates at 6.75 percent.

Most states levy an ad valorem tax on the revenues of sportsbook operators. Many states levy the tax on gross gaming revenues (GGR), an estimated measure of sportsbook profitability from gaming activity, prior to any deductions for operational expenses. The way in which promotional wagers affect GGR and the taxable base of sportsbooks continues to be a policy focus for several states.

A few states take a different approach to taxing sports betting activity. Tennessee levies a tax directly on the sports betting handle—the total amount wagered—and Illinois recently established an additional ad quantum fee of $0.50 per wager. Some states like Oregon grant themselves a monopoly on online sports betting within their state and establish a revenue share agreement for a share of operators’ proceeds. We convert these taxes to their approximate GGR levels for comparability with other states’ rates.
Taxes are not the only burdens that gamblers and sportsbooks must bear.

Consumer access to legal betting markets is limited primarily by high barriers to entry for sports betting operators who want to offer services in the state and by limits on the geographic locations where players are allowed to place bets.

State laws and regulations erect significant barriers to entry for operators. This is often in the form of expensive licensing fees or requirements for online sportsbooks to partner with existing in-state brick-and-mortar operators. For instance, Massachusetts demands sportsbooks pay a fee of $5 million and renew that payment every five years. Sportsbooks in Pennsylvania must pay an initial fee of $10 million and a $250,000 renewal fee every five years.

New Jersey requires online sportsbook operators to partner with a brick-and-mortar racetrack or casino licensed in the state, while Ohio offers online sportsbooks the option to partner with a professional sports organization approved by the Casino Control Commission to offer mobile sports betting.

Other states require a partnership with the state lottery commission or grant control of online sports betting markets to the state lottery commission directly. Online gaming operators in Connecticut must partner with an approved master gaming operator to legally offer services. Montana monopolized all sports betting under the Montana Lottery Commission. Florida allows online sports betting, but only through the Seminole Tribe’s single operator.

Whether via direct control, like in Montana, or an exclusive contract with a private operator, like in New Hampshire, states that grant a monopoly to one provider of sports betting services establish an insurmountable barrier to entry for other providers. These anticompetitive practices limit consumers’ options, which is likely to also limit the revenues states generate from sports betting taxes and economic growth from the gaming industry.

Washington, DC, provides a great case study of the impact of a monopolized sports betting market. The DC Council established a monopoly in 2019 but ended that monopoly in 2024 amid problems with customer satisfaction, performance, and fraud. After DC’s monopoly ended, GGR per adult in the population nearly tripled from about $83 in 2024 to about $240 in 2025.

Several states also restrict where players are allowed to gamble online. In New Mexico, North Dakota, and Wisconsin, consumers are only allowed to place bets from tribal casinos. South Dakota gamblers may place bets in tribal casinos or in licensed casinos in the city of Deadwood. Mississippi and Montana only allow consumers to place bets when physically present at retail casinos or state-operated facilities.

Online wagers are treated differently from other wagers in certain states. Arizona, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and the District of Columbia tax online wagers more heavily than retail (in-person) wagers.
The various burdens states place on sportsbook operators translate into worse odds and worse experiences for bettors participating in the legal market.

Sports betting is different, legally and economically, from prediction markets. The tax and regulatory treatment of prediction markets are not the same as that of sports betting, online or otherwise. However, efforts are ongoing across several states to try to bring prediction markets into the tax and regulatory framework that governs sports betting or other forms of gambling.

The same budget bill that increased taxes on sportsbooks in North Carolina also established a 6 percent tax on operators of prediction markets to begin in 2027. Kentucky has also provided for a broader 14.25 percent tax on prediction markets. However, the legal environment is rapidly developing as federal courts consider whether states can regulate these entities as gambling or authority rests solely with the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission as with financial products. Whether states can regulate them and whether they can tax them, and what that tax may look like, may also be separate questions.

Until federal courts or legislation answer these questions, the treatment of prediction markets at the state level is largely uncertain. Different courts have come to different conclusions thus far, so either Supreme Court input or congressional legislation is likely to be the only definitive solution.

Establishing and taxing a legal sports betting market has been quite lucrative for states. Sports betting taxes brought in more than $3.7 billion for states across the country in 2025, with New York receiving by far the most, with more than $1.3 billion, followed by Illinois with more than $495 million.

The market for sports betting will likely continue to grow substantially as more states allow legal operations or expand existing operations to online services. State governments are often enticed by potential tax revenues. As the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. grows, tax policy design becomes increasingly important.

Optimal sports betting design would ensure that rates are low enough to bring consumers into legal, regulated markets rather than gambling illicitly. Restrictions on where consumers are allowed to gamble, or limits on their choices from barriers to entry like exorbitant licensure or monopoly grants, are also likely to push consumers into black markets. Illicit gambling markets also tend to be more predatory and have fewer protections for consumers, especially problem gamblers, so this aligns with public health goals as well.

Tax revenues and public benefits from legal sports gambling may be further undermined by the recent change to the treatment of gambling income for federal income taxes. With only a portion of gambling losses now deductible, the unequal tax treatment threatens to drive gambling activity to other countries or illicit markets that are not so unfairly burdened.

Adam Hoffer is the Director of Excise Tax Policy at the Tax Foundation. Dr. Hoffer earned his PhD in Economics from West Virginia University and his undergraduate degree from Washington & Jefferson College.

Jacob Macumber-Rosin is an Excise Tax Policy Analyst with the Tax Foundation. Jacob holds a BS in economics (politics and the economy) as well as a BS in civic and economic thought and leadership from Arizona State University.

articles.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
articles.standfirst: Would AI be a good judge of whether you should get a mortgage, car loan or mobile phone contract?
paragraphs: Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.
Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.
It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.
"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.
Credit scores are "backward looking" says Funmi Olufunwa
Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.
"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.
Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.
"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.
"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.
Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.
But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?
In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.
But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".
But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.
"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.
Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".
While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.
She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.
"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."
Upstart says it is tackling that issue.

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.
Evangeline Atkinson (left) and Laura Mills co-founders of Noggin HQ
Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.
"I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls.
"When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies."
That experience inspired her to try to change the system.
In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.
Their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.
The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.
Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".
"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics."
Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August
Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.
Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".
As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.
"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there."
Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.
Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.
"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.
"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," says Olufunwa.

paragraphs: At Monday’s Lord Mayor’s Banquet, Andy Burnham repeated his argument at Labour Party conference that the “hard Brexit we were given is not good enough”. But for anyone already dreaming of racing through shorter passport queues next summer, today’s EU-UK delivers a deflating reality check. Big changes will take time. What we got today was a tweak-around-the-edges deal which rests heavily on agreements predominantly negotiated by the Starmer Government, covering food and drink, emissions trading and a new youth mobility scheme. More substantial changes to the UK’s relationship with the EU won’t come until after the next general election.

Nevertheless, Burnham has taken another step towards a conversation about ‘Brejoin’ (sorry) with the public, and with Europe, and is arguably signaling more ambition on Europe than any government since the referendum (or at least since Theresa May’s Government). A decade on, we can see what hard Brexit has, and has not, delivered. And with the world very changed since 2016, Burnham argues it is time to ask whether we still want to be on this trajectory.
So is he right about the costs of Brexit? And would reopening the debate carry new costs?

Burnham has a point. The clearest damage from our departure is to goods trade. The value of UK goods exports fell by around £10 billion between 2019 and 2024, even as world goods exports grew by a quarter, and the UK had the largest fall in goods export volumes in the G7, as this first chart shows. Services have held up better – they made up 59 per cent of UK exports in 2024, up from 48 per cent in 2019 – but that’s from goods shrinking, rather than services growing. In fact, our services exports have only just kept pace with the rest of the G7.

Add it all up and the hit to the economy may be bigger than expected before we breparted (sorry). The Office for Budget Responsibility assumes Brexit will eventually reduce productivity by around 4 per cent. We reckon GDP is already between 4 and 10 per cent lower.

On Monday, Burnham promised to open a discussion “about options for our long-term relationship” with the EU. The European Commission President seemed open to that at today’s press conference, but their joint statement is careful to make no official commitments. UK in a Changing Europe set out the options in June with its ‘staircase‘: from a ‘TCA-minus’ Brexit, through a customs union, a Swiss-style deal and single market (EEA) membership, all the way up to rejoining. Each step up means closer alignment with EU rules, and, on the higher steps, free movement of people, in return for bigger economic gains.

We’ve spent the past couple of years negotiating our way from the TCA to the ‘TCA-plus’ step, with a deal on food standards, emissions trading and youth mobility announced today. And while HMT estimates this could add a welcome half a per cent to GDP, Labour’s manifesto red lines have kept the higher steps out of reach.
But Burnham wants to put those higher steps back on the table.

Putting rejoin back on the agenda isn’t necessarily free. The uncertainty created by the vote to leave the EU in 2016 held back business investment: on one recent estimate, uncertainty explained most of a 12 per cent shortfall in business investment, relative to a world without Brexit, by 2023-24.

But round two should hurt far less. It’s hard to fully separate the effects of higher uncertainty and a weaker economic outlook on investment. In 2016, the two arrived together and spurred each other on. This time, uncertainty would come with the prospect of better access to EU markets, which should partly offset it. And if talks failed, the fallback would be the status quo rather than a cliff edge, and firms already know how EU rules work – meaning the overall level of uncertainty should be lower too. Credible commitments to improved market access can also pay off quickly. China’s entry to the World Trade Organization, which removed the threat of higher US tariffs, accounted for over a third of the growth in China’s exports to the US in 2000-05, a period in which they more than doubled.

That said, a long, open-ended process should still be avoided. Rejoining would require both a domestic mandate and the agreement of all 27 member states, AND firms and our EU partners would need to be convinced that it would survive a change of government.
The key lesson we should take from the post-Brexit years is that what held back investment wasn’t only where the UK was heading, but how long we took to figure it out.

Andy Burnham’s EU ‘reset’ deal highlights the problems of incrementalism sam.macrory Fri, 20/11/2026 - 16:07 This prime minister has largely completed Keir Starmer’s EU legacy. 5 Comment Jill Rutter Institute for Government Yes Prime Minister Andy Burnham addresses a media conference during the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. International relations Brexit Trade Immigration Foreign affairs Labour Burnham government
No

It may have been Andy Burnham’s cabinet lining up in Brussels today to shake hands with EU leaders, but this PM’s team have picked up the baton from Keir Starmer and his lead negotiator Nick Thomas-Symonds. Today’s “deals” mostly reflect the files opened at the UK-EU summit in May last year. The one which closed summarily at that summit, when the UK decided the price was too high to join the EU’s Security Action for Europe programme, has remain closed, but the UK announced last December that it would reassociate for one year with the EU’s Erasmus+ programme. 

Since then, negotiations have focussed on easing life for most agri-food exporters, through an agreement to “dynamically align” UK sanitary and phytosanitary laws with the EU, removing the need for checks at the EU border which have seen UK exports decline very substantially since Brexit. The UK will also link its emissions trading scheme (ETS) with the EU’s, allowing UK exporters to avoid the bureaucracy and costs of the EU’s Carbon Border. And there will be a new Youth Experience Scheme (YES) which will allow up to 100,000 young EU citizens (aged 18-31) to work or study in the UK every year for a maximum of three years – with the same number of young Brits able to move to individual EU countries. The prime minister explicitly lauded this scheme as bringing hope to a generation that policy-makers had neglected (and who, by implication, were victims of a Brexit vote they could not participate in). 

None of these “deals” come into force yet. The language on both agreements is that “negotiations have been concluded”, and that the agreements aim to be applied in 2028. The precise language speaks of “looking forward to the conclusion of these agreements (SPS and ETS) along with the Youth Experience Scheme”.  

Opponents are arguing that these breach the UK’s red lines by effectively moving us inside the single market for agricultural goods, that the UK has become a rule taker by accepting the EU design of emissions trading, and that the YES is tantamount to freedom of movement through the backdoor. However, the UK parliament could still decide not to accept new EU rules (though at the price that access newly gained would be lost) and the YES is a souped up version of working holiday schemes that the UK already has with nations like Australia, Canada and South Korea. Indeed, the EU could say that 100,000 is proportionally very low compared to Australia’s 45,000 annual quota. The big concession will come when/if the UK discounts tuition fees for EU students at UK universities – something not conceded to any of these other countries. That remains to be negotiated within the next six months. The language in the joint statement avoids pegging agreement to charging domestic fees and it remains to be seen whether the EU will settle for less.

Burnham’s Brexit Mission: From Brussels with Love?

Burnham’s Brexit Mission: From Brussels with Love?

The FT’s Stephen Bush joins the podcast team to discuss a big week on the international stage for the prime minister.

Listen to the podcast

Attention is now shifting to Made in Europe

But one of the major focus points in the negotiations was not on the table last year. Since Keir Starmer launched his reset, the EU’s “Made in Europe” agenda – designed to protect the EU’s industrial base from Chinese incursions – risked leaving the UK outside the EU’s procurement and subsidy wall and excluded from critical supply chains. The EU itself has been divided on whether Europe for these purposes includes the UK (and other friendly countries such as Canada, Japan and South Korea) or whether Europe should be interpreted more narrowly to comprise only single market members. 

The final joint statement contains a lot of commitments to work together in “a partnership for economic resilience” with a “Dialogue on Economic Security” (their caps) and to cooperate in managing critical supply chains. There is no explicit reference to the UK coordinating external tariffs – but quite a lot of implication that the UK needs to avoid becoming a backdoor to allow other countries to avoid EU controls.

We don’t know how Andy Burnham will manage the future EU options debate 

The UK government is going to move swiftly into action on getting the necessary legislation to allow the SPS and ETS deals to be implemented onto the statute book, with Burnham suggesting that job will be done this parliament when the agreements are completed. He then proposed “brainstorming” future options with the EU before the next summit, around this time next year – though quite how much time or inclination the EU has for that in the aftermath of a series of difficult election results in Spain, France and Poland remains to be seen.  

The 10 year plan, due this side of Christmas, may reveal more about what Burnham wants to say to the British public about his thinking on future options. The risk for the prime minister is the vacuum he has created is being filled by his critics who are already weaponising elements of these deals to argue that “control” is being handed back to Brussels. But it may make him think that if these limited moves trigger such a reaction, he might as well try to move further, faster after an election.

articles.title: ETF sales support the Bank of Japan’s balance sheet and fiscal financing
articles.standfirst: The Bank of Japan (BoJ) announced on October 30 that it will increase the pace at which it’s selling its holdings of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) on the open market. The additional revenue from capital gains will mitigate the rising financial cost of rate hikes for the BoJ, but also make the government increasingly reliant on the sales as fiscal revenue, inviting the risk of political interference.
paragraphs: The Bank of Japan (BoJ) announced on October 30 that it will increase the pace at which it’s selling its holdings of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) on the open market. The additional revenue from capital gains will mitigate the rising financial cost of rate hikes for the BoJ, but also make the government increasingly reliant on the sales as fiscal revenue, inviting the risk of political interference.

As rate hikes increase interest payments on current accounts, dividends and capital gains from the ETF holdings play an increasingly crucial role in maintaining the BoJ’s surplus, allowing it to continue rate hikes without weakening its balance sheet. According to an estimate by a private research firm, the BoJ would post an operating deficit of JPY1.3tn in FY2026 without the ETF-related revenue of JPY2.7tn.

The government, which needs to find alternative revenue sources of JPY15tn-JPY20tn, plans to incorporate the proceeds from the ETF sales into its fiscal plan. Payments from the BoJ to the national treasury have been about JPY1tn-JPY2tn in recent years – faster sales could provide additional revenue of JPY1tn per year.

We think the BoJ will accelerate the pace of its ETF sales gradually in the coming years, careful not to disrupt equity markets. As the government’s reliance on the BoJ’s revenue from its ETF sales grows, the bank could come under political pressure to increase its profits.

articles.title: How can tax and finance leaders prepare their function for an AI-enabled future?
articles.standfirst: Transforming tax and finance requires more than applying AI to existing processes. Functions have to adapt to rising regulatory demands while providing greater strategic value.
paragraphs: Transforming tax and finance requires more than applying AI to existing processes. Functions have to adapt to rising regulatory demands while providing greater strategic value. We surveyed 1,600 tax and finance executives globally, spanning 22 industries, to dig deeper into these themes, examining how leaders can combine technology, trusted data, and human judgement to build more responsive operating models.

Amidst geopolitical instability, shifting trade policies, and the expansion of digital tax administration, tax and finance teams are under growing pressure. Leaders must manage increasingly complex compliance requirements while responding quickly to changes across the markets in which their organisations operate.

At the same time, businesses expect tax and finance functions to look beyond their traditional responsibilities. Teams are being asked to identify emerging risks and contribute more directly to strategic decision-making. Our findings suggest that AI can help create the capacity needed to meet these expectations, but technology alone will not deliver transformation.

Max is based in the London office and supports the Thought Leadership team across business sectors and disciplines. Max graduated from the University of Warwick with a BA in Politics, International Studies and Quantitative Methods and an MSc in Behavioural and Data Science.

John oversees Thought Leadership projects with EMEA-based clients. He works across business sectors and disciplines, but specialises in issues relating to strategy and business operations, such as sustainability, digital transformation, employment and skills, finance, and performance management. He has directed the Thought Leadership contribution on some of Oxford Economics’ largest and most complex research programmes, for global consultancies and corporates, including Accenture, the Adecco Group, Cognizant, EY, Fujitsu and YouTube. Often this is in collaboration with his economist colleagues to blend qualitative and quantitative analysis, and to explore the impact of corporate actions at a business, industry and economy level.

John joined Oxford Economics in 2014, after 25 years as a Financial Controller, financial management consultant and, most recently, a thought leadership expert for IBM’s Institute for Business Value, focused on global public sector issues. John then worked on the independent Digital Government Review as input to the UK General Election. He is an Economics graduate from Sussex University and a Chartered Management Accountant (ACMA).

Alice Ramoff is a Research Intern within the Thought Leadership team based in London. Her current role focuses on business research and AI. Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Alice worked for a technology start-up focused on food sustainability. She holds a Master's degree from the University of Edinburgh and a Bachelor's degree from King's College London.
