articles.title: Spain’s 2026 Election: Diverging Tax Agendas and the Push for Full Expensing
articles.standfirst: Spain’s 2026 election presents a clear divide in economic policy, with the Socialist Workers' Party favoring higher taxes on capital and businesses, while the People’s Party and Vox advocate tax cuts to encourage investment, stimulate economic growth, and improve competitiveness.
paragraphs: As Spain approaches the November 2026 general election, voters face a choice between competing visions for the country’s economic future. While housing, immigration, and infrastructure security are expected to dominate campaign headlines, taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. policy may prove to be one of the election’s most consequential economic dividing lines.

The debate comes after a period of significant tax policy change under Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Since 2018, Spain has introduced a digital services tax (DST), a financial transaction tax, a solidarity wealth taxA wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary., a domestic minimum tax, and several sector-specific levies. Over the same period, Spain’s standing in international tax competitiveness deteriorated markedly, falling from 27th place in 2017 to 35th out of 38 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries in the 2026 International Tax Competitiveness Index (ITCI), fueling debate over whether the current tax framework supports long-term economic growth and investment.

The main parties offer sharply different answers. The governing Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) has generally favored higher taxes on capital, wealth, financial institutions, and large businesses, while the center-right Partido Popular (PP) and Vox advocate lower taxes on investment, income, and wealth, arguing that stronger growth is the best path to higher living standards and sustainable public finances. The election presents voters a choice between maintaining the current approach or shifting toward a more investment-oriented tax system.

Although smaller parties could influence the final outcome, PSOE, PP, and Vox currently lead the polls and represent the clearest alternatives on tax policy. This analysis focuses on their competing proposals and what they would mean for Spain’s tax system and economic competitiveness.

The PP’s economic program proposes a broad package of tax relief measures for households, entrepreneurs, investors, and businesses. Its plans include lower personal income taxes through higher personal and family allowances, targeted tax cuts for middle- and lower-income households, and refundable family tax credits. The party also supports automatic inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin indexation for minimum-wage earners and periodic indexation of income tax bracketsA tax bracket is the range of incomes taxed at given rates, which typically differ depending on filing status. In a progressive individual or corporate income tax system, rates rise as income increases. There are seven federal individual income tax brackets; the federal corporate income tax system is flat. to prevent fiscal drag. In addition, it proposes income tax rebates for young workers.

It also advocates a temporary 0 percent value-added tax (VAT) rate on basic food, VAT exemptions for small businesses with turnover below €85,000, and stronger tax incentives for research, innovation, and productivity-enhancing investment. In addition, it would remove investment-disincentivizing taxes, strengthen anti-tax-evasion measures with revenues recycled into further tax cuts, ensure neutral taxation of savings vehicles, and protect the tax autonomy of Spain’s Autonomous Communities. This stance could also imply the elimination of the solidarity wealth tax, which the party has consistently opposed.

The party’s housing agenda seeks to reduce the cost of housing for young people. Their proposal includes cutting VAT on first-home young buyers, seeking agreements with regional governments to reduce property transfer taxes on existing homes, and introducing a tax-favored “Young Home Savings Account,” allowing annual contributions of up to €2,000 with a 20 percent tax deductionA tax deduction allows taxpayers to subtract certain deductible expenses and other items to reduce how much of their income is taxed, which reduces how much tax they owe. For individuals, some deductions are available to all taxpayers, while others are reserved only for taxpayers who itemize. For businesses, most business expenses are fully and immediately deductible in the year they occur, but ot and tax-free returns when used to purchase a first home. For renters, the party would introduce an income tax deduction for tenants, with larger benefits for lower-income households. Landlords who renew leases for at least three additional years and limit rent increases below inflation would receive an income tax deduction or tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly..

However, perhaps the most economically significant proposal is Measure 181: expanding immediate expensing for business investment. The PP proposes allowing companies to fully deduct in the year incurred investments in machinery, equipment, digitalization, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, software, and patents. It would also allow innovative firms without current profits to access part of the incentive upfront.

This proposal represents a substantial shift toward investment neutrality and faster cost recoveryCost recovery refers to how the tax system permits businesses to recover the cost of investments through depreciation or amortization. Depreciation and amortization deductions affect taxable income, effective tax rates, and investment decisions..

Under normal corporate tax systems, companies often recover investment costs over many years through depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco schedules. Inflation and the time value of money reduce the real value of those deductions, effectively increasing the tax burden on new investment.

Full expensing eliminates this distortion by allowing firms to deduct the entire cost of qualifying investments immediately. Full expensing is one of the most growth-friendly business tax reforms because it lowers the tax penalty on investment while maintaining taxation of profits.
Our modeling suggest that full expensing for machinery and equipment and intellectual property would meaningfully improve Spain’s investment climate.

The reform significantly reduces the tax burden on new investment. The asset-wide marginal effective tax rate falls from 14.2 percent to 11.6 percent. By lowering the cost of capital by 1.6 percentage points, the reform is projected to increase business investment by 1.9 percent and expand the non-financial corporate capital stock by 2.8 percent. These gains would boost productivity, raising long-run GDP by 1.1 percent, wages by 0.93 percent, and the aggregate wage bill by 1.1 percent, while employment would increase only modestly (0.14 percent). The results suggest that the reform’s main benefits would come through higher capital investment, productivity, and wages rather than stronger employment growth, an important distinction for an economy that has faced weak productivity growth over the past two decades.

Additionally, the fiscal cost of accelerated depreciation is front-loaded, peaking in the early years and declining rapidly thereafter, since it only brings capital allowances forward without increasing their total nominal value. As a result, full expensing is one of the most cost-effective tax reforms, delivering significant investment incentives for a relatively low long-term fiscal cost.

While the full expensing proposal would have a significant impact on the Spanish economy and improve the neutrality of the Spanish tax system, other PP’s reform proposals move in the opposite direction. A temporary 0 percent VAT on basic foods (meat, fish, and conserves) would narrow the VAT base by 4.9 percentage points from 44.9 to 40 percent of potential taxable consumption and would cost around €4.4 billion annually, in 2025 prices. Additionally, the VAT exemptions for small businesses would further reduce the VAT base. This means that small businesses below the threshold are not required to collect VAT on their outputs sold to customers but will then also not receive a refund for VAT paid on business inputs. However, small businesses with negative VAT liability will tend to register voluntarily even when below the threshold.
If the PP’s tax agenda seeks to improve investment incentives, Vox offers a much more aggressive tax-cutting platform.

Vox’s fiscal agenda is centered on broad-based tax cuts, deregulation, and stronger incentives for work, investment, and family formation. The party proposes lower personal income taxes and VAT rates, a reduction in the corporate tax rate, lighter taxation of energy consumption, and a systematic review of all taxes and fees affecting households and businesses. It also advocates a zero Social-Security contribution for self-employed workers earning below the minimum wage and lower contributions above that threshold.

While Vox’s current manifesto provides few quantitative details, earlier proposals offer a clearer picture of its fiscal agenda. In previous plans, Vox advocated reducing the standard VAT rate from 21 percent to 18 percent. Its proposed corporate tax rate of 15 percent would place Spain among the lowest-rate corporate tax jurisdictions in Europe. On personal income taxation, Vox previously proposed exempting income up to €22,000, replacing the current central government tax system with just two tax brackets: 15 percent on income up to €70,000, and 25 percent on income above that threshold. Currently, the central income tax brackets go from 9.5 percent to 24.5 percent. The plan also included an additional four-percentage-point reduction in income tax liability for each dependent child, underscoring the party’s emphasis on supporting families through the tax code.

The party’s housing agenda has some similarities with PP’s housing tax proposal. Vox would also eliminate taxes on first-home purchases through a 0 percent VAT rate on new homes and a 100 percent exemption from the property transfer tax on existing homes, while restoring the homeownership tax deduction. The party also proposes tax incentives for long-term rentals, lower taxes on housing development and construction, and preferential tax treatment for investments that increase rental supply. A key difference from the PP is that Vox would partly finance its housing tax cuts by increasing taxes on speculative property transactions and purchases by non-EU buyers.

A key challenge for Vox would be financing these tax cuts while preserving fiscal sustainability in a country already burdened by large deficits, high public debt, and growing pension costs. That said, our modeling suggests the proposed reforms could stimulate investment and economic activity, expanding the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. and partially offsetting the initial revenue losses through higher tax collections over time.

Our modeling results suggest that the proposed Vox tax package, combining a reduction in Spain’s CIT rate and standard VAT rate, would deliver a notable boost to economic activity by improving investment incentives and lowering the tax burden on work and consumption. The corporate tax cut reduces the marginal effective tax rate on new investment from 14.2 percent to 7.5 percent, lowering the cost of capital by around 5.1 percent and driving most of the overall macroeconomic gains. As a result of these two tax reforms, long-run GDP will increase by 3.7 percent, investment by 6.5 percent, and the non-financial corporate capital stock by 9.5 percent, while the wage bill rises by 3.7 percent and employment by 0.7 percent.

The VAT reduction provides an additional, though smaller, stimulus by reducing the labor tax wedgeBroadly speaking, a tax wedge is the difference between the pre-tax price or return and after-tax price or return. For labor income, it is the difference between the total labor costs to the employer and the corresponding net take-home pay of the employee. and encouraging labor supply. Specifically, the proposed reduction in the standard VAT rate is estimated to result in an annual revenue loss of approximately €6.4 billion, in 2025 euros, equivalent to around 6.8 percent of VAT receipts. Although this makes Vox’s proposal approximately €2 billion more expensive than the PP’s proposed VAT reduction on basic goods, it also improves VAT efficiency by reducing tax-induced distortions and increasing the C-efficiency ratio from 44.9 to 48.7 percent. Nevertheless, VAT revenues are estimated to fall by only 3.9 percent, rather than the full 6.8 percent, as the stronger economic activity generated by the CIT rate cut expands the consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible. base and partially offsets the revenue loss.

Overall, the results indicate that this reform package could significantly strengthen Spain’s long-term growth prospects, with the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. reduction accounting for most of the positive economic effects.

Additionally, Vox’s proposed income tax reform, which would reduce the marginal tax wedge by 6.35 percentage points at an estimated cost of €48 billion, could significantly boost economic activity. By increasing workers’ after-tax earnings, the reform raises employment by 2.7 percent, investment by 3 percent, and long-run GDP by almost 3 percent. The resulting economic expansion would broaden the tax base and stimulate consumption, generating an estimated 3 percent increase in VAT revenues (approximately €2.85 billion) that would partially offset the fiscal cost of the proposed tax cuts.

Nevertheless, the reform raises significant concerns regarding fiscal sustainability. With an estimated cost of €48 billion, it is among the most expensive tax reform proposals. Although stronger economic growth would generate additional tax revenues, these gains are unlikely to fully offset the initial revenue loss. Without complementary spending cuts or alternative revenue measures, the reform could widen Spain’s budget deficit and increase public debt, raising questions about its long-term fiscal stability.

PSOE’s fiscal agenda largely builds on its current approach, combining higher taxes on wealth, capital, large corporations, and other perceived undertaxed sectors with targeted tax relief aimed at lower- and middle-income households. Key measures include increasing the taxation of capital income above current levels, with a top rate of 35 percent (from the current 30 percent) applying to capital income exceeding €300,000. This 5-percentage-point increase builds on a trend that began in 2019, bringing the cumulative increase to 12 percentage points if implemented. The manifesto also proposes expanding the existing DST and introducing new taxes on large technology companies and certain AI-related activities.

It plans to continue increasing business taxation and it proposes a new surcharge on listed companies where CEO compensation exceeds 100 times the median employee salary, with an additional tier for pay ratios above 200:1. The party would strengthen wealth taxation and double the financial transactions tax, increasing the Tobin tax rate from 0.2 percent to 0.4 percent. In parallel, it proposes new levies on luxury goods consumption with a significant carbon footprint, including private jets, mega yachts, and business-class flights, targeting what it describes as high-income and environmentally intensive consumption.

At the household level, PSOE program includes refundable tax credits for dependent children, continued tax protection for workers on low earnings or around the minimum wage, and temporary progressive income-tax deductions during periods of elevated inflation. Housing policy also highlights a clear divide while PP and Vox largely favor a “carrot” approach, using tax cuts, deductions, and incentives to encourage homeownership and expand rental supply; whereas PSOE leans more heavily on the “stick,” using higher taxes and penalties on vacant properties, speculative holdings, and large landlords to influence housing market behavior.

A key risk of PSOE’s approach is that higher taxes on capital, investment, and businesses could slow growth while raising less revenue than expected, as many of the new taxes target narrow tax bases. Combined with higher spending commitments, any revenue shortfall could eventually create pressure for broader tax increases or higher deficits.

The election debate raises a broader question: should Spain prioritize redistribution or competitiveness? Or more aptly put: could a more competitive tax system broaden the tax base sufficiently to generate greater revenues and, in turn, support more redistribution?
Voters face a clear choice among three competing tax policy models.
PSOE, the incumbent party, would largely continue the current approach of higher taxes on capital, wealth, financial transactions, and businesses to finance additional public spending.

The PP’s program focuses on improving investment and productivity. Rather than providing targeted subsidies or government spending programs, it seeks to improve economic performance by removing a tax barrier to investment through full expensing.
Meanwhile, Vox proposes a broader low-tax strategy centered on lower taxes on work, investment, business activity, and consumption with a higher initial revenue cost.

From an economic-growth perspective, the strongest proposals are those that improve incentives to invest, work, and save. The modeling results suggest that reforms such as full expensing, lower corporate tax rates, and lower taxes on labor income would boost investment, productivity, wages, and GDP more effectively than additional taxes on capital and business activity. By contrast, many of PSOE’s proposed tax increases target narrow tax bases that are unlikely to generate sufficient revenue, while discouraging investment, constraining economic growth, and encouraging capital flight.

Regardless of the election outcome, Spain would benefit from a broader pro-growth tax reform agenda. Policymakers should avoid further tax increases and consider introducing permanent full expensing and repealing several distortionary taxes introduced during the Sánchez administration, including the windfall profits taxA windfall profits tax is a one-time surtax levied on a company or industry when economic conditions result in large and unexpected profits. Historically, such taxes have targeted oil and energy companies when costs have risen, especially from war or other crises., DST, financial transactions tax, domestic minimum tax, solidarity wealth tax, and wealth taxes.

Our modeling estimates that eliminating Spain’s DST could boost GDP by 0.036 percent (€539 million annually), while increasing investment, wages, and employment. Notably, the estimated economic gains would be 67 percent greater than the tax’s current annual revenue of €323 million. The resulting expansion would broaden the tax base and generate additional revenues from other taxes, partially offsetting the initial revenue loss.

Combined with reducing the top tax rate on capital gains and dividends from 30 percent to 23 percent, these reforms would improve Spain’s investment environment and move the country from 35th to 20th place in the International Tax Competitiveness Index, making the tax system more supportive of long-term growth, investment, and rising wages. More broadly, the 2026 election will present voters with a consequential choice between competing visions for Spain’s tax system, with implications for the country’s long-term growth, investment, tax competitiveness, and wage growth.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.

articles.title: Modernising post-government employment rules is long overdue
articles.standfirst:
Modernising post-government employment rules is long overdue ellie.slee.lamb Wed, 18/11/2026 - 10:20 Reform of the business appointment rules is an important part of the bigger picture on opening up the civil service 5 Comment Hannah Keenan Institute for Government Yes Civil service Civil servants Civil service reform Burnham government
No

Restrictions on the type of work an official can do after leaving the civil service are governed by BARs – the business appointment rules. Once administered by the advisory committee on business appointments (ACOBA), the BARs for senior (directors general and permanent secretaries) civil servants and special advisers is, as of 2025, overseen by the civil service commission, the arms-length body that regulates recruitment into the civil service.  

It is a system which, the institute has long argued, is in need of overhauling – and so a new report by the civil service commission is welcome. It sets out recommendations which will, if accepted, contribute to a more porous and expert civil service, and government should reform the BARs in line with the review recommendations. It will then need to go much further to open up the civil service. 

Business appointment rules have been harming the civil service 

While developing people and skills is crucial, part of creating an effective workforce will always mean being able to access experience and expertise from outside when it is required. Something with which the civil service has long struggled.  

There are a whole host of reasons, cultural and structural, behind that. But BARs are one part of the picture. As the Institute’s research from 2022 set out, the BARs have been acting as a disincentive for external applicants, in particular senior ones to technical roles. The rules could, in theory, restrict you from taking up work in your field of expertise for up to two years after leaving the civil service. And in process terms, even if there are ultimately no restrictions on your future employment, it might take you months to get clearance to take up that role – by which time the window may well have closed. That is very real uncertainty, and a very real disincentive for outsiders to take up a role in the civil service. It is not the only reason external experts don’t come in, but it is a factor. 

Government should act on the commission's review 

That the civil service commission, which already regulates entry, is leading this work on exits for senior officials is a good start; career shapes are shifting and the service should be encouraging – with appropriate ethical safeguards – careers that move in and out of government. The rules have not been meaningfully updated since the 1970s, and no longer reflect the reality of modern work or the skills the service needs. This review should result in a much-needed update.  

Two things are particularly welcome. First, a recognition that the current rules conflate sector expertise with improper advantage, and that this must change. The civil service needs experts, and there should be a sizeable chunk of them who are able to come into government and return to their field of expertise without being unduly punished for doing so. Second, the recognition that much of this is about culture and process efficiency, rather than only about the rules themselves. There is no point updating the rules if the myths around them still hold, or if it will still take months for officials to receive the all-clear on low-risk roles.

The government should act on the commission’s review, reforming the system so that it provides greater clarity for officials, and more proportionality. The review recommends, for example, that for fixed-term appointments of a year or less, conditions should be agreed upon before employment is taken up. As the Institute has previously argued, it should be possible, before joining a role, to see very clearly what restrictions on your activity will look like after you leave. 

Opening up the civil service will need far more than BARs reform 

These recommendations are still only one small piece of the civil service’s ongoing struggle with porosity. As the cabinet secretary said in her recent lecture, “we disincentivise our brightest talent from stepping outside the Civil Service to gain vital experience, and bringing that critical knowledge back”.  

Unblocking this problem requires a series of inter-linked initiatives. More recruitment, especially in central government departments, needs to be done externally. New talent can’t find its way in if many job adverts are still only visible to civil servants. That in turn means addressing the underlying reasons, or perceptions, that drive recruitment from the existing pool of civil servants: security vetting takes too long; onboarding is patchy; there’s no consistent training offer so new team members need to already ‘get’ government; the recruitment process favours internal candidates anyway.

The government is making good steps on some of this, including the new national school of government and public service, and the decision to scrap the ‘success profiles’ currently used to recruit. There are pockets of excellence that show it can be done differently without the system falling over, such as the recruitment exemptions in place for the AI Security Institute.  

Being able to bring in more external people while controlling the size of the civil service also requires better tools to increase the number of leavers from the civil service. A sharper practice and culture around poor performance management, and tighter workforce planning are all part of the same picture.

BARs reform is a helpful piece of the puzzle of breaking open the civil service. But it is only one part of a much bigger ambition on porosity and reform.

articles.title: Three figures we should all pay attention to in the Milburn Review
articles.standfirst:
It’s finally here: the Milburn Review of young people and work was published today. It’s big (over 250 pages); it’s bold (“a new settlement for the next generation”); and it’s brash (if its recommendations were implemented in full, it claims the UK would be “NEET Zero” by 2036-7).   There are many, many numbers in … Continued
The post Three figures we should all pay attention to in the Milburn Review appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: It’s finally here: the Milburn Review of young people and work was published today. It’s big (over 250 pages); it’s bold (“a new settlement for the next generation”); and it’s brash (if its recommendations were implemented in full, it claims the UK would be “NEET Zero” by 2036-7).

There are many, many numbers in the report (the best ones, naturally, are citations of Resolution Foundation research…), but just three of them taken together tell us a lot about Milburn’s recommended programme for change.

First, the report contains a dizzying array of recommendations for investment in service provision: £5.8 billion-worth in 2036-37 (in current prices). Some of this would be restitution for the austerity years (think greater further education funding); some would fund genuinely new services like a permanent youth employment scheme or support for young people with mental health problems.

That £5.8 billion of extra support sounds like a big figure, but it still likely falls short of the level of spending we observe in the lowest NEET countries. For example, Milburn’s proposed additional £3 billion for employment support for under-25s would take the UK from being a low spender on active labour market policies for young people relative to other European countries, to roughly middle of the pack.

And getting all these services and schemes working in concert, which is central to the Review’s vision, would also be no mean undertaking. This would require multiple departments and indeed multiple levels of government to work together to boost youth participation. Milburn recommends introducing a “Youth Opportunity Test” that applies to every government department, plus new duties on schools and local government, to achieve just this.

Which leads us to the second number. The Milburn Review concludes that a combination of early intervention, improved health support, more education and training investment and active labour market policies would result in a ‘big bang’ when it comes to youth employment. By 2036-37, the Review estimates 440,000 more young people would be in employment as a result, and that this would save the state £2.4 billion in 2036-37 as higher taxes and lower benefits are paid.

But achieving that outcome, too, may prove quite the task. Dividing the £5.8 billion of extra support by the 440,000 extra young people the report says will get into employment as a result suggests the average cost of getting each additional young person into work will be around £13,000. Sounds like a lot? It’s not. Past employment support schemes have spent around £30,000 per additional young person employed. Milburn’s £5.8 billion on employment, health and other support would have to be about three times as effective to get 440,000 additional young people into work.

And finally, to number three. The Review finds that the extra spending and savings resulting from the various recommendations balance out after a decade, on the basis that there are £3.6 billion of savings from “welfare reform”, a polite term for benefit cuts achieved through restricted eligibility, lower levels and/or shorter award lengths.

Make no mistake, these are the savings from cuts not from extra employment. And for those worried they are not tough enough, note that this is equivalent to half of the estimated £7.1 billion youth health and disability benefit bill in 2036-37 (in 2026-27 prices). And these reforms won’t just affect young people that are NEET: almost two-thirds of PIP recipients aged 16-24-years are in education or employment for example, many of whom could lose large amounts of support.

But alongside that (very important) debate about winners and losers, there are other radical aspects of Milburn’s vision for the benefit system. The Review recommends localising large parts of the system (a new local Health and Disability Fund, for instance); the introduction of far greater discretion and simultaneous loss of statutory entitlements for young people whose health conditions are not deemed severe or long-standing; and the creation of a separate system for young people which will mean cliff edges galore when young people turn 18 and then again when they turn 25.
A system that pays for itself should not be an end in itself

In all, then, Milburn has proposed £5.8 billion of investment, £3.6 billion of benefit cuts, and believes that after a decade, higher youth employment will also save the state £2.4 billion more. Fiscal neutrality will be achieved!

But the Review also shows the extent to which public spending has been increasingly skewed to older people over time, with the gap between spending on children and young people versus spending on pensioners widening over the past two decades. In that context, whether or not the recommendations are cost neutral is arguably the wrong test.

What the report has shown today is that moving the dial on NEETs will require wholescale change and investment across the system. As the details are debated (and the recommendations will have to make their way through a White Paper, Budget and a Spending Review next year), that may be the most important lesson we should all take from the Milburn Review.

articles.title: Northern Ireland’s “government in name only” is failing to deliver
articles.standfirst:
Northern Ireland’s “government in name only” is failing to deliver sam.macrory Tue, 17/11/2026 - 20:11 Dominant parties in Northern Ireland don't seem to pay a price for their inability to deliver better outcomes. 4 Comment Jill Rutter Institute for Government Yes Stormont is the home of the Northern Ireland Assembly and Executive, but both government and parliament need to work better in Northern Ireland. Devolution Northern Ireland protocol Sinn Féin Democratic Unionist Party Social Democratic and Labour Party Deputy first minister of Northern Ireland First minister of Northern Ireland Northern Ireland executive
No

The last Conservative government finally persuaded the DUP to re-establish the Executive in February 2024 – two years after it collapsed when the DUP withdrew over the implementation of the then Northern Ireland Protocol. Rishi Sunak had failed to persuade the DUP that the Windsor Framework was sufficient reason to return, and it took almost another year for the DUP to extract enough concessions to agree to go back in. 

Initially it looked as though relations between Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O’Neill and deputy First Minster Emma Little-Pengelly were going well, as the new team launched with a spirit of optimism, common purpose and a willingness to get to grips with deep-seated policy problems. But initial progress has since stalled and relations have deteriorated to such an extent that the DUP are now refusing to join joint activities with the First Minister. This left Northern Ireland with no political representation at the prime minister’s recent National Economic Council with the leaders of the devolved governments. 

But a bigger problem is what Sam McBride of the Belfast Telegraph termed “government in name only” at our webinar on Northern Ireland. Decisions are not being made. The much poorer performance of the health service in Northern Ireland than in the other parts of the UK is still not being addressed, despite years of reports detailing how it needs to be rationalised. The NI Executive is rejecting the latest bail out offer from Westminster – and refuses to contemplate extra local revenue raising, preferring instead to look to UK taxpayers to underwrite them. They know the UK government usually blinks first and the moral hazard merry-go-round of failing to take tough decisions continues. 

There is a lack of accountability when voting is little affected by delivery 

In theory, Northern Ireland should have politicians capable of facing up to long-term decisions because power sharing means they face minimal electoral jeopardy. Indeed, identity voting reduces the electoral penalty for poor performance. But so far there is no evidence that the dominant parties pay a price for their inability to deliver better outcomes in Northern Ireland. 

Sinn Féin have benefited from Michelle O’Neill’s decision to stand with the citizens of the Garvaghy Road in opposition to the controversial Drumcree march, even if the DUP’s response has hamstrung the Executive. A recent LucidTalk poll put the party at an impressive 28 per cent, despite the other main nationalist party, the SDLP, being seen to have been making a good fist of Opposition. The incentives to play to the base will only increase as the next elections approach.

On the other hand, accountability may finally be catching up with the DUP, who are shedding votes to a reenergised UUP (who they displaced in the mid-2000s as the principal unionist party) on one side and to the even harder line TUV (Traditional Unionist Voice) on the other. That same poll showed the three unionist parties all in the lowish teens, with the UUP just edging ahead. Advocacy of Brexit, failure to deliver in government and the move from insurgent to party of government all seem to be catching up, and the battle over Assembly seats is hotting up for next May.

Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset should reduce the tension over the Windsor Framework

Any search for stability is also dependent on decisions in Westminster over relations wit the EU. The move for GB to dynamically align with EU sanitary and phytosanitary rules, expected to be signed off, should reduce the divergence between NI – still following most single market rules –and the rest of the UK. If Andy Burnham aims to go further when he sets out his options, the differences would diminish – though so too would any “best of both worlds” advantage. But if the Conservatives or Reform UK looked like approaching government, Northern Ireland would be forced yet again to address the consequences of a breakdown in UK-EU relations over their desire to leave the ECHR. It is far from clear any Executive could cope with those pressures. 

Northern Ireland needs its institutions to work better

The Good Friday Agreement set up institutions (with slight modifications since) designed for power-sharing arrangements, but both government and parliament need to work better in Northern Ireland. In our webinar, David Sterling, the former head of the Northern Ireland Civil Service, pointed to the possibility of the three smaller parties going into opposition when the next Executive is formed. Ann Watt explained what Pivotal, Northern Ireland’s independent policy think tank, would be looking at in their new project on possible reforms to make Stormont more effective. Andy Burnham has hinted the government is looking at that too. And Ulster University’s Deirdre Heenan asked (somewhat plaintively) what level of divergence in public service standards between different parts of the UK a responsible government in Westminster could really tolerate – a great issue to throw back at a prime minister whose big idea is devolution. 

Whatever his answer, Andy Burnham will, at least, face scrutiny for his decisions. For now, Northern Ireland’s politicians seem to keep getting away without making any.

articles.title: US Bifurcation, aging, and job growth are shaping the metro consumer outlook
articles.standfirst: Although AI-related investment has been a major driver of US growth over the past year, consumer spending remains the backbone of the economy. Identifying which households, spending categories, and locations are powering spending is crucial to pinpointing opportunities for B2C companies.
paragraphs: Household spending power has become more concentrated over time

Although AI-related investment has been a major driver of US growth over the past year, consumer spending remains the backbone of the economy. Identifying which households, spending categories, and locations are powering spending is crucial to pinpointing opportunities for B2C companies.

Spending has become more reliant on high-income, asset-rich households, buoyed by equity and housing wealth, while lower-income households have struggled. This bifurcation has likely been heightened by the inflation shock from the US-Israel war with Iran and will continue to influence spending going forward.

Another trend that will shape spending is the aging of the population. As seniors gradually take up a greater share of the population, where they live and what they buy will matter more for spending growth.

Although high-income metros (e.g., San Jose) and retiree hotspots (e.g., The Villages) feature toward the top of our medium-term spending growth rankings, many of the top performers are still those with the strongest job growth prospects (e.g., Austin), most of which are located in the Sun Belt. By contrast, several Northeast and Midwest metros are forecast to lag, hindered by sluggish employment and population prospects, and in some cases, exposure to the spike in the price of essentials.

Slower-growing but large metros should not be dismissed as offering limited opportunities. The sheer size of cities like Chicago means that lower growth rates can still translate into huge spending level gains.
We expect discretionary categories (e.g., recreation and culture) and health to record the fastest growth over the medium term, supported by high-income households and seniors, respectively.

articles.title: London’s safeguarded wharves demand and capacity research
articles.standfirst: Commissioned by the Greater London Authority, this Oxford Economics research forecasts the wharf capacity London will need to 2050. It finds a potential shortfall, with construction materials demand alone exceeding capacity by 622,000 tonnes, and shows that where capacity sits matters as much as how much
paragraphs: London’s safeguarded wharves play a vital role in keeping the capital supplied with the materials and goods it needs, while helping to take freight off congested roads and reduce transport emissions. But with pressure growing to release riverside land for housing and other development, how much wharf capacity will London need in the decades ahead? Commissioned by the Greater London Authority (GLA), this research by Oxford Economics examines the freight handled by London’s safeguarded wharves, identifies the factors driving future demand and forecasts the capacity required to 2050.

Drawing on ten years of freight data from the Port of London Authority, forecasts of industrial demand and interviews with wharf operators, the research provides a detailed picture of how the market could evolve. It examines seven commodity groups, from construction materials and agricultural bulks to metals, petroleum products and waste, and considers how demand will vary across the North East, South East and West regions of the Thames. The findings point to a potential capacity shortfall by 2050, with demand for construction materials alone forecast to exceed available capacity by 622,000 tonnes. The analysis also highlights important differences between regions, suggesting that the location of future capacity could be just as important as its overall level.

The findings have important implications for the future of London’s riverside infrastructure and its ambitions for growth. They highlight the need to consider not just how much wharf capacity the capital requires, but where it is located, which commodities it can handle and how efficiently it is used. The report also explores the uncertainties surrounding future demand and capacity, including the impact of major infrastructure projects, wharf closures and changing river connectivity. Together, the analysis provides an evidence base to inform decisions about the future safeguarding of London’s wharves and the role of the Thames in supporting a growing, more sustainable city.

Andy Logan leads our Consultancy offer on different industries for clients. He undertakes studies forecasting the demand for company’s products, analysing the drivers of different industries growth, and assessing the size of different markets and industries. He also investigates the competitive pressures and opportunities facing industries now and in the future. Another area, where he has a keen interest is in studies assessing the demand and supply of labour for different industries and occupations, identifying potential skill shortages and implications for migration.
He has worked with clients in most industries, and in many countries of the world.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Andy worked in a variety of economist roles at the Bank of England for 15 years. His research focused on the labour market, commodity and producer prices, UK trade flows, and the performance of UK banks. He holds an MSc. and BA. degrees from the universities of London and Leicester.

Emily is a Senior Economist on the Industry team where she supports bespoke industry projects in areas such as renewable energy, construction and insurance. She is also involved in other projects like economic impact studies.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Emily worked for 5 years as a government economist for the UK Civil Service, working in the Department for International Trade (DIT) and the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS). In DIT she worked on assessing the socio-economic impact of Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and Freeports. She also worked in a crisis covid-19 analytical team, providing supply chain analysis and reporting of critical goods to ministers. In BEIS, she used economic analysis to develop policy positions for manufactured goods for both Free Trade Agreements, the Northern Ireland Protocol and the UK's Global Tariff Schedule. Emily holds a Bsc in Economics from the University of St Andrews.

articles.title: The Economic Importance of Motorcycles to Europe
articles.standfirst: In 2024, motorcycle-related activity supported €35.1 billion in GDP, 481,600 jobs and €20.6 billion in tax revenues across the EU and the UK. This study shows how manufacturing, sales, repairs and events ripple through supply chains, and how trade barriers and competition shape Europe’s global position. It also models how more motorcycle commuting could cut travel time, costs and CO₂ emissions.
paragraphs: A Report for the European Association of Motorcycle Manufacturers (ACEM)

In 2024, motorcycle-related activity supported an estimated €35.1 billion in GDP, 481,600 jobs and €20.6 billion in tax revenues across the EU and the UK. These figures capture the sector’s own operations, its supply chains and the wider spending it supports, including spending by employees and visitors attending motorcycle events.

The analysis covers motorcycle manufacturing, sales and repairs, as well as accessories, sports and promotional events. Drawing on official statistics, industry data and economic modelling, it traces how these activities support businesses across the economy. For every €1 of GDP generated directly by the sector, a further €2.30 was supported elsewhere.

International trade is another important part of the picture. Around half of EU motorcycle and parts production was exported in 2024. The report examines Europe’s position in global markets and how trade barriers, growing competition and regulatory complexity affect the industry’s opportunities to invest and expand.

The study also explores how motorcycle use can reduce commuting times, operating costs, emissions and demand for urban space. Around 6.4 million people across the EU and the UK already commute by motorcycle. Under a modelled scenario in which 5% of car commuters switched to motorcycles, the report estimates potential annual savings of 28 million days of commuting time and 2.6 million tonnes of CO₂. It also considers how motorcycles can complement public transport and other modes within urban mobility plans.
Associate Director of Economic Consulting, Continental Europe

Stefan Gorgels is Associate Director for economic consulting services in Continental Europe, focusing on economic impact analysis and econometric analysis. He has a strong academic background in economics and extensive experience in managing consulting and research projects for national and international clients.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Stefan was a manager at DIW Econ - the consulting arm of the German Institute for Economic Research - where he managed economic consulting and research projects for a wide range of clients, including companies, industry associations, German government ministries and the European Commission.
Stefan Gorgels holds a B.Sc. in Economics from Maastricht University, an M.Sc. in Economics from the Barcelona Graduate School of Economics and a Ph.D. in Economics from New York University.

During her time there, Johanna led several high-profile projects assessing the economic impact of different industries and institutions, as well as projects addressing socioeconomic and environmental issues. Johanna holds an M.Sc. in Economics and Management from Leibniz University Hannover.

articles.title: Concrete’s role in meeting housing and infrastructure demand to 2050
articles.standfirst: Our new research for the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA) explores how global megatrends are reshaping infrastructure demand and highlights the critical role of cement and concrete in supporting economic development, improving living standards and building a more sustainable future.
paragraphs: Our new research for the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA) explores how global megatrends are reshaping infrastructure demand and highlights the critical role of cement and concrete in supporting economic development, improving living standards and building a more sustainable future.
The world is entering a period of unprecedented demand for infrastructure and housing.

Our latest research forecasts that global construction activity will increase by more than 70% by 2050, reaching US$16.6 trillion annually, up from US$9.7 trillion in 2025. Emerging economies across Asia, Africa and the Middle East will be major engines of growth. Delivering these assets will create substantial opportunities across the construction industry.

However, infrastructure need does not automatically nor quickly translate into funded projects. Capacity constraints and financing pressures can slow delivery, while expanding materials supply requires capital and long lead times. This creates a difficult investment decision: committing too early risks underused capacity, while waiting too long can mean supply is unable to respond when projects proceed.

For investors, infrastructure owners and policymakers alike, this means that understanding when and where this growth will occur, and the barriers to delivering it, is essential to planning ahead and capturing the opportunity.
The report identifies five interconnected forces that are driving the next generation of infrastructure investment.

The practical implication is that companies need to understand which sectors will expand, how quickly projects can proceed and whether their capabilities match the work coming through. Policymakers and asset owners need to anticipate where competing demands will stretch delivery capacity.
Cement and concrete sit at the centre of this outlook. Concrete’s durability, scalability and local availability make it essential to delivering the infrastructure underpinning modern economies.

Our research estimates that annual concrete demand from key infrastructure sectors will reach around 20 billion tonnes by 2050, demonstrating the scale of future opportunities for construction materials producers and suppliers. Transport sectors (roads, and rail and ports) stand out with faster demand growth than other sectors. Nevertheless, the utilities sector remains a large source of demand in absolute terms.

The report also highlights the important contributions the cement and concrete industry make beyond its physical applications. Importantly, these include its contributions to regional economic development and industrial capacity, as well as its crucial role in supporting the transition to a lower-carbon economy through resilience and whole-life asset performance.

The outlook presents a substantial opportunity, but meeting infrastructure needs will require more than expanding production. As the report details, growing infrastructure investment will need to meet increasingly demanding expectations for affordability, resilience and sustainability.

Innovation in materials, construction methods and circular economy practices will be essential in improving delivery. Clearer and more credible project pipelines and procurement arrangements can give suppliers greater confidence to invest. The opportunity is to deliver more infrastructure and economic value per tonne of concrete, per unit of carbon and per worker.

Understanding where demand is emerging, what could constrain delivery and how requirements are changing will help organisations make better decisions about the capacity, capabilities and assets needed over the coming decades.

The full Oxford Economics report exploring the global megatrends, economic evidence and strategic implications for infrastructure investment and the cement and concrete industry is available here. Head of Construction & Infrastructure Consulting, OE Australia

Adrian has over 23 years of economic analysis and consulting experience with Oxford Economics Australia, focusing on the infrastructure, building, maintenance and mining industries. Adrian has undertaken a wide range of consultancy projects for the public and private sector based on his detailed understanding of construction, mining and maintenance markets, their drivers and outlooks, the range of organisations operating in this space and the issues they face.

This work includes deeper industry liaison, contractor and competitive analysis, pipeline analysis, demand and cost escalation forecasting, and industry capacity and capability projects for the public and private sector. He is the lead author of major reports but also undertakes briefings and workshops for senior management, board members and industry associations, leads in-depth stakeholder consultation, and facilitates and chairs roundtables between government and industry.

articles.title: Washington Can Start Delivering on Affordability by Rejecting Trump’s Tariffs
articles.standfirst: This new Congress will need to address the existing policies hurting affordability, prepare for Social Security insolvency in 2032, and build a regulatory environment that allows American dynamism to flourish.
paragraphs: Voters in the last two election cycles have clearly shown that they care about the cost of living. In response to the inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin following the COVID-19 pandemic, voters handed the Democratic party a significant setback and put Republicans in charge of the House, Senate, and White House. And, after two years of decisions from Washington that have driven up prices at the gas pump, the grocery store, and the assembly line, voters have again rejected unaffordable policies.

Indeed, polling from August revealed that Americans want their costs to fall more than they want additional handouts or carveouts through the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. code. By a 20-point margin, respondents said they want the government to focus more on lowering costs rather than boosting wages.

Newly elected members of the House and the Senate shouldn’t ignore them. But next year, with the looming debt ceiling expiration and Democrats’ long list of spending priorities, they’ll be tempted to return to a tax and spend agenda. If history is any indication, it just won’t deliver the affordability Americans desire.

articles.title: IRS Filing Data Show Higher Refunds and More Itemizers Following OBBBA
articles.standfirst: New IRS data for tax year 2025 shows how tax refunds and taxes owed at filing time changed under the new tax breaks enacted as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
paragraphs: New IRS data for taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. year 2025 shows how tax refunds and taxes owed at filing time changed under the new tax breaks enacted as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

The OBBBA changed several provisions of the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source code, but some of the largest changes for tax year 2025 were the creation of several deductions: for tip income, overtime, senior citizens, and auto-loan interest paid. The standard deductionThe standard deduction reduces a taxpayer’s taxable income by a set amount determined by the government. Taxpayers who take the standard deduction cannot also itemize their deductions; it serves as an alternative. was larger ($15,750 for single filers and $31,500 for joint), as was the child tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly. (up $2,200 per child), and the itemized deductionItemized deductions allow individuals to subtract designated expenses from their taxable income and can be claimed in lieu of the standard deduction. Itemized deductions include those for state and local taxes, charitable contributions, and mortgage interest. An estimated 13.7 percent of filers itemized in 2019, most being high-income taxpayers. for state and local taxes paid (SALT, which was increased from $10,000 to $40,000).

Unfortunately, the data update does not provide any new information on the new OBBBA provisions. While we can analyze how refunds and taxes due at filing time changed across filers, we cannot analyze the uptake or usage of the new provisions themselves.

Most of the tax relief from the new OBBBA changes occurred during the filing season, as taxpayers either owed less to the IRS than they would have paid otherwise, or received larger refunds. We can compare this year’s filing season data, which covers through July 30, 2026, to last year’s filing season data through the same week, to analyze how the filing seasons changed.

The total amount of tax owed at filing time fell by 8 percent year over year, while the number of taxpayers owing a balance dropped more sharply by 21.3 percent. For tax year 2024, 40.6 million returns paid nearly $236 billion at filing time. For tax year 2025, far fewer returns, 31.9 million, paid a lower $216 billion at filing time.

While taxes owed went down, tax refunds went up, growing nearly 21 percent year over year. In tax year 2024, 100 million tax returns received $329 billion back from overpayments, and that rose to 109.6 million tax returns receiving nearly $397 billion back from overpayments for tax year 2025. The average refund size increased by $328 from $3,290 in tax year 2024 to $3,617 in tax year 2025.

The biggest percentage decrease in taxes owed at filing was experienced by filers making between $50,000 to $100,000 (falling 23.1 percent year over year), while the biggest percentage increase in total refunds received was experienced by filers making between $200,000 to $500,000 (rising 54.6 percent year over year).

Last filing season, 132.9 million filers took the standard deduction (90.9 percent) compared to nearly 12.7 million who itemized (8.7 percent). This filing season, more taxpayers itemized. About 130.7 million filers took the standard deduction (88.6 percent) while 16.2 million itemized (11.0 percent).

This 27.9-percent increase in itemization is a predictable consequence of one of OBBBA’s biggest individual tax changes for tax year 2025: the increase in the state and local tax (SALT) deductionThe state and local tax (SALT) deduction permits taxpayers who itemize when filing federal taxes to deduct certain taxes paid to state and local governments. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) capped it at $10,000 per year, consisting of property taxes plus state income or sales taxes, but not both. cap.

Taxpayers claimed $253.3 billion in SALT deductions through mid-July, compared to just $96.3 billion in deductions at the same point for tax year 2024 filings. Taxpayers with adjusted gross incomeFor individuals, gross income is the total of all income received from any source before taxes or deductions. It includes wages, salaries, tips, interest, dividends, capital gains, rental income, alimony, pensions, and other forms of income. For businesses, gross income (or gross profit) is the sum of total receipts or sales minus the cost of goods sold (COGS)—the direct costs of producing goods (AGI) between $200,000 and $500,000 increased SALT claims the most relative to last year. OBBBA increased the SALT cap from $10,000 to $40,000 for tax year 2025, but the higher SALT cap phases out for taxpayers earning more than $500,000.

The IRS data through July 30, 2026, provide no new information on claims for the “no tax on” provisions from OBBBA: the deductions for tips, overtime, auto loan interest, and the enhanced senior deduction.

The Treasury Department published a press release in June 2026 with limited data on how many taxpayers claimed the new deductions and the average deduction size. The IRS filing season data are more granular and allow researchers to examine total deductions claimed by AGI cohort.

Absent a filing season update, policymakers, researchers, and the public may have to wait until annual IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) data are released for tax year 2025 for more data on the “no tax on” provisions. Given IRS data lags, those data may not be published until 2028—the year these temporary provisions are scheduled to expire.

While we know that the OBBBA delivered tax relief for individual taxpayers—as millions fewer taxpayers owed at filing time and refunds were up—we still lack detailed data on how filers utilized the new provisions.

articles.title: Forecasting The Future Of Forecasting
articles.standfirst: Can AI forecast the economy better than models we already have? That depends. In one comparison for near-term UK CPI, a simple linear model has proven hard to beat, as...
paragraphs: NIESR and the University of Birmingham recently hosted a workshop on Economic Forecasting with AI. With presentations of five papers and a round table discussion, we learned how LLMs and other machine learning methods are potentially pushing the boundaries of macroeconomic forecasting. But a key question remains: what do we value more, accuracy or the mechanisms behind our forecasts? In this Monday Interview, Senior Economist Peter Dixon asks Associate Economist Charlotte O’Leary which methods are being applied, what AI is capable of and where the limitations lie.

That depends. In one comparison for near-term UK CPI, a simple linear model has proven hard to beat, as past inflation plus seasonality carries most of the signal. Our participants explained that this is because inflation is endogenous: when central banks see pressure building, they act, so the pressure never fully shows up, leaving inflation best predicted by its own past. Furthermore, data is scarce: monthly figures provide only a few hundred observations; even using CPI sub-components does not come anywhere near generating the millions of observations that methods like neural networks (NNs) require, so their extra flexibility tends to fit noise.

LLM forecasts, on the other hand, are nearly perfect. Or so they would seem. One of the presenters stripped the dates, series name and country from their dataset, and found that the LLM beat linear forecasts in almost every horizon. This, however, stems from a contamination problem. The LLM was able to name the exact quarter on two-thirds of occasions, and within one year 98.8 per cent of the time. When explicitly told to disregard all prior knowledge of the economy, the only thing that changed was its verbal compliance, its behaviour, did not. Hence, for now, out-of-sample testing is very limited.

Three places stood out. The first is measurement. Claude Opus 5 coded 56 years of Federal Reserve Beige Books, around 6,400 reports, into a usable time series in under one day for roughly $300 (~£225). Added to a standard real-time recession model, this text index managed to date business-cycle turning points more accurately, cutting the average timing error from about three months to under two.

The second is scenario analysis. A multi-recurrent neural network trained on UK data produced policy responses that depended on the state of the economy. The same combination of monetary easing had an estimated effect on GDP some four to five times larger in late 2008 than in 2015. The model also identified significant interactions between interest-rate and liquidity shocks, suggesting that their combined effects cannot simply be inferred by adding their individual impacts. Interestingly, the results also point to the importance of broad money in explaining economic developments during periods of financial stress. This resonates with the literature on Divisia monetary aggregates, which suggests that appropriately weighted measures of money can provide useful information about exchange-rate movements, particularly when conventional interest-rate indicators become less informative.

A third area of interest is simulation. Bank of England researchers used an LLM to create synthetic respondents to the Inflation Attitudes Survey. These matched average perceptions during the 2022-23 spike and offer a cheap laboratory for testing communication and survey design.

Discipline. Results need contamination testing, to ensure a clear separation between training, validation and test data. Moreover, researchers need to be open about the software frameworks, model specifications and implementation choices since these can give materially different results. In one paper, for example, the same Long Short-Term Memory neural network architecture gave noticeably different forecast errors when run using the Python frameworks TensorFlow and PyTorch. Reproducibility is a serious concern when using stochastic models, and when vendors change their default LLMs without notice this can seriously impact on the results. One participant noted that such a switch resulted in a loss of access to the temperature setting that their method relied on. One potential thing that could help is using locally hosted models with known training cut-offs and testing their forecasts only on the periods that follow.

This brings us back to the issue of accuracy versus mechanisms. For policymakers, the most accurate model is not necessarily the most useful as they need to know why a forecast has changed and what happens if policy changes. It is here that AI still falls short. The neural network’s scenarios are not structurally identified, and LLMs are even further removed from a structural model.

The consensus was, therefore, that the future is hybrid. Machine learning is good at finding nonlinear patterns, which are particularly helpful for events like the GFC, whereas econometrics and structural models impose causal discipline, where human judgement plays a role in interpreting the results. AI thus makes economics more important, not less. One member set out the challenge clearly: AI will have truly advanced when it can explain the reasoning behind its forecasts and produce credible conditional scenarios. We are not there yet.

articles.title: Not All Bipartisan Tax Ideas Are Created Equal
articles.standfirst: Unfortunately, not all bipartisan efforts will make for sound tax reform. Both parties have leaned into the “no tax on” trend in recent years, complicating the tax code and narrowing the US income tax base.
paragraphs: The midterm election results mean that Washington is heading towards another era of divided government, with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress and a Republican still in charge at the White House. While the two parties have plenty of disagreements over taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities., trade, and fiscal policy, there are areas where they might agree and compromise in 2027 and 2028.

Some of these areas could represent meaningful progress on sound tax policy, such as enhancing full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. for multifamily housing construction or improving taxpayer services at the IRS. Congress could also pursue a bipartisan opportunity to roll back some of the economically harmful tariffs the Trump administration has imposed in recent years—or, better yet, reclaim its legislative authority over trade and tariffTariffs are taxes imposed by one country on goods imported from another country. Tariffs are trade barriers that raise prices, reduce available quantities of goods and services for US businesses and consumers, and create an economic burden on foreign exporters. policy.

Unfortunately, not all bipartisan efforts will make for sound tax reform. Both parties have leaned into the “no tax on” trend in recent years, complicating the tax code and narrowing the US income tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.. Lawmakers are also considering new or revived carveouts for specific sectors of the economy, including the film and television industry and clean energy companies.
Below, we review the tax policy items—good and bad—that may attract bipartisan support in next year’s new Congress.

While Republicans have controlled both chambers of Congress and the White House for the past two years, lawmakers in both parties have been hard at work on several bipartisan priorities. Several bills may merit consideration during the “lame duck” session in November and December 2026, including:
In the new session of Congress, beginning on January 3, 2027, lawmakers may have several additional opportunities for bipartisan tax reform:

Several tax ideas have emerged with bipartisan support that would make the tax code more complicated, cost needed revenue, or provide targeted tax carveouts that distort economic activity at the expense of other taxpayers.

The new Congress may have several opportunities to change direction on tax, trade, and fiscal policy over the next two years. Bipartisan cooperation will be the key to unlocking any number of reforms in divided government.

But not all bipartisan tax policy is created equal. Lawmakers should keep the principles for sound tax reform—simplicity, neutrality, transparency, and stability—central when considering new tax policies in 2027.
