Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

articles.title: Bank Taxes in Europe, 2026
articles.standfirst: 13 European OECD countries have implemented financial stability contributions (FSCs), commonly referred to as “bank taxes.” Explore the 2026 data.
paragraphs: The 2007-2008 financial crisis triggered a global debate on whether—and, if so, how— taxation can be used to stabilize the financial sector and generate revenue to partially cover the costs associated with financial crises. The issue has returned to the spotlight since 2023, as banks have benefited from higher interest rates and governments have sought new sources of revenue in the wake of the 2022-23 inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin shock.
Following the financial crisis and the more recent inflation surge, policymakers and international organizations have explored several approaches:
Today’s map shows which European countries implemented financial stability contributions (FSCs), commonly referred to as “bank taxes.”

Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovenia, Sweden, and the United Kingdom all levy bank taxes. Almost all of these countries implemented the levy following the 2007-2008 financial crisis, with Greece (1975) the only exception.

Most countries levy their bank taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. on a measure of liabilities or a measure of assets. However, some countries decided on a different tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.. For example, France taxes the minimum amount of capital necessary to comply with the regulatory requirements.

While bank taxes raise relatively little revenue, they can reduce the sector’s capacity to support lending, investment, and economic activity. Over time, they may also reduce the amount of available capital, limiting banks’ ability to absorb losses and respond to unforeseen financial crises.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.

articles.title: Portland’s Proposed Fair Share Tax Yields Astronomical Tax Burdens
articles.standfirst: As Portland City Council considers the proposed tax increase, they should understand the city’s starting point—as arguably the highest-tax jurisdiction in the entire country—not one of the lowest.
paragraphs: Under the Fair Share Tax, a proposal pending before Portland City Council, some corporations could soon face a 26.2 percent state and local income taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. rate, plus a 1.57 percent gross receipts taxGross receipts taxes are applied to a company’s gross sales, without deductions for a firm’s business expenses, like compensation, costs of goods sold, and overhead costs. Unlike a sales tax, a gross receipts tax is assessed on businesses and applies to transactions at every stage of the production process, leading to tax pyramiding. rate (not accounting for a partial deduction for the cost of labor or cost of goods sold, which will vary by business). For a business with a 7 percent profit margin, that represents a 48.6 percent rate on net income just from state and local income and gross receipts taxes, before even considering federal taxes or local property taxes. But one of the proposal’s co-sponsors, City Councilor Mitch Green (D-District 4), argues the proposed tax shouldn’t be a concern because, he contends, Portland’s current business taxes aren’t actually high.

The Councilor’s proposal would add a multiplier to the existing city business license (income) tax with rates based on CEO compensation ratios, with the highest rate set at 15.6 percent—higher than the highest state corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. of 11.5 percent in New Jersey. This would be in addition to Oregon’s 7.6 percent top state corporate income tax rate, a 2 percent county tax, a 1 percent regional tax, and both city and state gross receipts taxes.

Councilor Green contends that Portland’s current business tax burdens are reasonable and specifically objects to our prior analysis, which finds that Portland has some of the highest business taxes in the country. But can his claim be true? Is it possible that, as his office purports to show, Portland’s business taxes are almost 40 percent lower than Pittsburgh’s and barely a quarter of Seattle’s?

The answer is, of course, no: Portland is a uniquely high-tax jurisdiction, and the calculations the Councilor relies on are deeply flawed. The results raise obvious red flags, such as the fact that the calculations for Seattle yield a 142 percent effective tax rate for a typical business from sales, payroll, and gross receipts taxes alone. Even without considering federal income taxes, local property taxes, or any other taxes, Councilor Green’s comparative tables show a Seattle business paying the entirety of its profits, and then 42 percent more, in state and local taxes. Seattle’s taxes are high, but they aren’t that high.

It’s worth understanding how these calculations went awry, because correcting the errors yields precisely the conclusion that the so-called Fair Share Tax’s sponsor attempts to disprove: Portland’s business taxes are already uniquely high.

Both Portland and the state of Oregon have gross receipts taxes, which are major drivers of the region’s high business tax burdens, though a constellation of state, regional, county, and city income taxes also contribute significantly to the overall tax bill. Oregon does not, however, levy a sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. —one of five states to forgo one. The Councilor’s analysis attempts an “apples-to-apples” comparison by converting other jurisdictions’ taxes into gross receipts tax equivalents, but errs in several respects, nowhere more significantly than in the conversion of general sales taxes into gross receipts tax equivalents.

The Councilor’s FAQ recognizes that sales tax calculations drive the results but fails to recognize that the calculations are gravely in error. After a table comparing Portland to several other jurisdictions, the text reads: “Notice that Portland’s various tax rates sum to a fairly large number, just under Seattle’s. But after converting to the equivalent tax on gross receipts, these rates become very small. Indeed, because Oregon and the jurisdictions therein do not have a sales tax, the actual tax burden is much lower than other cities.”

In Seattle, for instance, sales taxes are estimated to cost businesses 5.93 percent of gross revenue, which is almost 85 percent of the income of a business with 7 percent profit margins. Seattle’s sales taxes alone are estimated to impose as much as 243 percent of the total business tax burden calculated for Portland (2.44 to 2.54 percent of gross revenue), which is clearly mistaken.

The Councilor’s analysis converts sales tax rates into gross receipts equivalents by dividing the general sales tax rate by 1.78 percent, based on a misinterpretation of a paper that estimates 1.78 as the ratio of gross receipts to final consumption. The paper’s estimate is entirely reasonable and is essentially identical to the ratio of US gross output to GDP. It is a ratio of all transactions to consumption and has nothing to do with sales taxes.

Total consumption is not the same as taxable sales. It includes transactions largely excluded from sales tax bases (like healthcare, insurance, groceries, and legal services), and it even includes consumption that does not involve a transaction, like the imputed value of living in one’s own home. And while some business-to-business transactions are taxed, and their costs are at least partially borne by businesses, it’s also clearly mistaken to apply all the cost of sales taxes—a consumer tax—to businesses.

The magnitude of this error can be demonstrated by applying the Councilor’s methodology to sales taxes nationwide. That yields $2.37 trillion in business sales tax burdens in FY 2024, whereas total state and local sales tax collections were about $588 billion, including both consumer and business purchases.

To put this in further context, EY and the Council on State Taxation estimate that businesses paid about $245 billion that year, one-tenth of what Councilor Green’s methodology suggests. Federal corporate income tax collections were $472 billion in FY 2024, making the Councilor’s estimates of businesses’ share of state and local sales tax burdens five times what the federal government collects in corporate income tax revenue.

In other words, the primary reason Portland’s taxes look modest compared with other jurisdictions is that the analysis takes the one major tax Oregon lacks and overstates its burdens by a factor of ten.

The comparison also contains other errors and omissions. It applies Seattle’s Social Housing Tax, which applies only to compensation above $1 million per employee, and its JumpStart Housing Tax, which applies only to larger businesses, to all wages. It lists Pennsylvania’s corporate income tax but drops it from Pittsburgh’s total tax calculation, omits California’s corporate income tax entirely, excludes Oregon’s TriMet employer payroll taxA payroll tax is a tax paid on the wages and salaries of employees to finance social insurance programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Payroll taxes are social insurance taxes that comprise 24.8 percent of combined federal, state, and local government revenue, the second largest source of that combined tax revenue., applies Portland’s Clean Energy Surcharge to all businesses, and disregards deductions under the Oregon CAT. These errors cut both ways, but they indicate a haphazard approach. Property taxes (on real property as well as machinery and equipment), which represent about 34 percent of all state and local taxes paid by businesses, are also omitted, though this omission is acknowledged.

The Councilor’s own analysis yields a 36.3 percent effective rate on a business with 7 percent profit margins from state and local business income and gross receipts taxes alone, even before the new tax, which is astonishingly high. It’s too high, in fact, due to several calculation errors. But the reality is that Portland’s taxes are very high, and the Councilor’s analysis does nothing to contradict that. It merely compares it favorably to vastly inflated rates in other jurisdictions.
These are not just calculation errors. They also flow through into the broader analysis.

The Councilor’s FAQ argues, for instance, that low-margin businesses like grocery store chains will be able to handle an increased tax burden in Portland since the increase is supposedly minuscule compared to “the actual sales taxes in Vancouver, Washington, where there are plenty of grocery stores despite state and local taxes 45 times higher than this ordinance proposes.” Not only does this rely on the previously mentioned miscalculation of sales tax burdens, converting an 8.9 percent sales tax into a 5 percent tax on grocers’ gross receipts—an impossible 250 percent effective rate from sales tax alone, based on the Councilor’s correct identification of grocery store profit margins as about 2 percent—but it misses the fact that Washington, like most states, exempts groceries from the sales tax.

Portland already has anomalously high business taxes, and the proposed tax would make those rates astronomical. Business taxes imposed based on sales into a jurisdiction tend to show up in prices, meaning Portland consumers would bear a substantial share of the increased tax burden, even if large corporations are the ones to remit the tax. Some businesses may find that they can no longer afford to operate in Portland at all, reducing consumer choice and undercutting local employment.
As Portland City Council considers the proposed tax increase, they should understand the city’s starting point—as arguably the highest-tax jurisdiction in the entire country—not one of the lowest.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.
Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: Are We In The ‘Foothills’ Of AI-Driven Growth?
articles.standfirst: It seems we finally have some good economic news to cheer about. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in Q3, making the UK the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7, behind...
paragraphs: It seems we finally have some good economic news to cheer about. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in Q3, making the UK the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7, behind only the US. This was the fastest quarterly growth since the end of 2017 excluding the post-pandemic recovery (although growth at this rate was normal before the pandemic). So, in this post we dig into whether we are seeing the start of an AI-driven growth boom as some in government have claimed, drawing out the implications for the labour market and interest rates as well as the broader economy.

The first place to look for the effect of AI is in the investment needed for its infrastructure. Spending on data centres, servers, semiconductors, connections to the power grid, and the software itself should show up as a boost to investment. In that context, it’s encouraging that investment has been strong in recent quarters – contributing around half of GDP growth in Q3. More compellingly, if we look at the assets that are being invested in – as shown in Figure 1 – it’s ICT equipment and buildings where investment is concentrated. So this picture is at least consistent with a growth bump from AI investment, albeit this is very much circumstantial evidence. It’s also important to stress that the contribution to UK GDP will depend on the extent to which this new infrastructure is imported, and how much is produced at home and in that context, it’s striking that net trade was a drag on GDP in the latest data. This is something that we should expect to continue.

More importantly for a service-based economy like the UK’s, it is AI adoption across knowledge-intensive business services that will start to drive process improvement which will show up in the GDP statistics as higher value added in these sectors. By automating routine tasks, improving research and analytical capabilities, and enabling firms to deliver more output with fewer labour inputs, AI should raise productivity. (As an aside, there are also big measurement challenges around capturing AI – so we should take the latest data with a pinch of salt (for more on this see the 2026 Deane-Stone lecture from the ONS’s James Benford on measuring the effects of AI). In this context, while significant differences in AI adoption remain across sectors, uptake has been on an upward trajectory over the past three years (Figure 2). If the link between AI usage and output growth persists, continued expansion across firms points to more broad-based economic gains in the future.

So, what can the data tell us about the benefits of adopting AI? Again, we don’t have direct evidence, but the signs are good. As Figure 3 shows, the latest pick up in output has come with a boost from growth among a group of industries that are likely to be providing AI services (a definition coined by the Bank of England). Growth in sectors likely to adopt AI – including financial and business services – has also picked up sharply through the course of this year. Together, these sectors account for around three-fifths of the pick up in growth through the course of this year.

Note: AI services encompass SIC 58, SIC 62, and SIC 63, following the Bank of England November 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Early adopters are SIC sections J (excluding AI services), K, and M. Public services are SIC sections O, P, and Q. Source: ONS, NIESR calculations

To be clear, this does not quantify the contribution of AI to growth; rather, it shows that the sectors driving growth this year are precisely those where one would expect AI-related gains to show up first.

Seeing early signs of AI-related activity is particularly encouraging given that there are good reasons to think such gains should emerge slowly. Any company starting to use a new technology may initially see productivity fall given time taken to understand how to use the technology and, for example, make the complementary investments required to realise its potential. This includes significant complementary investments in intangible capital, including redesigning processes, training workers, restructuring the organisation and developing new products and approaches. This means AI may actively reduce measured output and productivity in the near term. But, as firms exploit the technology the gains should become apparent. Academic work for the US that digs into this AI J-curve finds that unmeasured intangible investment associated with computer hardware and software raises so-called total factor productivity. As Robert Solow put it during the ICT boom of the 1990s: “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics”

To put some flesh on the bones of our AI-related inferences, we can look to the ONS Business Insights and Conditions Survey, which has tracked AI adoption across firms since late-2023. Unsurprisingly, the ICT sector leads the pack with 60 per cent of firms confirming their use of AI in the latest vintage, up from 30 per cent in the first. Professional services follow in second place, at two-fifths of firms. At the other end of the scale, fewer than 20 per cent of firms in the hospitality and construction sectors report AI usage. Figure 4 shows that differences in adoption have broadly mapped onto output growth over the past year: not only have AI-intensive sectors led growth, but year-on-year declines in output have been concentrated in sectors with fewer than one in five firms using AI.
Source: Business Insights and Conditions Survey, NIESR calculations

The first thing to say here is that there is a lot more of this to come. One way to look at this is to ask: how far does the AI infrastructure buildout still have to run? A recent Brookings paper tackles this head on, finding that around 57 GW of US data-centre capacity was in place by the middle of this year compared with a pipeline of more than 500 GW. Such estimate should be taken with a healthy pinch of salt – not least because there are good reasons to doubt that all of this capacity will ultimately come on stream. Nonetheless this estimate makes clear that – even in the US – we might only be a tenth of the way through the buildout currently envisaged. To put this in perspective, the work estimates that to deliver this would mean investment of nearly 4 per cent of US GDP in the coming years – way more than was spent during periods of previous general purpose technology rollouts, for example during the railroad, electrification, highway and telecommunications booms.

As we show in simulations from NIESR’s global econometric model NiGEM, published in our recent Economic Outlook, such a scenario is not all good news for the UK, however. There are gains in the form of exports to the US. But, as already mentioned, we are not big players in the data-centre supply chains, so these effects are modest. More importantly, they are likely to come with chunky increases in longer-term interest rates as demand for investment capital globally spirals. Indeed, as set out in our recent Market Anatomy, around a third of the rise in gilt yields since February seems likely to be attributed to the rise in demand from AI investment. If we are only a tenth of the way through the buildout, there will be more upward pressure on interest rates, tightening financial conditions and dampening UK economic activity. An implication of this is that the Chancellor should certainly not bank on a fall in the cost of borrowing providing a substantial boost to the public finances in the near future.

The other potential dark cloud to the silver lining of AI-driven growth could come from the labour market. The context here is the warning issued this week from central banks that AI – among other factors – is leading to lower labour demand, putting downward pressure on hiring. Figure 5 provides some extra evidence here, showing that around one in ten businesses expect AI to reduce their headcount in the future, roughly double the 6 per cent already reporting AI-related reductions. By contrast, only 2 per cent anticipate a positive impact. In short, if we are in the foothills of AI-driven growth, then we are likely also at the very beginning of the labour market churn that comes with it.
Note: Figure refers to all businesses excluding those with 0-9 employed. Source: Business Insights and Conditions Survey, NIESR calculations

It’s become widely accepted that the UK is in a rut when it comes to growth. And there is a broad political consensus that this is the key policy challenge we face. Recent data do not change that fact and writing a blog about 0.7 per cent quarterly growth should itself provide a reality check about the position we find ourselves in. Nonetheless, the casual nihilism about our growth prospects should at least be tempered by these tentative signs that new technology can deliver growth. Nurturing these green shoots should certainly be a priority for policymakers – this is definitely not the moment to declare victory. But we must also think hard about what AI-driven growth comes with. If we are moving into a future of higher interest rates and rising unemployment, the challenge is not just to avoid choking off the ‘green shoots’ of growth, it is also how we learn to live with what the growth of the future comes with.

articles.title: You’ve got mail (finally): your Milburn cram sheet inside
articles.standfirst:
Afternoon all, If you’re reading this then we have survived not only doomsday but also an email free Friday – hope you enjoyed it. And avoiding the end of the world is not the only forecast to be improved upon this week. GDP grew 0.7 per cent in Q3, putting our year-to-date growth second in … Continued
The post You’ve got mail (finally): your Milburn cram sheet inside appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: If you’re reading this then we have survived not only doomsday but also an email free Friday – hope you enjoyed it.

And avoiding the end of the world is not the only forecast to be improved upon this week. GDP grew 0.7 per cent in Q3, putting our year-to-date growth second in the G7, behind only the US. Sadly, household incomes aren’t following – while real GDP per person has grown by 2.6% over the past two years, real household disposable income per person has been essentially flat.

Next week, there’ll be only one story in town as the Milburn review’s final report drops. Our mini-Milburn special has reads on young people’s experiences of work, a cheat sheet to help you cram, and a Chart of the Week showing how the UK’s balance between benefits and employment support stacks up against our OECD neighbours.

Plus – know an audio-visual whizz looking for a public policy role? We’re hiring a maternity cover Communications Manager who would (among other things) have the joy of working with me on our High Resolution podcast. Do share if you know a good candidate.

Catch-22-year-olds. In the last year, more than half of young jobseekers heard nothing back from any of their job applications. Have employers given up on the young? Not according to this Reed survey of 2,000 UK firms: 73 per cent say hiring early-career talent is a high priority. Nonetheless, there’s concern there about the skills and qualities they think young people are lacking: understanding the working environment (34 per cent), communication (33 per cent) and reliability (32 per cent). This brings us back to the age old ‘experience paradox’, where young people need experience to get a job, but a job to get experience. Employers’ preferred fix is (record scratch, freeze frame) a tax cut. 72 per cent say scrapping employer NICs for under-25s would boost hiring. Scroll to Something for the weekend to find out what a more cost-effective measure would look like.

Mental maths. Economics research on mental health has ballooned, and this sweeping review takes stock. The costs are large: stress, depression and anxiety accounted for 55 per cent of UK working days lost to work-related ill health in 2024-25, and research from Denmark found that people diagnosed with depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia earn 31 to 73 per cent less than their siblings. But the authors argue rising caseloads don’t necessarily mean worsening mental health: UK survey data show distress among 16-19 year olds edging up only modestly since 2008 (from 9 to 11 out of 36 for boys), far less than diagnoses suggest. But that view is contested. Peter Fonagy’s review for the Government found the rise in common mental disorders among English adults (from 16 to 23 per cent since 1993) “cannot be explained by greater awareness alone”. Either way, economic shocks take a real toll. In Brazil, parental job loss raised children’s chances of mental health diagnosis by 6 percentage points. Support helps: in New York, guaranteeing legal representation to families facing eviction cut new mental health diagnoses among children by 7 per cent.

Parent trap? Making people spend time applying for jobs is a huge part of the Universal Credit system – but does work search conditionality actually get people into work? New research from our friends at the IFS assesses the Lone Parent Obligation in search of an answer. Between 2008 and 2012, the age of youngest child at which single parents had to look for work was cut from 16 to five. Employment rose by 4.4 percentage points – although the typical job paid just £8,000 a year, yielding little tax. Meanwhile, disability benefit claims rose, and among children already struggling at school, GCSE results fell and absence rose. Almost 90 per cent of the gross saving disappeared, as the cuts incurred other fiscal costs in the form of alternative benefits and lower future tax payments. So conditionality got some additional parents into work, but the savings were much smaller than expected and there were downsides for the kids.

Remote control. Next week’s focus may be young people, but remote working could be part of the answer to boosting employment for other groups. Treating the pandemic jump in UK home working as a natural experiment, this blog compares occupations where it took off with those where it didn’t, and finds a boost to the employment rates of older and physically disabled workers. Each one-point rise in home working lifted full-time employment by nearly 1 per cent for disabled workers and 0.4 per cent for 50-64-year-olds. Home working explained roughly three-quarters of the rise in full-time disabled employment. Given we need to boost the employment rates of old and young, we should be cautious about rowing back from all of the pandemic flexibilities. Might need outlook to work though…
The long-awaited Milburn review lands next week – here’s key facts for you ahead of the publication (more on our Substack):

Alan Milburn wants you to know that for every £1 spent on employment support (training, job search help, wage subsidies) for young people, £25 is spent on their benefits. His review will aim to shift that balance and it looks like he’ll suggest doing so by both cutting benefits and increasing employment support. But how do other countries compare? For Chart of the week, we’ve plotted benefit spending (the x axis) against spending on employment support (the y axis) as a proportion of GDP across OECD countries. Important caveat: to get internationally comparable data we look at all ages here, not just young people. If you’re in the bottom left quadrant, you’re not spending a lot (hello America), but anyone in the top right quadrant is a big spender on both fronts (hello Denmark). The coloured lines show you where different ratios sit: if you’re on the green line (and only a handful of countries – including Sweden, Denmark and Korea – exceed it) then you’re spending five times as much on benefits as on employment support. The latest available UK data puts us comfortably on the red line meaning we spend twenty times as much on benefits as we do on employment support. It is low employment support spending, rather than high benefit spending, that is causing our high ratio. Hopefully the balance of Alan’s recommendations will reflect that.

articles.title: Senator Moreno’s 100% Federal Tax on Data Center Incentives Would Usurp Sound State Sales Tax Policies
articles.standfirst: Senator Bernie Moreno’s proposed RECLAIM Act (S. 5689) would impose a 100 percent tax on state and local “incentives” for large AI data centers, including state sales tax exemptions for servers and chips.
paragraphs: Sen. Bernie Moreno’s (R-OH) RECLAIM Act (S. 5689) would impose a 100 percent federal taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. on any state or local “incentive” received by a large AI data center. By our reading, the proposal would “top up” the sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. on data center servers and chips in the states that exempt them by imposing a federal tax equal to the exemption amount. We expect that, generally, the state would respond by imposing the tax itself, thereby collecting the revenue the federal government otherwise would collect (the “top up” logic is thus very similar to global minimum taxation).

This “top up” tax on exemptions usurps sound state sales tax policies. State sales tax exemptions for data center inputs are not subsidies or incentives: a sales tax is meant to fall on final consumption, and thus provisions that remove business inputs like servers from the base are integral to a well-designed sales tax. We estimate at least 31 states would be affected by the proposal. (Some states, like Ohio, have paused new exemptions; we therefore count them as already taxing these investments, though exemptions already granted would still be affected by the proposal.)

The proposal would impose a tax “equal to 100 percent of the amount of any prohibited State or local incentive received by the data center operator.” The tax would apply only to “covered data centers,” which are certain large AI-focused facilities. The bill also has a federal component, which would affect data centers’ federal tax treatment.

A face-value reading of the bill suggests its effects may reach far beyond state sales tax exemptions. Indeed, as written, the bill could turn the income tax on a covered data center into something closer to a tax on gross receipts. Prohibited state or local incentives include “any state or local grant, loan, loan guarantee, cooperative agreement, tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly. or deduction, exclusion, exemption, abatement” in addition to other state or local incentives. This broad language could include denying deductions for business inputs, such as the usual deductions for wages and capital depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco. If this is not the policy intent, the proposal should make clear which types of deductions or exemptions are not covered by the policy.

In public statements, the bill’s sponsor appears clear about his intent. “Taxpayers will not subsidize data centers, period,” Sen. Moreno said in the press release announcing the bill, which further says the bill would tax “any state or local grant or tax exemptionA tax exemption excludes certain income, revenue, or even taxpayers from tax altogether. For example, nonprofits that fulfill certain requirements are granted tax-exempt status by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), preventing them from having to pay income tax.” that hyperscalers use for data centers. Before introducing the bill, Sen. Moreno had singled out a sales tax exemption on equipment, calling the exemption a “$4.5 million subsidy.”
The bill thus counts exempting business equipment from the sales tax as a special incentive, and if enacted, it would top up the sales tax in many states that provide these exemptions.

Our analysis relies on a recent state-by-state survey for the National Taxpayers Union by Tax Foundation’s Jared Walczak, whose classification shows 31 states exempt data center equipment only through conditional or discretionary programs. These are the clearest cases, since these policies are clearly an “exemption . . . for the development or commercial operations of a covered data center,” as described in the proposal.

Two states we assess as less certain, because their policies are structured closer to a by-right exemption, which makes it unclear whether they would be interpreted as incentives under the proposed law.

The remaining 18 jurisdictions would face no top-up (at least on new projects). California, New Jersey, and 11 others (including the District of Columbia) already tax data center equipment at full rates, so there is no exemption to tax. Oregon and four other states have no sales tax at all.

A retail sales tax is meant to fall on final consumption once. A well-designed sales tax exempts all intermediate business inputs. If the sales tax is instead imposed on business inputs, the tax is built into the price of whatever those inputs produce and then taxed again at the next sale, which economists call tax pyramidingTax pyramiding occurs when the same final good or service is taxed multiple times along the production process. This yields vastly different effective tax rates depending on the length of the supply chain and disproportionately harms low-margin firms. Gross receipts taxes are a prime example of tax pyramiding in action.. Tax neutrality is lost, as the total sales tax rate depends on the structure of the supply chain. Tax transparency is lost, as the tax the consumer ultimately pays varies across goods in unobservable ways.

Data center equipment is a business input just like any other. Most states already accept the principle for factories, with 41 exempting manufacturing machinery and equipment by right. What makes data center exemptions look like favors is their legal form only: in most states, data center equipment escapes the sales tax only through special policies. That legal form is irrelevant to the economic point that these exemptions should be applied broadly on business inputs.

Indeed, Tax Foundation’s latest State Tax Competitiveness Index scores states more highly when they exempt data center equipment from sales tax, calling such purchases “a business-to-business transaction that should rightly be exempted along with other business inputs.” By focusing on legal form, the RECLAIM proposal would counteract states’ attempts to adopt sound sales tax treatment for these business inputs.

As an elegant economic analogy, a sales tax on equipment is a uniform negative investment tax credit: while an investment tax credit at rate k cuts the price of a machine by k percent, a sales tax at rate s raises it by s percent. In 1976, the economist Emil Sunley showed that a uniform investment tax credit is not neutral across asset lives: it favors short-lived assets, which get the credit much more frequently—every time they are repurchased after wearing out or becoming obsolete—than long-lived assets. A uniform sales tax is the mirror image. Consequently, the sales tax can translate into a very high effective tax burden on short-lived assets.

This is especially relevant for data centers. The chips used in data centers wear out or become obsolete very quickly. A 7.5 percent sales tax might sound like a modest tax rate, but when it’s paid again every few years, it translates into a very high effective rate.

In 1978, the economist David Bradford, extending Sunley’s work, derived the pre-tax return (net of depreciation) an asset must earn when it receives an investment tax credit. We apply his formula (page 291, equation 9) to study the sales tax by treating it as a negative investment tax credit and convert the estimate into a marginal effective tax rate.

To illustrate, at a typical sales tax rate of 7.5 percent, a 5 percent real required return, and a short asset life (an annual depreciation rate of one-third, corresponding to replacement every 3 to 6 years assuming that a third to a seventh of the asset value remains at retirement, respectively), the sales tax alone amounts to a marginal effective tax rate of about 37 percent on the return on a chip. For comparison, CBO estimates that federal taxes impose a marginal effective tax rate of about 4 percent on new investment in equipment in 2026, now that the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act allows full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs.; under prior law, with 20 percent bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs., the rate would have been about 16 percent.

The RECLAIM proposal is broader than a top-up tax for state sales tax exemptions. For example, it also tops up data center property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. abatements, which are in many cases non-neutral tax subsidies that are difficult to justify. Whether the federal government should intervene in such cases of non-neutral special treatment is a question of fiscal federalism. The state sales tax exemptions on data center equipment inputs are, however, not special tax incentives, and usurping them would be overturning sound tax policy.

Dr. Richard DiSalvo’s research focuses on how artificial intelligence will affect the tax system, on the taxation of business investment (including real estate), and on new taxes aimed at the technology sector. He previously served as a senior economist at the Joint Economic Committee of the US Congress and at the New York City Independent Budget Office, and he taught at Princeton University’s School of Public and International Affairs.

articles.title: Senator Kelly’s Plan to “Make AI Work for Americans” Is Funded by Three Poorly Designed Taxes
articles.standfirst: If lawmakers want to pay for new government spending, better approaches include broadening the income tax base, reforming the corporate tax, or taxing consumption.
paragraphs: Motivated by concerns that artificial intelligence (AI) adoption may lead to substantial and rapid changes in labor markets, Sen. Mark Kelly’s (D-AZ) proposed Make AI Work for Americans Act includes federal funding for several labor insurance and worker training programs. AI’s impact on the labor market remains debated, but some observers project that many workers will need to switch jobs.

To fund the additional spending, the proposal includes three new taxes: a digital advertising taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities., a bit tax, and an excess profits tax.

Sen. Kelly should be commended for attempting to pay for additional spending. With the federal government’s debt burden and interest on the debt at near-record levels and projected to increase further, policymakers should not propose new spending without identifying ways to pay for it. However, Sen. Kelly’s proposal may end up increasing deficits, since his proposal spends gross revenues but does not account for expected declines in other taxes, such as income and payroll taxes.

Each of the three taxes would take effect on January 1, 2027. We estimate that without any changes in behavior or economic growth in response to the tax, in the first year, the digital ad tax would raise $15.8 billion, the excess profits tax $6.5 billion, and the bit tax only $23.2 million.

Ten-year projections are challenging, since the growth rates of the affected tax bases are highly uncertain. Moreover, we have not modeled behavioral responses, including avoidance behavior, nor macroeconomic effects, and so our estimates overstate the revenue that would be raised. We estimate that over 10 years, the three taxes could raise a combined $380 billion, but this should be seen as a ceiling because it does not incorporate any feedback effects.

All three tax proposals are unsound. The digital ad tax is a gross receipts taxGross receipts taxes are applied to a company’s gross sales, without deductions for a firm’s business expenses, like compensation, costs of goods sold, and overhead costs. Unlike a sales tax, a gross receipts tax is assessed on businesses and applies to transactions at every stage of the production process, leading to tax pyramiding. that can be charged several times along the advertising chain; the bit tax may constitute a growing share of the cost of using AI and serve as a brake on technological development; and the excess profits tax may fall largely on one taxpayer.
If lawmakers want to pay for new spending, broad-based taxes—preferably on consumption—would do so at a far lower economic cost.
While Sen. Kelly may be the first lawmaker to package these three taxes together, none of them are new ideas. In fact, all have historical precedents at the federal, state, or international levels.

Digital ad taxes have been most popular at the state level. Maryland, Illinois, and Utah have all enacted digital ad taxes in recent years, though Maryland’s Tax Court struck down the state’s digital ad tax in August in a highly followed case. (The state of Maryland has appealed the Tax Court ruling.)

The bit tax has a longer history than digital ad taxes. The 1990s-era bit tax would amount to $80 per gigabyte (GB) today—arguably not the intention of its proponents, but an indicator that taxes that seem reasonable in one era can be completely impractical in the next.

Sen. Kelly’s tax amounts to $0.11 per GB. That may seem small today; chatting with an AI platform may only use one to five megabytes per hour, or 0.001 to 0.005 GB. In a decade or two, though, as AI platforms become more capable, the tax may become prohibitively large.

Excess profits taxes have an even longer and more well-worn history. Federal policymakers have often proposed an excess or “windfall” profits tax on oil and gas producers when energy prices rise. As Tax Foundation’s Alex Muresianu wrote in May 2026:

Several analyses of the 1980 Windfall Profits Tax have found it reduced domestic production and increased reliance on imports. A Congressional Research Service paper found that the tax reduced domestic oil production by between 1.2 and 8.0 percent, and increased reliance on foreign oil by between 3 percent and 13 percent between 1980 and 1988 (when the tax was eventually repealed).

The 1980s tax also brought in a fraction of the revenue projected, $80 billion actual compared to $393 billion projected. Sen. Kelly’s excess profits tax would have a narrow base—potentially, almost entirely one company—making it especially precarious.

Sound tax policy is neutral, simple, transparent, and stable. Kelly’s proposed taxes are narrowly targeted, complicated to administer, and rest on tax bases that can change wildly due to growth, technological change, or tax avoidance.

The digital ad tax is a gross-based tax on a business input. The US has opposed similar digital service taxes abroad. These types of taxes distort production, can pyramid through supply chains, encourage vertical integration and other inefficient restructuring, and fall hardest on low-margin businesses.

Academics and policymakers have expressed concerns that AI is built on the uncompensated work of human creators—authors and artists, for example. A closely related economic concern is that AI chatbots will divert traffic and reduce monetization opportunities, leading to an underproduction of human-created content. Since many creators ultimately derive revenues from digital ads, a digital ad tax would be partially borne by these content creators. In short, a tax introduced in a bill to cushion the effect of AI on workers would ironically be partially borne by workers threatened by AI.

The structure of the bit tax is similar to the 1990s versions, which were proposed as “dollars per unit of data” taxes. If adopted, these would have raised little revenue at first, but would have quickly become an astronomical tax burden as internet traffic doubled annually and costs collapsed. If AI use takes off in a way similar to the internet—and AI costs per unit collapse—the proposed bit tax would quickly turn into a substantial burden on the adoption of this technology.

Changing the bit tax to an ad valorem tax, such as in the token tax proposal by Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX), would largely fix the problem of an escalating burden. However, it would still distort production away from the use of AI models and toward less efficient input choices. The bit tax would also add significant tax complexity, especially in policing technical avoidance strategies, including service offshoring.

The excess profits tax applies a high rate on a narrow base. The tax would likely be paid by few firms—our analysis suggests that in 2027, almost all of the tax would be paid by one firm. Singling out certain firms for additional tax based on arbitrary financial conditions and industry participation is non-neutral tax policy. The tax could also be avoided through firm restructuring or financial engineering, ultimately causing economic distortions while raising much less revenue than our estimates. Finally, insofar as it is paid, the tax captures the payoff to successful innovation at a high rate while the costs were deducted earlier at a lower rate; that intertemporally asymmetric treatment would deter innovation.

While Sen. Kelly differs from other lawmakers in attempting to pay for new spending under his Make AI Work for Americans Act, his proposed AI taxes miss the mark. The digital ad tax is inefficient and complex, potentially targeting revenue that has little or nothing to do with AI. The bit tax may not stand the test of time, especially as consumer- and business-facing technologies grow and data usage increases. And the excess profits tax suffers from a very narrow base, meaning actions of just one or a few companies could render the tax moot.

Lawmakers seeking to pay for new spending—or reduce unsustainable federal deficits and debt—would do better to broaden the income tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates., reform the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax., or tax consumption instead of income. Several of these options and more are featured in Tax Foundation’s Options for Reforming America’s Tax Code 3.0.

We estimate the revenue effects of the three proposed taxes without capturing any behavioral feedback. We multiply the projected tax base by the proposed tax rate. Because the estimates do not account for the responses of taxpayers—including tax avoidance—they should be treated as illustrative.

Our revenue estimate for the digital ad tax starts with the Interactive Advertising Bureau’s (IAB) revenue report, which puts 2025 US internet ad revenue at $294.6 billion. The vast majority of ad revenues (92 percent) came from the top 25 companies, which serves as our base for the digital ad tax; five percent of that is about $13.6 billion. We checked this by producing a separate estimate from the SEC filings of public companies, which yields a similar estimate of about $14 billion. Both approaches likely understate the tax base (due to considerations of gross vs. net ad revenue, and ad revenue missing from our SEC filing search), so we start with the $14 billion estimate and increase it by 20 percent. Grown at the IAB’s average annual growth rate for 2021 to 2025 (about 12 percent), revenue is about $21.1 billion in 2027, or $15.8 billion after the 25 percent income and payroll taxA payroll tax is a tax paid on the wages and salaries of employees to finance social insurance programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Payroll taxes are social insurance taxes that comprise 24.8 percent of combined federal, state, and local government revenue, the second largest source of that combined tax revenue. offset, and about $278 billion over 10 years after the offset.

Our revenue estimate for the bit tax begins with reported AI image generation from OpenAI and Google, which total about 225 billion images per year. We assume images are the main source of the tax in the near term; switching to other mediums, such as video or streaming video games, is baked into assumed growth rates. At about 2.5 MB per image, that is about $62 million of tax before the exemption. We assume that all consumers would fall below the 10 GB exemption amount and be exempt, but that businesses would often have usage above the exemption amount and be taxed. About a quarter of Google’s token usage is through its API. We take this as a proxy for the business usage share, so we assume a quarter of usage would fall above the 10 GB per-user exemption. We assume usage doubles annually, as internet traffic did for about a decade, yielding about $30.9 million in 2027, or about $23.2 million after the 25 percent income and payroll tax offset. Continuing to assume an annual doubling, the tax would raise $24 billion over 10 years after the offset.

We assess that the excess profits tax affects only a handful of companies. Using SEC filings, we estimated taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. for publicly traded companies and identified those above the 40 percent of receipts threshold. Private AI labs appear to be loss-making, though a few private firms may owe tax we do not capture. We estimate the tax would collect about $7.6 billion in 2027 (almost all from one company) under a narrow—and our preferred—reading of the bill, and about $11 billion under a broad one. We apply a 13.6 percent offset for this tax, rather than the 25 percent offset for the other two taxes. This 13.6 percent offset is the ratio of corporate tax receipts 2027-2036 over corporate taxable income from CBO’s February 2026 projections. This offset is justified under the assumption that the excess profits tax is deductible against the corporate income tax and therefore reduces corporate income tax receipts. Applying this offset reduces 2027 revenue to $6.5 billion. Grown at four percent annually, in line with nominal GDP, it raises about $79 billion over 10 years, after the offset.

Dr. Richard DiSalvo’s research focuses on how artificial intelligence will affect the tax system, on the taxation of business investment (including real estate), and on new taxes aimed at the technology sector. He previously served as a senior economist at the Joint Economic Committee of the US Congress and at the New York City Independent Budget Office, and he taught at Princeton University’s School of Public and International Affairs.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

articles.title: Digital Services Taxes in the United Kingdom and Belgium Create Large Economic Harms per Unit of Revenue
articles.standfirst: Evaluations of digital services taxes in the UK and Belgium show tiny annual revenue collections relative to the total treasury revenue raised by the government. Our dynamic modeling shows digital services taxes reduce both labor and capital supply, lowering investment, GDP, and labor compensation.
paragraphs: Digital services taxes (DSTs) are taxes on gross revenues that large companies earn from certain digital activities. Most cover revenue from digital advertising or other intermediation, though designs vary. The most economically significant DSTs are typically levied by European countries and aimed at very large software companies, most of which are based in the United States.

A significant flaw in DSTs is nonneutrality, which creates economic inefficiencies. The nonneutrality comes from discrimination by industry or business model, implicit discrimination through thresholds or carveouts that define the list of in-scope payers, and the gross receipts base.

As a result of these qualities, DSTs are comparatively harmful, relative to other taxes, per unit of revenue raised. This paper will discuss the economic theory undergirding this claim and examine two specific examples.

One of these is Belgium; Tax Foundation Europe most recently made this argument in testimony before the Belgian Finance and Budget Committee on August 31, 2026.[1] The testimony described several drawbacks of the Belgian DST proposal and employed both quantitative and qualitative analyses.

This paper will recap the Belgian analysis and extend its methods to the United Kingdom’s DST as well. Then it will discuss the foundations, methods, and limitations of quantitative modeling in Tax Foundation’s DST work.

Tax Foundation’s quantitative and qualitative analyses are consonant with each other; they come from the same roots in key public finance works studying tax neutrality, and generally support neutrality as a pillar of sound tax policy. However, the quantitative and qualitative analyses serve different roles. In some cases, quantitative work makes effects more understandable and tangible—and in other cases, qualitative analysis might help describe effects for which quantitative modeling methods do not exist.

The results below concern the effects of DSTs on the supply of labor and capital—and ultimately, the gross domestic product—of both Belgium and the UK. The model results are simplifications in many respects, but the simplifications are for practical reasons. More robust or complex modeling of DSTs may even strengthen the case against them.

For Belgium, Tax Foundation Europe’s testimony included modeling of a tax proposal that is not explicitly named as a DST, but mirrors one in intent and economic properties. Though DSTs have typically been assessed as a tax on gross receipts, the Belgian proposal adds an extra step. Rather than taxing gross receipts directly, it calculates an imputed income from a static deemed profitability percentage. This deemed profitability is assumed, not demonstrated via accounting. Then, the policy taxes a percentage of that deemed income. This intermediate step does not, however, change the form of the tax to something notably different from a DST; gross receipts multiplied by two percentages (the deemed profitability, then the tax rate) can reduce mathematically to gross receipts multiplied by one percentage, as the written testimony shows.
The DST proposal is by any measure a very small tax relative to the total size of the Belgian economy, so all the effects described are modest. However, the overall results are not favorable.

The DST is modeled as a proportional tax on gross output, with its corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. deductibility feature partially reducing its burden on capital. The model finds a reduction in GDP and total labor compensation coming from two different sources: roughly, people working slightly less efficiently, and people working slightly less overall.

The DST slightly reduces the overall returns to work, in part by simply reducing the after-tax purchasing power for Belgian consumers, and in part by reducing the overall productivity of Belgian work, including by discouraging investment by Belgian firms. These effects combine to reduce after-tax returns to work, and in turn, the modeled workers are more likely to engage in non-market activities.

The revenue modeling of Belgium’s tax borrows revenue-estimating techniques from the already-existing French DST, while the economic modeling is based on neoclassical production functions, a number of long-established public finance results, and a few critical economic elasticities used consistently throughout Tax Foundation’s work.[2]
The United Kingdom’s digital services tax raised £808 million in tax year 2024/25. As for Belgium, this tax is modelled with similar effects as a proportional output tax.
The DST is deductible from corporate income tax according to British law.[3] A non-deductible DST would have a stronger negative effect on output.

Its less sizable effect on output is largely explained by Britain’s taxing labor more moderately at the margin than Belgium. The DST adds a small wedge to the tax on labor, and labor supply responds to the after-tax wage.

Because additional labor compensation is already taxed at about 35.9 percent in Britain against 65.0 percent in Belgium (or 49 and 84 percent after consumption taxes) for a single worker earning the country’s average wage, the same proportional wedge adds a larger hit to what a Belgian worker keeps, so labor supply and total output contract more strongly.[4]

Digital services taxes present some significant challenges for dynamic policy modeling, including by Tax Foundation. Tax Foundation has often used qualitative critiques of digital services taxes, such as highlighting their complexity, nonneutrality, and pyramiding. However, these properties—those that make DSTs poor tax policy—often are the same properties that make them more challenging to model. The overall result is that our modeling of the harms of DSTs is in many respects conservative or understated, because the data, the elasticities, or the computations required to fully show the harms of DSTs are impractical or unavailable.

Digital services taxes create several different economic deadweight losses. Some are common among tax policies, and others are present only in taxes with particular structural defects. Below, we will discuss the different possible deadweight losses and the challenges they present for modeling.

One common effect of many taxes, no matter how well-structured, is that they raise the relative value of activities outside of formal markets: for example, for leisure and socialization rather than market work used to pay for market consumption.

Non-market activities are still valuable activities, and ones we would expect even in the absence of any tax burden. But these become more attractive relative to the alternative if the alternative is taxed. A tax on market activity encourages people to forgo some of those market activities and instead do non-market activities, a decision that would not have been freely made in the absence of tax.

This is a moderate but well-studied effect, quantifiable through a labor supply elasticity. Tax Foundation Europe’s modeling here uses 0.2 for these purposes, meaning that a 1 percent reduction in real after-tax compensation results in 0.2 percent less work effort.[5]

Importantly, this tax burden holds in general equilibrium regardless of whether one considers the tax “passed on” to the consumer or “passed back” to the worker. In either case, it reduces the value of market activity after a complete closed loop from earning money to spending it on consumption.

Additionally, this tax burden is integrated across different types of taxes. For example, taxes on worker income interact with excise taxes, creating a greater combined impact than the sum of the two impacts calculated independently. The “Harberger triangles” representing deadweight loss vary with the square of the tax rate, so calculating excise or commodity taxes independently of the underlying general tax regime will understate their burden.[6]

Tax Foundation integrates consumption and excise taxes together with labor taxes to form the overall tax burden on market activity; this interaction, which is more severe in Belgium than in the UK, is the primary factor explaining why Belgium’s tax incurs a greater impact per unit of revenue raised.

A uniform tax on consumption distorts only the margin described above, between nonmarket or “leisure” activities and market activities. A nonneutral consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible.—one that falls on some goods but not others—adds a second form of distortion. This distortion lies within the realm of market activities, rather than on the market-nonmarket margin. When consumption taxation is nonneutral, people have an incentive to shift consumption from heavily taxed goods or services to lightly taxed goods or services. The incremental amount of change that consumers make only in the presence of the uneven tax regime reduces consumer surplus.

There are some noted exceptions to the optimality of neutral taxation, often concerning internalizing externalities, or approximating a user feeA user fee is a charge imposed by the government for the primary purpose of covering the cost of providing a service, directly raising funds from the people who benefit from the particular public good or service being provided. A user fee is not a tax, though some taxes may be labeled as user fees or closely resemble them. for a government service. However, the benchmark of neutrality shown by Anthony Atkinson and Joseph Stiglitz (1976) remains the default frame of reference.[7]

Unfortunately, adequately representing this inefficiency at scale and in detail exceeds the scope of data availability, researched elasticities, and general model-building capacity, whether at Tax Foundation or elsewhere. It would in principle require a vast catalog of goods and services in the economy, along with elasticities of substitution between each of them. (An elasticity of substitution measures the amount that consumers shift their budget from one activity to another possible alternative as a result of a tax.)

Consumers may, for example, largely shift to close substitutes that roughly resemble the forgone option, but also shift some spending to weaker substitutes and unrelated goods that are substantially different from the forgone option. The complexity of such calculations can expand polynomially with the quantity of potential spending options, as each one has a relationship with the others. Furthermore, the deadweight loss comes in part from lost consumer surplus—the difference between what a consumer paid and what a consumer hypothetically would have been willing to pay for the good received. This quantity is not easily derived; economists can typically only infer that it has been reduced in the tax-motivated consumption change.

A tax on gross receipts, like a DST, with no crediting or deductibility system to avert double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income., further extends the nonneutrality problems of differential consumption taxation, while also producing a few new issues as well.

The problems of gross receipts taxes are especially salient for multi-firm chains where the same value-added ends up an explicit or implicit cost of revenue for several in-scope businesses throughout the chain.

Economists have understood the drawbacks of gross receipts taxation for decades, and advised against taxing intermediate inputs.[8] Unfortunately, the taxation of intermediate inputs is relatively common in DST design, and a specialized chain of diverse software providers can quickly find itself paying a DST multiple times on the same activity, as Tax Foundation has recently shown with stylized examples.[9]

Some of the drawbacks of nonneutrality from pyramiding are virtually the same as those described above, but amplified: there is an even greater range and variety of effective tax rates across different patterns of economic activity. The incentive for buyers to substitute away from multiply taxed goods and services becomes even stronger. Indeed, as deadweight losses tend to vary with the square of tax rates rather than linearly, double taxation is more than doubly distortive.

But there are also a few extra distortions from taxing business inputs that are not quite fully captured in models of nonneutral consumption taxes. Business inputs impact production allocation, not just consumption allocation.

These concepts are related, but not entirely the same. In either case, the economy produces, for tax reasons, something less than what would maximally make consumers happy. In a closed economy that consumes its own output, these are arguably the same effect, and the difference is driven by who makes the tax-motivated decision.

But in an open economy, like the typical European economy, a nonneutral tax on business inputs can artificially change the profitability of different production processes for export industries, introducing a new kind of inefficiency that would not be present in any kind of consumption tax system. Roughly, companies in a DST-levying country may choose to export less valuable services purely to avert the DST on the production inputs of the otherwise more lucrative export.

Difficulties in quantifying these DST drawbacks, of course, are even more substantial. The model of the different consumption options and substitution elasticities between them would have to extend to the intermediate inputs and model different production options for different firms, with changes in decision-making coming from the taxes on intermediate inputs. These inefficiencies are real and relatively simple to show in a stylized example with only a handful of products, where a consumer or producer shifts to a less-desirable or less-profitable product, simply for tax reasons. But these effects are impossible to quantify systematically in a large dynamic economy with many goods and unknown preferences.

Taxes on business inputs may, in some cases, impact investment. The effect that will be described below is arguably an extension of the production efficiency concerns described above. But it deserves special discussion because of the role of capital in typical models of macroeconomic growth, including our own.

An economy’s available productive capacity is often shown as a function of factors including labor and capital; the original form, developed by Paul Douglas and Charles Cobb, is commonly taught in early textbooks.[10] (A production function may include other terms or residuals as well; an efficient or inefficient tax code driving efficient or inefficient production allocation would likely be called a form of “total factor productivity” in a typical production function.)

If a DST contributes to the cost of a capital good, it may have an impact on the cost of capital in business decisions, and ultimately, the time structure of production: not just what or how to produce in any given period, but how much to create capital goods—such as equipment, software, or ideas—that assist in production in future periods. Tax the process that creates capital goods, and one ultimately gets fewer of them.

Tariffs in the US have spurred a high-quality discussion of taxes on business inputs and their impact on investment behavior in the United States. A seminal framework for an after-tax user cost of capital, developed by Robert Hall and Dale Jorgenson, undergirds much of this work.[11] Calculations published by Tax Foundation in July 2026 show that even under a corporate income tax system with full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs.—which eliminates the tax wedgeBroadly speaking, a tax wedge is the difference between the pre-tax price or return and after-tax price or return. For labor income, it is the difference between the total labor costs to the employer and the corresponding net take-home pay of the employee. on marginal investments in the basic Hall-Jorgenson model—a distortive tax on business inputs can still impact the user cost of capital.[12] A more detailed extension of these insights was published by American Enterprise Institute and Tax Policy Center scholars later the same year.[13]

Though this research was aimed at a US audience and US policy, much of this discussion would apply to European DSTs as well. DSTs have some similar properties to tariffs, as discussed explicitly in Tax Foundation research.[14] And they too can constitute an unrebated tax wedge on the creation of a capital good, for example, when software or physical capital are created with goods or labor located through online search or digital marketplaces.

Overall, there is good reason to model gross-receipts taxes generally, and DSTs specifically, as falling in part on the capital production factor, not just the labor factor. This explains the modeling choices made by Tax Foundation for DSTs; they are modeled to fall on gross output, not consumption, but the incidence on capital is reduced in part by corporate income tax deductibility, where applicable.

Overall, our modeling of the economic effects of DSTs may be conservative. Though it captures the extensive margin of economic production versus leisure, and the margin of investment versus consumption, both of which are important, it does not capture the significant substitutions within those categories that come from inefficient differential taxation of production and consumption. In other words, our modeling does not fully capture the insights that key pillars of public finance literature like Diamond-Mirrlees and Atkinson-Stiglitz might have to offer on DSTs.
This modeling conservatism is attributable primarily to the limitations of data, the economic literature, and calculation, not doubt in the overall value of tax neutrality.

Moving beyond pure models of taxes and economic decision-making behavior to capture messy real-world realities would be further outside the scope of Tax Foundation modeling, but it merits some mention: Tax Foundation testimony on the Belgian DST proposal notes legal disputes, relabeling disputes, treaty obligations, and administrative complexity as additional drawbacks of DSTs. These legal, compliance, and enforcement issues are outside of the quantitative modeling tradition from which Tax Foundation operates, but economic insight can be applied to them. Disputes over taxes occupy productive resources, such as skilled professionals, who could better be put to use in more productive parts of the economy.
Overall, even though the modeling results above show significant drawbacks from DSTs, they do not quantify all of the drawbacks. A more complete assessment could be even more negative.
