States are not allowed to pay interest costs directly from the state’s unemployment trust fund. Twenty-eight states and the District of Columbia have these taxes on the books, though they fall under several names, such as advance interest tax and bond assessment tax (Colorado) and temporary emergency assessment tax (Delaware).

Reserve Taxes. Reserve taxes are levied on employers, to be deposited in a reserve fund separate from the unemployment trust fund. Since the fund is separate, the interest earned on it is often used to create other funds for purposes such as job training and paying the costs of the reserve tax’s collection. Four states have these taxes on the books: Idaho and Iowa (reserve tax), Nebraska (state UI tax), and North Carolina (reserve fund tax).

Surtaxes for UI Administration or Non-UI Purposes. Thirty-one states and the District of Columbia levy surtaxes on employers, usually to fund administration but sometimes for job training or special improvements in technology. They are often deposited in a fund outside of the state’s unemployment fund. Some of the names they go by are the state training and employment program (Arkansas), reemployment service fund tax (New York), wage security tax (Oregon), and investment in South Dakota future fee (South Dakota).

Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI). A handful of states—California, Hawaii, New Jersey, New York, and Rhode Island—have established a temporary disability insurance (TDI) program that augments the UI program by extending benefits to those unable to work because of sickness or injury. No separate tax funds these programs; the money comes right out of the states’ unemployment funds. Because the balance of the funds triggers various taxes, the TDIs are included as a negative factor in the calculation of this subindex.

Voluntary Contributions. Twenty-seven states allow businesses to make voluntary contributions to the unemployment trust fund. In most cases, these contributions are rewarded with a lower rate schedule, often saving the business more money in taxes than was paid through the contribution. The Index rewards states that allow voluntary contributions because firms are able to pay when they can best afford to instead of when they are struggling. This provision helps to mitigate the nonneutralities of the UI tax.

Time Period to Qualify for Experience Rating. Newly formed businesses, naturally, do not qualify for an experience rating because they have no significant employment history on which to base the rating. Federal rules stipulate that states can levy a “new employer” rate for one to three years, but no less than one year. From a neutrality perspective, however, this new employer rate is nonneutral in almost all cases since the rate is higher than the lowest rate schedule. The longer this rate is in effect, the worse the nonneutrality. As such, the Index rewards states with the minimum one year required to earn an experience rating and penalizes states that require the full three years.

Rather, they are the result of stock appreciation due to corporate activity such as increasing retained earnings, increasing capital investments, or issuing dividends. Stock appreciation becomes taxable realized capital gains when the stock is sold by the holder.

[28] States have sought to limit this sales tax competition by levying a “use tax” on goods purchased out of state and brought into the state, typically at the same rate as the sales tax. Few consumers comply with use tax obligations.
[29] Timothy J. Bartik, “Small Business Start-Ups in the United States: Estimates of the Effects of Characteristics of States,” Southern Economic Journal (April 1989): 1004-1018.

[30] For example, in early 1993, Intel Corporation was considering California, New Mexico, and four other states as the site of a new billion-dollar factory. California was the only one of the six states that levied its sales tax on machinery and equipment, a tax that would have cost Intel roughly $80 million. As Intel’s Bob Perlman explained in testimony before a committee of the California state legislature, “There are two ways California’s not going to get the $80 million: with the factory or without it.” California would not repeal the tax on machinery and equipment; New Mexico got the plant.

[31] Sales taxes, which are ideally levied only on sales to final users, are a form of consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible.. Consumption taxes that are levied instead at each stage of production are known as value-added taxes (VAT) and are popular internationally. Theoretically, a VAT can avoid the economically damaging tax pyramiding effect. The VAT has never gained wide acceptance in the US, and only two states (Michigan and New Hampshire) have even attempted a VAT-like tax.
[32] Alaska does authorize local governments to levy their own sales taxes, however, which is reflected in the state’s sales tax component score.

[33] The average local option sales tax rate is calculated as an average of local statutory rates, weighted by population. See Abir Mandal, “State and Local Sales Tax Rates, Midyear 2026,” Tax Foundation, Jul. 6, 2026.
[34] J. Moody and Scott and Wendy P. Warcholik. “How Tax Competition Affects Cross-Border Sales of Beer in the United States,” Tax Foundation, March 2004.
[35] See Adam Hoffer, “Cigarette Taxes and Cigarette Smuggling by State, 2022,” Tax Foundation, Nov. 26, 2024.
[36] See Ulrik Boesen, “Tax Foundation Comments on Maryland’s Digital Advertising Tax Regulations,” Tax Foundation, Nov. 10, 2021.
[37] See Timothy J. Besley and Harvey S. Rosen, “Sales Taxes and Prices: An Empirical Analysis,” NBER Working Paper No. 6667, July 1998.
[39] Jared Walczak, “State Sales Tax Breadth and Reliance, Fiscal Year 2022,” Tax Foundation, Jul. 23, 2024, https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/sales-tax-revenue-reliance-breadth/.
[40] See Matt Moon, “How Do Americans Feel about Taxes Today?,” Tax Foundation, Apr. 8, 2009.

[41] Andrew Phillips and Caroline Sallee, “Total State and Local Business Taxes: State-by-State Estimates for Fiscal Year 2024,” Council on State Taxation (COST) with Ernst and Young LLP and the State Tax Research Institute, December 2025.

[42] Stephen T. Mark, Therese J. McGuire, and Leslie E. Papke, “The influence of taxes on employment and population growth: Evidence from the Washington, DC metropolitan area,” National Tax Journal 53:1 (2000): 105-123.

[43] Timothy J. Bartik, “Business Location Decisions in the United States: Estimates of the Effects of Unionization, Taxes, and Other Characteristics of States,” Journal of Business and Economics Statistics 3:1 (January 1985): 14-22.
[44] Timothy J. Bartik, “Small Business Start-Ups in the United States: Estimates of the Effects of Characteristics of States,” Southern Economic Journal (April 1989): 1004-1018.

[45] Tangible personal property taxes can also affect business decisions and are now part of the new Index. For a comprehensive review of these taxes and reform recommendations, see Jared Walczak, “Tangible Personal Property De Minimis Exemptions by State, 2024,” Tax Foundation, Mar. 5, 2024, and Joyce Errecart, Ed Gerrish, and Scott Drenkard, “States Moving Away from Taxes on Tangible Personal Property,” Tax Foundation, Oct. 4, 2012.
[46] See Joseph Johns, “Tangible Personal Property De Minimis Exemptions by State, 2025,” Tax Foundation, Apr. 29, 2025, https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/tangible-personal-property-taxes/.
[47] Some states, like Kentucky, are often considered not to impose an intangible property tax but continue to levy a low millage on financial deposits.

[48] For a summary of the effects of the estate tax on business, see Congressional Budget Office, “Effects of the Federal Estate Tax on Farms and Small Businesses,” July 2005. For a summary of the estate tax in general, see David Block and Scott Drenkard, “The Estate Tax: Even Worse Than Republicans Say,” Tax Foundation, Sep. 4, 2012.
[49] See Joseph Bishop-Henchman, “Unemployment Insurance Taxes: Options for Program Design and Insolvent Trust Funds,” Tax Foundation, Oct. 17, 2011.

[50] According to the US Department of Labor, “Average High Cost Multiple (AHCM) value uses actual trust fund balances as of 12/31/2025 and estimated wages for CY2025. This measure compares the state trust fund balance to the average of the three highest years of benefit payments.” The full report is available at https://oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/docs/trustFundSolvReport2026.pdf.

[51] Alaska is the only state to use the payroll experience method. This method does not use benefit payments in the formula but instead the variation in an employer’s payroll from quarter to quarter. This is a violation of tax neutrality since any decision by the employer or employee that would affect payroll may trigger higher UI tax rates.

Katherine has testified before legislators in seven states and DC and has authored or coauthored tax reform options guides on Kansas, Kentucky, Nebraska, and Wisconsin. Her work has been cited in The New York Times, The Economist, USA TODAY, Forbes, Bloomberg, the Associated Press, and numerous state media outlets across the country.

articles.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
articles.standfirst: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt...
paragraphs: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt interest) is forecast to improve by 3 per cent of GDP over the next 5 years, from a deficit of 1.5 per cent in 2025-26 to a surplus of the same size by 2030-31. The IMF singled the UK out this month as one of the few advanced economies where action on the deficit has been taken decisively.

The trouble is that few people outside the Fund expect this squeeze to be delivered. Most of the tightening is scheduled for 2029-30, which could well be the run-up to the next election. This is the familiar pattern of promising fiscal prudence tomorrow, what Charlie Bean once called the “Augustinian approach” to fiscal policy.

None of this is a criticism of the OBR. Its remit requires it to forecast on the basis of the government’s stated policy, so what it publishes is a forecast conditional on the plan being implemented. That is a useful thing, but it’s also not a best guess of what is likely to happen because the stated policies are themselves unlikely to be unbiased.

In this week’s blog, I set out what I think is a credible path for the UK’s public finances. I use the historical record of borrowing forecasts against outturns to discipline how the fiscal plans are likely to be revised in the years ahead. On this path, the primary balance improves but stays in deficit over the next five years. The current budget is in deficit by around £30 billion in 2029-30, so the fiscal rules are missed by a significant margin. The debt ratio rises throughout the forecast, reaching 101 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. My guess is that this is closer to the market’s expectation than the official forecast, and it may help resolve the puzzle of why the UK’s borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7 despite the IMF’s praise.

Figure 1 explains why. It reconstructs one the OBR published in its 2025 Fiscal Risks and Sustainability Report, comparing the OBR’s forecasts for the debt ratio since 2010 with what actually happened. The forecasts are hump-shaped: on average, they show the debt ratio deteriorating for two years and then improving over the later years of the forecast. The outturns are linear: the debt ratio just keeps rising with the forecast horizon. The improvement that every forecast has pencilled in for years three to five has never arrived.
Public sector net debt (as % of GDP), OBR forecasts compared to outturns, 2010-present

What explains this? I can think of three candidate explanations. The first is bad luck: the economy has been hit by a series of adverse shocks over this period. The second is a planning fallacy: planners tend to be overly optimistic about their ability to deliver. The third is that the plans are built to satisfy the fiscal rules and were never meant to be delivered.

To tell these apart, we follow the approach of Beetsma, Giuliodori and Wierts, in a 2009 paper they provocatively titled “Planning to cheat: EU fiscal policy in real time”. The idea in a nutshell is to take the OBR’s forecast errors for borrowing and split them into a part due to government decisions on taxes and spending and a part due to everything else, above all macroeconomic news. Helpfully, the OBR’s own publications make this possible in a way that would be more difficult in most other countries. We use two of its datasets: every official forecast, so we know what was planned each year; and every revision between one forecast and the next, which the OBR itself splits into the effect of policy decisions announced in the interval, classification changes, and underlying changes to the economy and debt interest. The policy estimates include both the direct cost of measures and their indirect effects on the forecast through the economy, such as higher receipts when spending raises GDP.

For each forecast and each year of its horizon, we add up the policy revisions made in every later forecast for that year. Since each forecast reports its revisions relative to the one before, the sum is the total effect on that year’s borrowing of all the decisions taken after the plan was published. An example hopefully helps fix the intuition. Take the March 2021 forecast for borrowing in 2023-24. The six forecasts that followed attributed revisions to 2023-24 of £11bn, £1bn, £31bn, £19bn, £8bn and £0.3bn to policy, £70bn in all or 2.5 per cent of GDP. Over the same period, the economic outlook improved, which is why the outturn missed the forecast by only 1.4 per cent of GDP in the end. In other words, the method measures how much each plan was undone by later decisions, and differentiates this from how much the economy helped or hurt.

Table 1 shows the results, with the forecasts split into those made between June 2010 and March 2014 and those made from December 2014 onwards (excluding Covid years). In the first period, borrowing came in about 1 per cent of GDP above plan by year 3, and this entirely reflected macro news. Evidently, this was a period where the coalition government held to its plans and the economy fell short. In the second, borrowing has come in fully 2 per cent of GDP above plan by year 3, and three-quarters of that is accounted for by policy decisions taken after the forecast was made. These decisions raised borrowing in the third year of every one of the 24 forecasts since December 2014. So this latter period is not explained away by bad luck.
Notes: Per cent of GDP. Target years 2020-21 to 2022-23 excluded; windows complete to 2026-27, with 2026-27 measured against the October 2026 forecast.

Which decisions explain these slippages? The OBR’s policy measures database records every measure since 2010 by the tax or spending line it affects, so the slippage can be attributed accordingly. Figure 2 does that for the third year of each forecast since December 2014.

The direct cost of the measures announced after each forecast added 1.8 per cent of GDP to year-3 borrowing on average (their indirect effects, mainly the extra receipts that higher spending generates, bring that down to the 1.5 in Table 1). Of the 1.8 per cent, 1.5pp is departmental spending and it is positive in all 15 forecasts. A further 0.2 is the devolved and local authority spending that follows from it via the Barnett formula. Welfare measure net to almost nothing. Fuel duty contributes 0.1, small but present in all 15, because the planned rise is cancelled every time. Tax measures as a whole net to zero at year 3, though by year 5 tax rises outweigh cuts.

The departmental slippage comes in two forms. Spending Reviews give departments budgets for a fixed number of years, currently to 2028-29. Beyond that the forecast rests on a Treasury assumption about total spending growth. Our results say that it is when the next Review replaces that placeholder with settlements that the total comes out higher. In particular, where a forecast’s third year lay beyond the Review period, later departmental decisions added a median 2 per cent of GDP to borrowing, and two-thirds of that arrived at the Review itself. Where the third year already had settled budgets, the additions were smaller and more varied.

So to summarise: of the three explanations we started with, borrowing slippages since 2014 have not in the main been driven by bad macroeconomic news, although there certainly has been plenty of that. They instead reflect departmental spending outstripping forecasts, primarily in the years beyond the planning horizon of the Spending Review. Whether the assumption for those years reflects a planning fallacy of the kind that afflicts most long-range plans, or the incentives the fiscal rules create to pencil in restraint where it costs least, is not settled.

The credible path takes the OBR’s forecast and subtracts from it the typical amount by which later decisions have undone past plans. Concretely, we take the median policy slippage at each horizon from the second panel of Table 1, nothing in the year of the forecast, 0.1 per cent of GDP in year 1, 0.6 in year 2, 1.5 in year 3, 1.6 in year 4 and 1.8 in year 5, and subtract it from the planned primary balance. The band around the result is the interquartile range of the same record. There is no estimation involved—this is just the plan minus what slippage normally occurs.

One point to note before we discuss the results. We focus here solely on slippages from policy decisions, not from macro news. Macro forecasts will also be wrong, and the assumptions underpinning them can be optimistic. For example, the OBR has been criticised for a trend growth path strong than many outside forecasters assume. But the OBR was set up precisely to make those expert, independent judgements, and they are matters on which reasonable people disagree. We are looking instead for the places where a systematic bias is plausible, and Table 1 says that since 2014 that has been in the policy assumptions.

In making these translations we assume that 85 per cent of the slippage lands on the current budget rather than on capital, which is its historical share, and that the extra debt is financed at 4.5 per cent.

To be clear, this is a conditional forecast of how the plan is likely to proceed: it assumes the policy process of the past decade continues, and in particular that next year’s Spending Review raises departmental budgets for 2028-29 to 2030-31 well above the figures the OBR’s forecasts are built on.

That does not seem like a bad assumption. Inflation has run higher than expected since the current settlements were fixed in June 2025, so the OBR now puts the departmental limits at £7bn a year less in real terms than when they were set, and it estimates that unprotected departments would need £11bn more by 2031-32 simply to avoid real cuts from 2028-29. On top of that sits the defence commitment, social care and whatever the Milburn and Timms reviews recommend. None of this is in the credible path above. It rests purely on historical slippage alone.

But the same arithmetic describes a big opportunity. The 2027 Review is the first moment since 2014 at which a government could settle the target year’s budgets at a level in the forecast, and if it did, the gap in the charts above would mostly close. In other words, we would update our priors on the credible path significantly were this to happen.

The prize here would be lower gilt yields. NIESR’s Laubach-style regression results suggest that each percentage point of projected deficit adds 15-20 basis points on the 10-year gilt yield. So a plan that credible delivers 1.5-2 points of primary surplus relative to the credible path could be expected to take 25 to 40 basis points off gilt yields, worth over £10bn each year in debt interest—with wider effects for the whole economy. That would be a credibility dividend worth buying.

articles.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
articles.standfirst: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council...
paragraphs: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged.

Therefore, while today’s Budget appears to have not resulted in a backlash from the markets, maintaining a backloaded path for tax rises and deferring major fiscal decisions on defence and other spending until the 2027 Spending Review to buy time is not a credible fiscal strategy.

The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 100 basis points since February, to around 5.3 per cent. As explained in this blog, some of that rise can be traced to the war in the Middle East and would presumably unwind if there were a resolution. But over half of it likely reflects other factors, including heavy government borrowing worldwide and the AI investment boom, which have pushed up global long-term real interest rates. These are forces that could exert a persistent effect on gilt yields.

The DMO’s financing remit for 2026-27 has been modestly revised up today by £7.4 billion, taking planned gilt issuance to £250.6 billion. This means taking on additional debt at what could prove to be a persistently higher cost of borrowing.
Successive economic shocks this century have ratcheted up the debt-to-GDP ratio. After both the global financial crisis and the pandemic, debt stabilised at a higher level.

But for fiscal policy to act as a shock absorber, the government needs to have adequate capacity to step in and act when the next shock hits the economy. A consistently high debt ratio limits this ability. Therefore, the minimal test of credibility of for today’s budget was whether the Chancellor was willing to stop the debt rising even further.

The OBR forecasts that policies announced in this budget will lead to increased borrowing over the next three years of £12.4 billion, which will then be followed by a reduction of £7 billion on average in the years after. Based on the forecast paths laid out by the OBR today we can see that our minimal test of credibility was not met with Public Sector Net Debt peaking at around 97 per cent of GDP in 2028-29 before falling only slightly to 96 per cent of GDP in 2031-32, higher than the ratio in August this year of 94 per cent.
Today’s Budget comes against a fragile global backdrop as the risk of adverse shocks appears to have increased over the past year. Bond markets are jittery and looking for the next shoe to drop

UK ten-year gilt yields remain the highest in the G7, leaving the public finances exposed to shifts in market sentiment. In our judgement, this strengthens the case for building fiscal buffers. The Chancellor’s decision to reduce headroom by £9 billion therefore leaves the government vulnerable to future shocks.

This is underscored by the path for debt interest now being higher than was set out in March 2026. By the end of the decade UK debt interest is expected to rise to around £150 billion annually – more than the government currently spends on education.

A credible fiscal strategy could help to reduce debt interest. Even modest fiscal restraint could deliver a credibility dividend of 10-20 basis points off gilt rates (worth around £1-2 billion a year by the end of the parliament).

Today’s Budget measures do not attempt to place the debt-to-GDP ratio on a sustained downward path in the medium term. Difficult decisions have, once again, been deferred, leaving the integrity of public finances contingent on good fortune. But hoping for the best is not a credible basis for managing the public finances. This approach leaves the UK government more exposed to renewed market scrutiny in the months ahead.
The longer the Chancellor delays the necessary adjustment, the larger, and more difficult, these adjustments will be.

articles.title: Proposing heating efficiency standards for Europe
paragraphs: More than half of the European Union’s natural gas imports are burned to keep buildings warm, with the heating and cooling of buildings using fossil fuels responsible for 12 percent of the bloc’s greenhouse gas emissions in 20241. Both the gas import bill and emissions could be reduced if the installation of heat pumps in EU buildings were ramped up. Europe has a strong manufacturing capacity and innovation base for producing heat pumps, which are beneficial for the climate, energy security, affordability and European jobs.

However, heat pumps cost more to buy and install than gas boilers: up to five times more, depending on the country (Toleikyte et al, 2024). Because a heat pump is about three times as efficient as a boiler, it is cheaper to run only if electricity costs less than about three times as much as gas. In 2025, this cost ratio was 1.9 in France but 3.2 in Germany2, meaning the extra cost of a heat pump is recouped in about three years in France but 13 years in Germany (LCP Delta, 2025).

In July 2026, the European Commission published an Electrification Action Plan (European Commission, 2026), with a goal of making electricity cheaper relative to gas, including through tax reform. In relation to heat pumps, the Commission said it would explore a “clean heat market mechanism” to narrow “the upfront cost difference for heat pumps”. At the time of writing, no further details have been offered on how such a system might work.

In this analysis, we propose basic principles for such a scheme. We draw inspiration from the EU’s carbon dioxide emission standards for new cars, which have spurred sales of electric vehicles3. We also look at lessons from what we regard as an unsuccessful attempt by the United Kingdom to introduce a heating market mechanism and draw on a comprehensive analysis of options by Agora Energiewende (2025). We begin with a brief overview of the market for heat pumps in the EU, then discuss how to design a scheme based on the efficiency of heating appliances as a useful benchmark. Finally, we set out three arguments on the benefits of such a system.

Despite their relatively higher cost, EU sales of heat pumps have grown since 2019, reaching 28 percent of sales of water-based heating systems in 2025 (Figure 1). Sales jumped in 2022 and 2023 during the European energy crisis and have since fallen back slightly. Heat pumps make up 97 percent of heating sales in Sweden and 70 percent in Denmark. In Germany, heat pumps outsold gas boilers for the first time in 2025, comprising 48 percent of all sales4.

About half (53 percent) of Europeans heat their homes with self-contained systems, 27 percent use central heating shared by their building and 13 percent are connected to district heating networks5 (Eurostat, 2026). Across this building stock, approximately 68 million gas and 18 million oil boilers are installed, compared to around 11 million hydronic heat pumps6. Thus, about one in ten heating systems are heat pumps, many of which serve several households (in apartment blocks, for example).

Rather than generating heat – like a boiler does by burning fuel – a heat pump extracts heat from outside air and transfers it indoors for space and water heating7. This makes heat pumps remarkably efficient. One unit of electricity delivers around three units of heat. By comparison, an efficient gas or oil boiler typically delivers around 0.9 units of heat per unit of energy consumed. The heat-pump efficiency gain could cut heating bills by up to 60 percent (European Commission, 2026).

The scheme’s aim would be for the share of heat pumps in overall heating sales to increase steadily from about 30 percent today (see Figure 1). This could be achieved by setting heat pump sales quotas that tighten each year for the companies that manufacture and sell heating systems. Companies that fail to meet their quotas would be fined proportionately to how far from the target they are. Companies that sell more heat pumps than required, including companies that manufacture only heat pumps, would generate credits that can be sold to lagging firms.

In April 2025, the UK launched a Clean Heat Market Mechanism, which requires manufacturers to sell specified numbers of heat pumps relative to gas boilers, with a £500 fine for each unit below the target8. Early evidence suggests that manufacturers that sell both technologies have responded by discounting heat pumps to meet the target, rather than by purchasing credits from other manufacturers (Agora Energiewende, 2025). This suggests that an EU scheme must set ambitious targets and sufficiently high fines. If the target is not ambitious enough, demand does not increase, and the result is to shift sales away from heat-pump-only manufacturers to those that also sell boilers.

A second lesson from the UK scheme is how to define what counts towards the target. Heat pumps come in different shapes and sizes, with varying efficiencies. The UK scheme covers only hydronic heat pumps, excluding air-to-air units9. Instead of listing technologies in scope, an EU scheme should be based on appliance energy efficiency.

Heating appliances sold in the EU are already rated for energy efficiency10. These ratings could provide the basis for manufacturer-wide efficiency standards, tightened annually. More-efficient heat pumps would contribute more towards the quota than less-efficient units, while hybrid units would contribute less. Manufacturers exceeding their quotas would generate credits that can be sold to those falling short. The approach would be similar to EU vehicle emissions standards, under which annual fleet-wide carbon dioxide emissions targets are applied to carmakers11.

A complication is that heating appliances differ in their capacities and uses. While hydronic heat pumps typically provide enough heat for a whole home, air-to-air units often serve individual rooms, and multiple units can be installed in single homes. Air-to-air units are also used for cooling; excluding them, as the UK scheme does, is not appropriate. However, counting them in full would be disproportionate. A fractional credit could be applied based on rated heating capacity and estimated potential to displace fossil-fuel heating.

Boosting heat pump sales is uncontroversial as a way to cut emissions and gas imports. Heat pumps are the most cost-effective technology to decarbonise heating at scale (Rosenow, 2022). Heating efficiency standards, as proposed above, should offer three main benefits.

Most households face borrowing or spending constraints. Upfront rather than lifecycle costs weigh substantially more on decision-making when purchasing energy technologies such as solar panels or heat pumps (De Groote and Verboven, 2019; ICF, 2024).

EU policy on heat pumps focuses currently on reducing their running costs. The European Commission’s Electrification Action Plan asks countries to bring household electricity prices to no more than 2.5 times the price of gas by 2030, mainly by cutting taxes and levies on electricity (European Commission, 2026). In addition, from 2028, a carbon price will be put on fuels used for heating in the EU12. This will improve the investment case for heat pumps, though the carbon price would need to be very high in certain markets. In Germany, a carbon price of around €350 per tonne of CO2 would be needed to repay a heat pump’s extra cost within ten years13. That is more than twice the roughly €150 per tonne analysts expect by 203014.

A heating efficiency standard would complement these policies by creating a direct financial incentive for manufacturers to compete aggressively to make heat pumps more affordable. Each additional heat pump sold would help manufacturers meet their obligations and avoid fines or the cost of purchasing credits. Manufacturers could also pass some of the cost of compliance onto gas boiler sales. Over time, a larger and more predictable heat pump market should also reduce costs by providing investment certainty for production, distribution and financing models.

Household decisions on what kind of heating unit to adopt depend heavily on advice from installers. Gas boilers have been the incumbent option for decades. Shifting to heat pumps requires overcoming path dependence.

One in four heating systems in the EU is replaced only following a breakdown (Energy Systems Catapult, 2026). Heat pumps are then often not a practical alternative, not least because there is a relative shortage of specialists trained in heat pump installation (LCP Delta, 2025; HPA UK, 2024).

Boiler manufacturers incentivise installers, much as carmakers set sales targets and bonuses for their dealers. Most installers are trained and certified in academies primarily funded by boiler manufacturers (Toleikyte et al, 2024). Manufacturer loyalty schemes pay installers for each boiler fitted; Ideal Heating, for example, pays £20 to £55 per boiler registered15.

A heating efficiency standard would push manufacturers to invest in commercial loyalty schemes for efficient installations, giving installers an incentive to recommend heat pumps. Following the introduction of the UK Clean Heat Market Mechanism, manufacturer Worcester Bosch began paying installers £500 for each heat pump fitted, matching the £500 fine per missing heat pump16.

EU factories have a manufacturing capacity of 7.7 million heat pumps per year, but sold only two million units in 2024 (Volt et al, 2025). The sector employed about 80,000 people in the EU in 2023, and Europe accounts for almost half of global heat pump patent families (inventions patented in one or more countries) filed since 2000 (Bruegel, 2026). Steady demand would help European producers fill idle capacity and reduce costs.

National subsidies in Europe have boosted heat-pump take-up, but have also been stop-start. Sales of air-to-water heat pumps fell by 35 percent in Italy in 2024 when a tax credit covering up to 110 percent of renovation costs ended. Austria saw a sales dip of 17 percent in 2025 after federal grants for replacing fossil heating systems expired (EHPA, 2025a; EHPA, 2026). A clear annual trajectory would provide manufacturers with more certainty about demand.

articles.title: The Minimal Credibility Test For The Autumn 2026 Budget
articles.standfirst: The ground has been prepared for a quiet Budget, albeit one in which the Chancellor’s buffer against the fiscal rules comes in perhaps £10 billion lower than the £23 billion...
paragraphs: The ground has been prepared for a quiet Budget, albeit one in which the Chancellor’s buffer against the fiscal rules comes in perhaps £10 billion lower than the £23 billion the OBR found in March. This so-called “headroom” is nothing more than the margin by which the OBR expects the current budget to be in surplus three years out, the point at which the fiscal rules are now tested. Running it down means a higher expected level of borrowing three years from now than previously planned (and nothing about the years in between).

In this week’s blog, Ben Caswell and I consider whether that is the right call from a macroeconomic standpoint. Our answer is no, for three reasons. First, the economy does not need a fiscal stimulus. Second, the rise in borrowing costs this year looks mostly persistent, so the argument for borrowing through a temporary shock does not apply. Third, markets are jittery and looking for the next shoe to drop. This is the environment to strengthen our fiscal position, not weaken it, and the case is stronger still if one believes the risk outlook has deteriorated.

Assuming we do end up with extra borrowing at the Budget, the minimal test of credibility is whether the higher borrowing through year three of the forecast is accompanied with correspondingly lower borrowing in the years after it: whether, in the language of control theory, the framework delivers “integral control”, so that overshoots in the stock of debt are made up later rather than forgiven. It is the minimal test because the government’s planned consolidation path is already time-inconsistent: back-loaded towards the last possible date for the next general election, when governments are not traditionally incentivised to deliver fiscal restraint. Our recent survey with Ipsos suggests that the public are ahead of the politicians in understanding the scale of fiscal retrenchment needed to bring the public finances into good shape.

Growth has proved far more resilient than almost anyone expected in March. GDP has grown by 1.8 per cent so far this year, with four months still to go. That is remarkable, and it exceeds anyone’s estimate of trend; our own is 1.3 per cent. The labour market tells the same story. Unemployment has fallen since the start of the year and is now half a percentage point below the OBR’s March forecast.

Inflation, meanwhile, is above target and rising. CPI inflation was 3.5 per cent in September, up for three months running, and with energy prices higher again since the summer most of the shock has still to reach consumer prices. We expect inflation above 4 per cent in the first quarter of next year. Some of the direct effect of the energy shock of course. But pay growth is running close to 4 per cent, against the 3 per cent or so the Bank of England regards as consistent with the target, and the main round of pay settlements falls early in the new year, when inflation will be above 4 per cent. The risk of second-round persistence has grown.

If we take the OIS curve literally, markets already price 100 basis points or more of increases in Bank Rate over the next twelve months. A Budget that adds to demand would push that path higher still; the looser the fiscal stance, the more of the work falls to the Bank of England. The policy mix the economy needs is tighter fiscal policy and, in time, easier monetary policy, not the reverse.

The case for dipping into the buffer rests on a respectable piece of economics: borrowing should be used to absorb temporary shocks, while taxes and spending should adjust to permanent ones (Barro, 1979). Borrowing through a permanent shock, however, postpones the adjustment and makes it bigger. So the judgement call for the Chancellor is whether the shock he would be borrowing through will pass.

Our assessment is that part of shock to global yields will dissipate if there is a resolution to the conflict in the middle east. The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 110 basis points since the conflict began in February, to about 5.4 per cent, its highest since 2007, and the rise has been global. Roughly a third of the UK move reflects higher inflation compensation and the policy rates expected to deal with it.

The rest is likely to prove persistent. The real rate the market prices for 2031 to 2036 has risen by 75 basis points in the UK and by almost 100 in the US. That is harder to square with a temporary energy shock story. It is easier to rationalise as a global shift in the real interest rate, driven by the AI investment boom and the scale of government borrowing everywhere, with a term premium on gilts that has been rising since July on top. Around two-thirds of the rise in borrowing costs, on this reckoning, is here to stay.

The interest rate on new government borrowing is now above the growth rate of the economy, which turns the debt arithmetic from a tailwind into a headwind: the primary surplus needed simply to hold the debt ratio steady has risen, and every pound borrowed at today’s rates adds to that bill. With interest rates at 5 per cent, say, and a primary deficit of -1.5 per cent of GDP, the economy would need to grow in cash terms by 6.5 per cent annually to keep debt stable.

None of this is certain of course. But standard frameworks for decision-making under uncertainty point to fiscal conservatism. A Bayesian would treat most of the move as persistent, because changes in real rates historically are. A robust control approach asks which mistake is worse: tightening now and finding that rates fall back is a reversible error. Borrowing more and finding that they stay high may be harder to reverse.

The environment in which the Budget will be delivered next week is not a forgiving one. Global bond markets are looking for the next weak link. Attention is on France today, but the UK has been there twice in four years, in autumn 2022 and January 2025, and its 10-year yield is already the highest in the G7. It is not hard to imagine how the UK could come under the bond market’s spotlights in the months ahead. The risk outlook has, in our judgement, deteriorated: adverse shocks are more likely than they were a year ago. These are circumstances in which to build fiscal buffers, not run them down.

The public share the concern. In our survey with Ipsos, 52 per cent think a severe loss of market confidence in the UK’s ability to repay its debt is likely within five years, and 16 per cent of which think it very likely. Those are sobering numbers.

There is also an opportunity here, and an asymmetry. A Budget that markets judged credible could take 10 to 20 basis points off gilt yields through a lower term premium, worth £1 to 2 billion a year by the end of the Parliament. A Budget that they did not could cost several times that: on the OBR’s own reckoner, a 50-basis point repricing adds around £6 billion a year to debt interest by the end of the decade. The downside is larger than the upside, and the buffer is the one thing in this the Chancellor controls.

Suppose the Chancellor does borrow more. The minimal test of credibility is whether higher borrowing through the third year of the forecast is matched by correspondingly lower borrowing in the years after it, so that the stock of debt (relative to GDP) returns to the path planned in March rather than settling on a higher one. Engineers call this approach “integral control”—monetary economists will recognise it as the difference between a price-level target, which claws back an overshoot, and an inflation target, under which bygones are bygones.

The figure below illustrates this strategic choice facing the Chancellor. Both borrowing paths meet the fiscal rules (which do not require integral control), but only one delivers the same debt reduction path planned in March.1

It is a minimal test because the plan it would be applied to is already back-loaded and already hard to believe. The March forecast requires the primary balance to improve by around £100 billion a year by the end of the decade, a swing from the current primary deficit of 1.5 per cent of GDP to a primary surplus of the same magnitude. Almost all of it comes after 2027, with the largest single step in 2029-30, the year of the latest possible general election. If borrowing costs remain elevated, the debt interest bill could be £11-17 billion higher by 2030-31, raising the surpluses required further still. And at today’s borrowing costs, this would do no more than hold the debt ratio at 95 per cent.

The record on delivering surpluses of that kind is shown below. With the exception of the forecasts made at the height of the pandemic, every OBR forecast since 2010 has shown a primary surplus within its horizon. None of them has arrived; the UJ has not run one since 2001.

There is a further risk to the plan. The March forecast and the Spending Review settlements were set before the conflict pushed up inflation. On unchanged plans, the same cash buys 2.1 per cent less by 2030 than departments were promised. The flip side is that higher inflation flatters the near-term public finances precisely because cash spending plans stand still while cash receipts rise, and the OBR’s Budget forecast is likely to show that gain. It is only real if the squeeze is delivered. The record suggests it will not be, and the pressure points are already visible: pay review bodies reporting against inflation above 4 per cent, and the calls to raise real spending on the NHS and defence.

Pulling this together, the case for higher borrowing at this Budget is thin. It rests on a gamble that that the Bank of England won’t respond to the fiscal stimulus by raising Bank Rate; that market yields will fall back to pre-conflict levels; that there are no further adverse shocks; and that the government will deliver a 2 per cent annual real spending squeeze on departmental budgets relative to what it promised a year ago.

It also seems blind to the scale of debt reduction the country needs to deliver over the medium term. On this, the public appear to have a better appreciation of the problem than is evident in political discourse. In our survey with Ipsos, 58 per cent expect further significant steps to reduce debt within five years, beyond what is already planned, and four in ten of those expect them only after the next election. Two-thirds expect higher taxes at this Budget. When half the sample was shown the facts on debt and debt interest, neither expectation moved, because people already knew. Voters are divided on how the adjustment should fall, between taxes and spending and between high earners, business and waste, which is why the conversation to have now is about its size and timing rather than how. The public, it seems, are ready for that conversation.

1 The current fiscal rules are analogous to inflation targets. The stability rule tests whether the current budget is in balance in the third year of the forecast; the investment rule tests whether the debt ratio is falling in that same year. Both are tests of a single year, and neither asks where the debt ratio is relative to where it was meant to be.

articles.title: Inflation Could Climb Above 5% in Early 2027
articles.standfirst: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month.  Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4...
paragraphs: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month. Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4 per cent compared to 0 per cent in 2025, leading to the increase of 0.4 percentage points in annual inflation.

The monthly inflation of 0.4 per cent corresponds to an annualised rate of 4.9 per cent and flows on from the high monthly inflation of 0.5 per cent in August. This suggests that the continuing energy supply issues caused by the American war on Iran are feeding into general price inflation. These effects are likely to escalate until a resolution to the conflict is found. Under our preferred forecast scenarios, inflation looks set to reach
The Bank of England will face pressure to tighten policy as inflation continues to increase.
If we look at the broad categories of inflation over the last 12 months, we see:

Services inflation this month is pretty much in line with wage data reflecting a cooling labour market: the latest ONS figures on wage increases excluding bonuses, covering June to August 2026, came in at 3.7 per cent.
The biggest contributors to the change in headline inflation between August and September were:

However, these overall contributions combine the “base effects” of inflation dropping out from the previous year with the new inflation “dropping in”. We need to unwrap these to get the true picture. Figure 1 (below) shows the sectoral contributions to overall inflation, with the previous year’s monthly inflation dropping out (blue) and the current month’s new inflation dropping in (brown). The overall impact is the sum of the two, shown by the burgundy line.

Focusing on the new monthly inflation (brown), eight sectors registered an increase in prices this month, with two registering falls (interestingly these two were Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). The blue dropouts from the previous year are negative or close to zero in eight sectors, and positive in two (also Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). Overall, the burgundy line, showing the total effect for each sector, is significantly negative in one sector, and significantly positive in three sectors, as listed above.

We can look ahead over the next 12 months to see how inflation might evolve as the recent inflation “drops out” as we move forward month by month. Each month, the new inflation enters the annual figure and the old inflation from the same month in the previous year “drops out”. We depict the following scenarios for future inflation dropping in:

The Iran war makes the future path of inflation highly uncertain. In my initial blog, The Possible Effects on UK Inflation in 2026 of the US-Iran Conflict, published on 23 March, I contrasted the possible effects of two scenarios, a “good scenario” with a short conflict that left most of the energy infrastructure in the Gulf intact and an “ugly” scenario with a prolonged conflict in which most of the infrastructure is destroyed. With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and now the additional closure of the Bab-el-Mandeb, we seem to be heading into the “ugly” scenario, with a major inflationary spike. In addition, the direct conflict between Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah (the Houthis) has led to the destruction of significant pipelines and refineries in Saudi Arabia. Unless the conflicts are resolved soon, there is likely to be more inflation coming our way and also negative impacts on output and employment across much of the world as we move into 2027.

I have therefore revived our old friend from 2022, the “sanctions” scenario, now renamed the “Hormuz” scenario. This and the very high scenario seem to be most relevant at present, and we also depict the high and medium scenarios for reference. The low scenario seems unlikely to be relevant so we have not depicted it.

If we look at the very high and Hormuz scenarios, inflation might be at 4.2-4.7 per cent in December 2026. Even the medium and high scenarios suggest that inflation will be at 3.4-3.7 per cent by December. So, under all scenarios, inflation looks set to rise in the final quarter of 2026.
For further analysis of inflation in the United Kingdom, see:
Seasonal Adjustment of CPI and CPIH, Huw Dixon and Monica George Michail. NIESR Policy Paper 45, May 2025

articles.title: The Return of the Energy Shock
articles.standfirst: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of...
paragraphs: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of the year, following the February, May and July 2026 blogs. Three things have changed since July:

The July blog made a testable claim: our recommended Intermediate Energy MRN projected 3.0 per cent for June 2026, easing to 2.7 per cent by August, before rising to a 4.5 per cent peak in February 2027. The outturns were 2.6 per cent in June and 3.1 per cent in August. The model was 0.4 percentage points too high in June and 0.4 points too low in August, and the sign of the error flipped exactly as the geopolitics did. In June the peace announcement was pulling energy prices down faster than the model’s training data allowed for; by August the collapse of that deal was pushing them up faster. We flagged the first possibility explicitly in July (“a June print materially below this range would suggest the peace-deal energy price fall is passing through faster than the model anticipates”). We did not anticipate the second, and nor, on the evidence of its July Report, did the Bank of England, whose central projection assumed oil prices would drift from $76 to $71, and inflation would peak at 3.2 per cent in the fourth quarter of 2026. Two lessons follow. The first is that the MRN carries no oil price assumption at all; it extrapolates from the energy history it has seen. So its twelve-month path is best read as an unconditional projection of where the data were pointing at end-August. The Bank’s and NIESR’s forecasts are conditional on an assumed path for oil prices. Part of the gap between us is therefore a difference in what is being forecast, not only in how; the fair test is whether the unconditional path keeps moving the right way when the world moves, as it did between June and August. The second is that readers of our May blog will recall that the then-current MRN had inflation “well beyond 5 per cent in early 2027”; the July update, trained during the brief peace, pulled that back to 4.5 per cent. The present round returns to the May reading.

Figure 1 shows the current forecast of two classes of MRN model: the Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which uses CPI level and month-on-month change, ONS UK energy CPI, the monthly Brent average and, new in this round, Bank Rate; and the Intermediate Energy MRN, which adds real GDP, PPI, the 10-year gilt yield and the sterling effective exchange rate to that set. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects annual CPI inflation of 3.7 per cent in September 2026, 4.1 per cent in November, 4.4 per cent in December, and then a step up to 5.4 per cent in January 2027, holding at 5.4 per cent in February and March before easing to 4.3–4.4 per cent in April–May and drifting back up to 4.9 per cent by July and August 2027. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN follows a similar path but peaks later and higher, at 5.7 per cent in June 2027. The Average MRN peaks at 5.3 per cent in February and does not fall below 4.5 per cent at any point in the forecast window. The quarterly averages are 3.9, 5.2 and 4.8 per cent for the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first two quarters of 2027, respectively.

We must state two things about this path clearly. The first is that the peak has moved up by almost a full percentage point since July, from 4.5 per cent to 5.4 per cent, while its timing has stayed put in the first quarter of 2027. That revision is almost entirely the energy channel doing what it is designed to do: the price of Brent crude oil is 50 per cent higher than when the July models were trained, UK wholesale gas prices have risen 78 per cent since the Bank’s July Report, and the Ofgem energy price cap has gone from £1,477 in Q2 to £1,663 in Q3 and £1,723 for October–December, with Cornwall Insight now forecasting £1,999, a 16 per cent rise, for January 2027. The second is that part of the January step is arithmetic rather than economics. The CPI fell by 0.5 per cent month-on-month in January 2026; so, roughly half a point of the first quarter peak is that base effect. It is real, in the sense that the headline rate will print it, but it does not imply a fresh burst of price pressure in that month.

This is the first round in which we forecast the policy rate, and the two classes disagree in a way we think is informative rather than embarrassing. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which sees inflation, energy and the rate itself, but nothing of the real economy, has Bank Rate rising from 3.75 per cent to 4.0 per cent by February 2027 and 4.5 per cent by June. The Intermediate Energy MRN, which also sees GDP, producer prices, gilt yields and sterling, has it falling to 3.5 per cent by November, 3.25 per cent by January and 3.0 per cent by March, before settling at 3.25 per cent. The average of the two dips to 3.5 per cent through the winter, touches 3.25 per cent in March, and is back at 3.75 per cent by June 2027.

Read the two classes as the two sides of the Monetary Policy Committee’s own argument. At its 17 September meeting the Committee held at 3.75 per cent by six votes to three, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill voting for an immediate quarter-point increase on the grounds that slack “may have already peaked” and that raising rates is “a better risk-management strategy when faced with uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects”. The six who held pointed to “very limited evidence of emerging second-round effects” and to slack “still evident in a range of indicators”, with Alan Taylor arguing that policy “should respond to evidence of propagation rather than mechanically to volatile ticks in headline energy prices”. The Simple class, which has no measure of slack and reacts to headline energy, is the hawkish minority’s direction of travel. The Intermediate class, which can see weak activity and the restrictiveness of financial conditions, is the majority’s. We do not claim the network understands this debate; we claim that the two feature sets encode the two positions, and that is exactly why we report both rather than only the average.

The September 2026 inflation number from the ONS is due on 21 October and is the first direct test of these forecasts. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects 3.7 per cent, the Simple Energy + MPC MRN 3.9 per cent and the Average 3.8 per cent, all well above August’s 3.1 per cent, reflecting the motor-fuel surge the Bank has already documented. A September number in the 3.6–3.9 per cent range would validate the near-term path; something nearer 3.3 per cent would suggest the VAT cut and the G7 reserve release are biting faster than the model allows. The second test is the 6 November MPC decision: the Simple MRN class implies the hawks gain ground, the Intermediate MRN class implies the first cut arrives by November, and the two cannot both be right. The third is the Ofgem announcement for January 2027, due in late November, which will fix the single biggest input into our peak in the first quarter of 2027. The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook and the NIESR Autumn Economic Outlook both appear before our next update, and we will report how the MRN stands against their revised paths.

1 The modelling approach is described in Binner, J. M., Kelly, L. J. and Tepper, J. A. (2025) ‘Professional Forecasters vs. Shallow Neural Network Ensembles: Assessing Inflation Prediction Accuracy’, Journal of Risk and Financial Management, 18(4), 173 (MRN methodology). https://doi.org/10.3390/jrfm18040173.
